title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Flange-Sealed Thermocouples
text: In industrial sectors such as petrochemicals, coal gasification, metallurgical smelting, high-temperature vacuum furnaces, and nuclear energy, reaction vessels often operate in environments characterized by extreme temperatures, high pressures, and complex media that are highly corrosive, flammable, or explosive. As critical temperature-sensing components in these demanding conditions, flange-sealed thermocouples require a flange structure to ensure highly reliable physical isolation and pressure sealing, while relying on internal sensing elements to provide accurate and rapid temperature feedback. In the ultra-high temperature range exceeding 1,300°C—or even 2,000°C—CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) thermocouple wires have become the material of choice for the vast majority of extreme temperature-sensing applications involving flange-sealed thermocouples, thanks to their irreplaceable high-temperature thermoelectric properties. I. High-Temperature Thermoelectric Properties of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium alloy wire is a solid-solution material composed of tungsten and rhenium; common pairings include WRe3-WRe25 and WRe5-WRe26. In the field of high-temperature thermoelectric measurement, tungsten-rhenium wire demonstrates outstanding overall performance: Ultra-high temperature measurement limit and high thermoelectric potential: Tungsten has a melting point of 3,410°C, and rhenium melts at 3,180°C. Through rhenium alloying, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples exhibit exceptionally high thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) and excellent sensitivity across a broad temperature range of 0–2,300°C, with thermoelectric output significantly higher than that of noble metal (e.g., platinum-rhodium) thermocouples. High-temperature recrystallization resistance and improved toughness: Pure tungsten wire tends to become brittle and fracture easily after undergoing recrystallization at high temperatures. The addition of rhenium produces a significant "rhenium effect," effectively lowering the alloy's ductile-to-brittle transition temperature and enhancing ductility and resistance to vibration fatigue—both in the annealed state and after high-temperature service. Excellent Chemical Stability: In environments such as high-purity vacuum, hydrogen, or inert gases (e.g., argon, helium), CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wire exhibits exceptional chemical stability and a very low high-temperature volatilization rate, while also resisting corrosion from common acids and alkalis. II. Compatibility of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire with Flange Sealing Structures The core design of a flange-sealed thermocouple involves using a flange, a metal gasket, or a flexible graphite seal to securely mount the temperature-sensing probe onto the reactor wall, thereby ensuring zero leakage against high pressure and hazardous media. CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wire is an ideal material for heating or temperature sensing in such sealing structures because its material properties align perfectly with the mechanical, physical, and environmental requirements of the flange assembly. High Environmental Compatibility with Sealed Protective Chambers: Flange sealing structures create a relatively isolated, sealed chamber for temperature measurement. Since tungsten-rhenium wire oxidizes rapidly in air at temperatures above 400°C, the flange structure provides a reliable seal for the internal sheath, facilitating evacuation or the introduction of high-purity inert gas (such as argon). The wire's exceptional chemical stability in vacuum or inert/reducing atmospheres works synergistically with the sealed chamber, effectively overcoming its susceptibility to oxidation. Structural Compatibility with Mechanical Stress and Vibration: Flange connections are often zones where thermal expansion stress, medium pulsation, and mechanical vibration converge. Modified with rhenium, CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wire possesses excellent toughness and elongation; it effectively withstands the bending and tensile stresses encountered as the thermocouple passes through the flange neck and terminal box, preventing brittle fracture caused by stress concentration during prolonged vibration and thermal cycling. Thermal Expansion Compatibility with Insulating Seals: Within the flange sealing assembly, the thermocouple wires must pass through rigid insulating beads—typically made of high-purity alumina or magnesium oxide—and connect to glass or ceramic seals at the terminal end. CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium alloys feature a low and stable coefficient of thermal expansion (approximately 4.3 × 10⁻⁶/K). This ensures excellent thermal expansion compatibility with corundum insulation tubes and high-temperature sealing materials, significantly reducing the risk of insulation beads crushing the thermocouple wires or seal failure caused by uneven thermal expansion and contraction. III. Applications of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire in Flange-Sealed Thermocouples Flange-sealed thermocouples equipped with CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wire offer an exceptionally high temperature measurement range, superior thermoelectric stability, and excellent mechanical toughness, making them suitable for a wide range of critical industrial applications. Coal Chemical and Gasification Units: In core equipment such as coal-water slurry gasifiers and pulverized coal gasifiers, reaction temperatures often reach 1300–1600°C, accompanied by high internal pressures and the presence of reducing synthesis gases (e.g., CO, H₂). The flange-sealed structure prevents the leakage of highly toxic, high-pressure gases, while the internal tungsten-rhenium wire—housed within an inert-gas-protected thermowell—provides high-precision, continuous temperature monitoring. This yields critical data for assessing the service life of the gasifier's refractory bricks and for process control. Petrochemicals and High-Pressure Reactors: In heavy oil deep-processing units—such as those for hydrocracking and residual oil hydrotreating—reactors operate in environments characterized by high temperatures (400–1400°C), high pressures, and strong corrosivity (involving sulfur and hydrogen). Leveraging the tungsten-rhenium wire's high thermoelectric sensitivity and fatigue resistance, these flange-sealed thermocouples can precisely detect minute temperature drifts within the reactor, effectively preventing the risk of thermal runaway. Metallurgical Smelting and High-Temperature Vacuum/Inert Gas Furnaces: In equipment such as vacuum smelting furnaces for refractory metals (e.g., titanium alloys, tungsten, and molybdenum), hot isostatic presses (HIP), and high-pressure single-crystal silicon growth furnaces, operating temperatures frequently exceed 1800°C. The flange sealing assembly ensures a high-vacuum or high-pressure inert gas environment within the furnace body; a temperature-sensing probe—equipped with fine-gauge tungsten-rhenium wire—can reach directly into the molten pool or the edge of the heating zone, enabling rapid-response temperature measurement in ultra-high-temperature areas. Semiconductor and Nuclear Industries: In semiconductor epitaxial growth equipment and auxiliary high-temperature circuits of nuclear reactors, there are dual, stringent requirements for absolute sealing and exceptional temperature measurement stability. The excellent radiation resistance and low vapor pressure of tungsten-rhenium wire make it indispensable for such high-purity, high-risk applications involving flange-sealed temperature sensing. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Thermocouples with Recrystallized Silicon Carbide Tubes
text: In the field of high-temperature measurement, contact-based temperature sensing constantly faces challenges regarding material limitations. When temperature requirements rise to 1,500°C or even above 2,000°C, traditional thermocouple materials—such as platinum-rhodium and nickel-copper alloys—often prove inadequate. The advent of tungsten-rhenium thermocouples has opened a new pathway for precise, ultra-high-temperature measurement. The core component of the tungsten-rhenium thermocouple is the tungsten-rhenium wire—an alloy of tungsten and rhenium—which currently stands as the metal thermocouple material with the highest resistance to high temperatures. However, tungsten-rhenium wire is highly susceptible to oxidation at elevated temperatures; consequently, it must be used within a protective atmosphere or isolated from oxygen using a protective tube. Recrystallized silicon carbide tubes, prized for their exceptional resistance to high-temperature oxidation and chemical stability, serve as an ideal choice for the outer protective housing of these thermocouples. Together, these components form a high-temperature measurement system capable of withstanding extreme operating conditions in sectors such as metallurgy, aerospace, and nuclear energy. I. Material Properties and Key Advantages of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium wire holds an irreplaceable position in high-temperature measurement due to its unique material properties. (1) High melting point and broad measurement range. Tungsten possesses the highest melting point of any single metallic element; the tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wire produced by CTIA GROUP has a melting point exceeding 3,000°C. Under standard application conditions, thermocouples made from this wire operate stably within a range of 0°C to 2,300°C. This extensive temperature coverage makes the material unique in the realm of ultra-high-temperature measurement, catering to applications in high-temperature metallurgy, aerospace, the nuclear industry, and beyond. (2) Breakthroughs in mechanical properties driven by the "rhenium effect." Although pure tungsten boasts an ultra-high melting point of 3,410°C, its inherent brittleness at room temperature severely limits its practical application. Adding 3%–25% rhenium to tungsten promotes the formation of extensive twin structures at grain boundaries; this enhances ductility by approximately 300% while maintaining high strength, effectively overcoming the inherent brittleness of tungsten. Consequently, CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wire offers a combination of advantages, including high strength at both room and elevated temperatures, good plasticity after recrystallization, and excellent welding performance. (3) Excellent thermoelectric properties. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples feature a linear relationship between temperature and electromotive force (EMF) and offer reliable thermal stability. They deliver high-precision thermoelectric signals; for instance, at 1200°C, the deviation in thermoelectric EMF non-uniformity across a full coil of wire is controlled within the 40–80 μV range. Common types include Tungsten-Rhenium 3/25 (Type D: positive electrode 97% W/3% Re; negative electrode 75% W/25% Re) and Tungsten-Rhenium 5/26 (Type C). CTIA GROUP can customize tungsten-rhenium wire specifications—such as diameter and precision—to meet specific customer requirements. (4) Comprehensive cost advantages. Precious metal thermocouples are expensive and have limited upper temperature ranges; in contrast, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples offer higher temperature limits and good stability at a fraction of the cost of platinum-rhodium thermocouples. This superior cost-performance ratio has led to the widespread adoption of tungsten-rhenium thermocouples in industrial temperature measurement applications. II. Protective role of recrystallized silicon carbide tubes Despite their outstanding performance, tungsten-rhenium wires are prone to oxidation. In an oxidizing atmosphere, they rapidly oxidize and fail, resulting in an operating temperature far below their theoretical maximum. Therefore, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are typically restricted to use in vacuum, hydrogen, or inert atmospheres. To enable high-temperature measurement in oxidizing environments, a protective tube is essential to effectively isolate the tungsten-rhenium wire from oxygen. Recrystallized silicon carbide tubes were developed specifically for this purpose. Recrystallized silicon carbide (also known as recrystallized SiC) is a specialized ceramic material formed through a specific process that allows silicon carbide grains to recrystallize and grow at high temperatures. It exhibits excellent high-temperature resistance and chemical stability, making it suitable for operating conditions where surface temperatures do not exceed 1500°C. In an oxidizing atmosphere, recrystallized silicon carbide tubes can be used for extended periods at temperatures up to 1600°C. It is important to note that there are strict material compatibility requirements regarding the pairing of recrystallized silicon carbide tubes with tungsten-rhenium wires. During assembly, silicon carbide should not serve as the material in direct contact with the tungsten-rhenium thermocouple, as complex chemical reactions occurring at high temperatures could cause the thermocouple to fail. Consequently, the recrystallized silicon carbide tube functions solely as an outer protective sheath; insulating material must be packed between the tungsten-rhenium wire and the inner protective tube to maintain proper isolation. III. Application of Tungsten-Rhenium Wires in Recrystallized Silicon Carbide Thermocouples The combination of tungsten-rhenium wires and recrystallized silicon carbide tubes creates a thermocouple assembly that offers a reliable solution for precise temperature measurement in high-temperature oxidizing atmospheres. (1) In the metallurgical industry, these thermocouples are widely used to measure temperatures in various industrial furnaces and kilns—including those for metallurgy, chemical processing, and refractory material production—as well as in coal gasifiers and sulfur recovery units. (2) In the aerospace sector, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are employed for ultra-high-temperature measurements, such as monitoring engine exhaust plumes. (3) In semiconductor manufacturing, thermocouples utilizing tungsten-rhenium wires are integrated into MOCVD equipment to monitor deposition temperatures of 1500°C within the reaction chamber in real time. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Corundum-Sheathed Thermocouples
text: In the field of high-temperature measurement, tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) thermocouples are renowned for their exceptional high-temperature performance. However, bare tungsten-rhenium wires are extremely sensitive to oxygen; the use of corundum sheaths (high-purity alumina sheaths) provides a reliable technical solution for fully leveraging the high-temperature capabilities of W-Re thermocouples in oxidizing atmospheres. 1. High-Temperature Characteristics of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium wires produced by CTIA GROUP (China Tungsten Intelligent Manufacturing) offer outstanding advantages, including a high melting point, high recrystallization temperature, high thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF), and high sensitivity. They exhibit excellent linearity in the temperature-EMF relationship and reliable thermal stability, making them the ideal choice for thermocouple wires in ultra-high-temperature measurement applications. W-Re thermocouples made from these wires can measure temperatures up to 2300°C in vacuum, hydrogen, or inert atmospheres, all at a cost that is half—or even less—than that of platinum-rhodium thermocouples. Common W-Re thermocouple graduation types include WRe5-WRe26 (positive electrode: 95% W, 5% Re; negative electrode: 74% W, 26% Re) and WRe3-WRe25 (positive electrode: 97% W, 3% Re; negative electrode: 75% W, 25% Re). 2. The Critical Role of Corundum Sheaths Corundum (Al₂O₃) sheaths are among the most commonly used protective casings for tungsten-rhenium thermocouples. High-purity corundum tubes feature high density, excellent high-temperature strength, and good resistance to chemical corrosion, allowing for long-term use in oxidizing atmospheres at temperatures up to 1600°C. With a gas permeability as low as ≤0.2%, high-purity corundum tubes effectively block external oxygen and water vapor, creating a stable operating environment for the tungsten-rhenium wires. In terms of structural design, the sheathing can flexibly utilize single-layer, double-layer, or even triple-layer protective tube configurations. For single-sheath designs, high-purity corundum tubes are used directly; for double-protection structures, an outer high-purity corundum tube is combined with an inner tube made of corundum, molybdenum, or molybdenum disilicide to further enhance protective capabilities. The interior is filled with high-temperature insulating material and vacuum-sealed to ensure the absence of residual oxygen. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples featuring double-layer sheaths (corundum and molybdenum) can also operate in oxidizing atmospheres at temperatures up to 1600°C, creating the technical conditions for tungsten-rhenium thermocouples to replace noble metal thermocouples in most applications. 3. Application of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire in Corundum-Sheathed Thermocouples Corundum-sheathed tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are widely used across numerous high-temperature industrial sectors, including metallurgy, chemicals, and refractory materials. In the metallurgical industry—where products are often manufactured in reducing atmospheres (such as hydrogen) or exposed to harsh environments involving high temperatures and highly corrosive media—solid-structure, oxidation-resistant tungsten-rhenium thermocouples utilizing corundum tubes have seen stable, long-term use; they serve as effective replacements for expensive platinum-rhodium thermocouples while offering significantly longer service lives. In the chemical industry, high-temperature cracking furnaces have successfully employed CTIA GROUP tungsten-rhenium wire—paired with composite corundum tubes—to replace platinum-rhodium thermocouples, achieving excellent performance in reducing atmospheres at 1400°C. Additionally, these thermocouples are widely used in industries such as ceramic firing, glass melting, heat treatment, and coking, covering a temperature measurement range of 0°C to 1800°C, with some products capable of long-term operation at 2000°C. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Tantalum-Sheathed Thermocouples
text: In industrial environments characterized by extreme temperatures and severe corrosion, standard nickel-copper thermocouple wires often fail to meet measurement requirements. Tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) wire from CTIA GROUP—distinguished by its high-temperature resistance, flexibility, and excellent thermoelectric properties—serves as the core component of ultra-high-temperature sensors when paired with a protective sheath made of the refractory metal tantalum (Ta). This combination offers a suite of advantages, including extreme temperature tolerance, chemical corrosion resistance, and airtight protection. 1. Characteristics of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wire is a refractory alloy composed of tungsten (W) and rhenium (Re). With a melting point exceeding 3000°C, it operates stably over long periods at extreme temperatures ranging from 1300°C to 2300°C. Additionally, it offers a high thermoelectric output and sensitivity, providing a more cost-effective alternative to traditional platinum-rhodium noble metal thermocouples. Common pairings for these thermocouple wires include WRe3-WRe25 or WRe5-WRe26, where the numbers indicate the rhenium content percentage. However, tungsten-rhenium wire is prone to oxidation; it undergoes rapid, destructive oxidation when exposed to air at temperatures above 400°C. Consequently, practical applications require strict control of the environment—utilizing vacuum, inert gas, or reducing atmospheres—along with superior airtight protection. 2. Characteristics of Tantalum Sheaths Tantalum (Ta) is an exceptionally rare refractory metal with a melting point of 2996°C. At room and moderate temperatures, it exhibits outstanding corrosion resistance against most acids (such as hydrochloric acid, nitric acid, and aqua regia) and liquid metals, with the notable exceptions of hydrofluoric acid (HF), sulfur trioxide, and strong alkalis. Unlike brittle ceramic protection tubes made of materials like corundum or quartz, tantalum offers excellent mechanical strength and ductility. It can be fabricated into slender, seamless tubes with high airtight integrity, providing robust physical isolation for the internal tungsten-rhenium wire. Technical advantages of combining a tantalum sheath with a tungsten-rhenium wire: (1) The tantalum sheath protects the internal tungsten-rhenium wire from external harmful gases, preventing oxidation at ultra-high temperatures. (2) The metal tantalum sheath withstands rapid thermal cycling and mechanical vibration, avoiding the cracking issues common to traditional ceramic protection tubes during sudden temperature fluctuations. (3) In high-temperature reaction environments containing corrosive vapors, strongly reducing gases, or specific liquid metals (such as lithium, sodium, or lead-bismuth alloys), the tantalum sheath provides excellent shielding. 3. Applications of Tantalum-Sheathed Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wires for tantalum-sheathed thermocouples are primarily used in specialized industrial and high-end scientific research scenarios that demand exceptional temperature resistance, hermetic sealing, and corrosion resistance. Nuclear industry and liquid-metal-cooled reactors: Used to monitor high-temperature liquid levels and temperatures in liquid metal circuits (e.g., liquid lithium or sodium-potassium alloys); tantalum exhibits superior resistance to dissolution corrosion by liquid alkali metals. Vacuum high-temperature heat treatment and sintering furnaces: Used in the sintering of aerospace materials, processing of carbon-carbon composites, and vacuum induction furnaces to provide precise closed-loop temperature control within the core high-temperature zone. Single-crystal growth and semiconductor materials: Used for temperature control in ultra-high-temperature equipment, such as sapphire single-crystal growth furnaces and silicon carbide (SiC) crystal growth systems. Defense and aerospace ground testing: Used for ultra-high-temperature thermal analysis in hypersonic wind tunnels, on the outer walls of rocket engine combustion chambers, and in high-temperature gas flow paths. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Compression-Spring Thermocouples
text: A compression-spring thermocouple—also known as a spring-loaded thermocouple—is a temperature sensor that utilizes spring pressure to maintain firm contact between the sensing tip and the surface of the object being measured. Its core design principle involves using the elastic force of an internal compression spring to press the sensing tip tightly against the object's surface or the bottom of a cavity, ensuring reliable, low-thermal-resistance contact between the sensor and the measurement point. The structure typically consists of a protective tube, a mounting bolt, a locking ferrule, a spring, and thermocouple lead wires; some models also include a terminal box. Tungsten-rhenium wire is an alloy composed of tungsten and rhenium and serves as a core material for manufacturing high-temperature thermocouples. Tungsten-rhenium wire from CTIA GROUP features an extremely high melting point (exceeding 3000°C) and offers advantages such as high strength at both room and elevated temperatures, good ductility after recrystallization, high electrical resistivity, and a low temperature coefficient of resistance. It exhibits excellent chemical stability in non-oxidizing atmospheres. These wires are widely used in industries such as metallurgy, construction materials, aerospace, aviation, nuclear energy, and chemicals, as well as in ultra-high-temperature measurement applications involving high-temperature electronic thermal systems, space vehicles, and nuclear reactors. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires from CTIA GROUP are characterized by a linear temperature-to-EMF (electromotive force) relationship and reliable thermal stability. At 1200°C, the deviation in thermoelectric inhomogeneity is controlled within the range of 40–80 μV. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are among the metal thermocouples capable of operating at the highest temperatures; in non-oxidizing atmospheres, they can withstand short-term operating temperatures of up to 3000°C. Common models include WRe3/25 and WRe5/26. By combining the compression-spring structure with tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wire, the resulting compression-spring tungsten-rhenium thermocouple integrates the convenience and reliability of spring-loaded mounting with the core advantages of tungsten-rhenium materials for ultra-high-temperature measurement. The primary applications of compression-spring tungsten-rhenium thermocouples include the following areas. 1. High-Temperature Measurement in the Power Industry Designed specifically for power plants, compression-spring tungsten-rhenium thermocouples meet the temperature measurement requirements of generator units (such as 300 MW and 600 MW capacities) and their auxiliary equipment. They are capable of directly measuring the temperatures of liquids, steam, and gases, as well as solid surfaces, during various production processes. 2. Metallurgy and High-Temperature Industries In sectors such as metallurgy and building materials, compression-spring tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are used to measure the temperatures of fluids, steam, gases, and solid surfaces across a range of 0–1800°C (or even higher). They can serve as an alternative to platinum-rhodium thermocouples, acting as ultra-high-temperature measurement tools for advanced metallurgical industries. 3. Chemical and Cement Industries Compression-spring tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are widely used in chemical and cement plants, capable of directly measuring the temperatures of liquids, steam, gases, and solid surfaces within the 0–1300°C range. Their spring-loaded sensing elements offer excellent vibration resistance, a wide measurement range, high mechanical strength, and superior pressure resistance. 4. Aerospace and Nuclear Energy Sectors Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples play a vital role in cutting-edge industries such as aerospace and nuclear energy. The spring-loaded structure enhances reliability in high-vibration environments, making them suitable for demanding applications such as monitoring aero-engine exhaust plumes and measuring ultra-high temperatures in nuclear reactors. 5. Temperature Measurement in Explosion-Proof Applications Certain spring-loaded tungsten-rhenium thermocouples feature a dual-chamber explosion-proof design with a rating of up to dⅡCT6. They are suitable for temperature measurement in environments containing gases classified up to Group ⅡC with an ignition temperature class of T6. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Sheathed Thermocouples with Compensation Leads
text: Tungsten-rhenium wire (also known as tungsten-rhenium alloy wire) is a type of thermocouple electrode wire used for ultra-high-temperature measurement. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples typically consist of a pair of tungsten-rhenium alloy wires with different compositions serving as the positive and negative electrodes; these are welded into a closed loop to form a measuring junction and a reference junction. When the temperature at the measuring junction changes, a thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) proportional to the temperature difference between the two junctions is generated; by measuring this EMF, the temperature at the measuring junction can be calculated. Common tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wire pairings include: WRe3/25 (Type D; positive electrode approx. W-3%Re, negative electrode approx. W-25%Re), WRe5/26 (Type C; positive electrode approx. W-5%Re, negative electrode approx. W-26%Re), and WRe5/20 (Type A; positive electrode W-5%Re, negative electrode W-20%Re). Tungsten-rhenium wire produced by CTIA GROUP features a melting point exceeding 3000°C, high thermoelectric EMF, and high sensitivity. It is more cost-effective than platinum-rhodium (noble metal) thermocouples and is suitable for ultra-high-temperature measurements ranging from 0°C to 2300°C, with short-term measurement capabilities up to 2800°C. However, due to its susceptibility to oxidation, it is primarily used in vacuum, hydrogen, or inert atmospheres and is unsuitable for oxidizing environments containing ordinary air. A sheathed thermocouple is a temperature-sensing device featuring an assembly of thermocouple wires, insulating material, and a metal sheath. Common materials for the thermocouple wires include tungsten-rhenium, platinum-rhodium, or copper-nickel alloys. Insulating materials typically include magnesium oxide (MgO), aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃), or hafnium oxide (HfO₂). The metal protective sheath is generally made of stainless steel, molybdenum, or other high-temperature alloys. The sheathed structure provides resistance to moisture, fire, acids and alkalis, high pressure, and vibration. Compensation leads configuration refers to a design where, instead of using a standard terminal box, a section of compensation lead wire (also known as a compensation cable or extension wire) is directly extended from the connection point. For tungsten-rhenium thermocouples, the corresponding compensation cable types are WC3/25 (for use with WRe3/25) or WC5/26 (for use with WRe5/26). Typically made of copper and copper-nickel alloys, these cables match the thermoelectric characteristics of the tungsten-rhenium thermocouples within the 0–200°C range; they extend the cold junction (reference junction) to a location with a stable temperature before connecting to display instruments, thereby minimizing errors caused by cold junction temperature fluctuations. Sheathed tungsten-rhenium thermocouples with compensation cables are primarily used in sectors such as metallurgy (e.g., continuous temperature measurement of molten steel, iron, and copper), petrochemicals (e.g., temperature monitoring in heavy oil cracking furnaces and coal gasifiers), power generation (e.g., monitoring temperatures in power plant boilers, steam pipelines, and turbine units), building materials (e.g., temperature detection in the glass industry), aerospace (e.g., measuring combustion gas temperatures in solid-propellant rocket motors and exhaust plume detection), and the nuclear industry (e.g., measuring nuclear reactor core temperatures). title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Dual-Element Thermocouples
text: Tungsten-rhenium wire for dual-element thermocouples is the core temperature-sensing material specifically designed for manufacturing dual-element (dual-channel) tungsten-rhenium thermocouples. Utilizing tungsten-rhenium alloy wires as thermoelements, it converts ultra-high-temperature signals into measurable electromotive force (EMF) via the thermoelectric effect. It is widely used in sectors such as iron and steel production, aerospace, the nuclear industry, and high-temperature furnace operations. Compared to traditional platinum-rhodium thermocouples, tungsten-rhenium wire offers a higher maximum operating temperature, a greater thermoelectric output, and significant cost advantages, making it one of the most cost-effective refractory metal thermocouple materials for ultra-high-temperature measurement. 1. Working Principle of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Dual-Element Thermocouples The temperature-measuring function of a thermocouple is based on the Seebeck effect: when two conductors or semiconductors of different compositions are joined to form a closed loop and the two junctions are at different temperatures, a thermoelectric electromotive force is generated in the loop; the magnitude of this force is approximately proportional to the temperature difference. The measuring junction (hot junction) is welded together and placed in the high-temperature environment being measured, while the reference junction (cold junction) is maintained at a known temperature (usually managed via compensation cables or cold-junction compensation circuitry). The thermoelectric EMF resulting from the temperature difference is converted into a temperature reading by secondary instrumentation. Tungsten-rhenium alloys from CTIA GROUP are particularly well-suited for extreme temperature measurements exceeding 2000°C due to their exceptionally high melting points (approximately 3120–3360°C), excellent high-temperature strength, and high thermoelectric output. However, it should be noted that tungsten-rhenium wire is highly susceptible to oxidation failure in oxidizing atmospheres; therefore, it must be used in conjunction with airtight protective tubes or solid anti-oxidation structures. The unique feature of the dual-element structure is the simultaneous arrangement of two independent sets of tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires—totaling four wires—within a single protective tube or sheathed assembly, forming either shared or separate measuring junctions. This configuration allows for the simultaneous output of two independent signals, enabling redundancy, simultaneous display and control, or dual-system monitoring, thereby significantly enhancing the reliability and safety of temperature measurement. 2. Common Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire Pairings In tungsten-rhenium thermocouples, the positive leg typically consists of a low-rhenium alloy (e.g., W-3%Re or W-5%Re), while the negative leg consists of a high-rhenium alloy (e.g., W-25%Re or W-26%Re). Common pairings include: WRe3/25 (Type D)—positive leg approx. 97% W + 3% Re, negative leg approx. 75% W + 25% Re; WRe5/26 (Type C)—positive leg approx. 95% W + 5% Re, negative leg approx. 74% W + 26% Re; and WRe5/20 (Type A), among others. 3. Application Scenarios for Dual-Element Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire Thanks to their high-temperature capability, redundancy, and cost-effectiveness, CTOMS's dual-element tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires play a critical role in the following scenarios: (1) Iron, Steel, and Metallurgy Industries Rapid temperature measurement of molten steel and iron; temperature monitoring in high-temperature zones such as vacuum induction furnaces, electroslag remelting furnaces, and continuous casting tundishes. The dual-element structure allows for simultaneous signal transmission to operator display instruments and automatic control systems, or enables an immediate switch to the backup element should one fail. (2) Aerospace and Engine Testing Temperature measurement in ultra-high-temperature zones such as aero-engine exhaust plumes, combustion chambers, and turbine blades; testing of thermal protection systems for hypersonic vehicles. The dual-element design meets stringent reliability requirements for primary and backup measurements during testing. (3) Nuclear Industry and Specialty Materials Monitoring of high-temperature components in nuclear reactor cores, high-temperature gas-cooled reactors, and nuclear fusion devices; process control for the sintering and heat treatment of refractory metals and ceramic materials. (4) High-Temperature Industrial Furnaces and Chemical Processing Vacuum heat treatment furnaces, silicon carbide crystal growth furnaces, coal gasifiers, sulfur recovery units, refractory material kilns, etc. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples featuring solid anti-oxidation structures can operate at temperatures up to approximately 1600°C in certain oxidizing atmospheres, while the dual-element configuration facilitates process control and safety interlocking. (5) Scientific Research and Special Equipment Precision temperature measurement in high-energy-density applications such as plasma equipment, electron beam melting, and laser processing. title: Packaging Requirements for Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire
text: Tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires (common grades include WRe3/25, WRe5/26, etc.) are critical materials for high-temperature measurement, suitable for use in vacuum, hydrogen, and inert atmospheres with an operating range of 0–2300°C. Due to their fine-wire nature (diameters typically ranging from 0.08 to 0.5 mm) and sensitivity to oxidation and contamination, strict packaging protection is essential to ensure the uniformity of thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF), surface quality, and long-term stability. Packaging requirements are primarily based on standards such as GB/T 29822-2013 "Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires And Temperature-Electromotive Force (EMF) Tables" and JB/T 5401-2013 "Expendable Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires" regarding supply methods, packaging, and labeling, while also incorporating common industry practices. Packaging typically employs a structure consisting of an inner vacuum layer and an outer protective layer. The wire is wound into coils (or onto spools)—either separated by polarity or as matched pairs—with a typical weight of 400–600 g per coil and a length of approximately 250–260 m per kilogram; winding is performed on clean spools or paper tubes to prevent cross-tangling and localized pressure. Inner packaging preferably utilizes vacuum-sealed plastic bags or aluminum-plastic composite bags; where necessary, inert gas filling and desiccant inclusion are employed to effectively isolate the wire from air, moisture, and contaminants, thereby preventing surface oxidation or moisture absorption. Outer packaging consists of sturdy cardboard boxes, reinforced with woven bags or wooden crates if required, and includes internal cushioning materials to prevent wire deformation, breakage, or surface scratching caused by vibration or impact during transport. Packaging boxes must be securely sealed and accompanied by a product certificate of conformity and an inspection report. Labeling must be clear, complete, and durable, including information such as product name, grade (e.g., WRe3/25), diameter and tolerance, batch number, quantity/weight, date of manufacture, applicable standard number, manufacturer name and trademark, and polarity identification marks. The outer packaging must bear appropriate shipping and handling symbols, such as "Keep Dry," "Handle with Care," and "Do Not Throw." During transport, the product must be protected from rain, moisture, and severe jolting, and must not be shipped alongside corrosive substances. Storage should be in a dry, well-ventilated, and clean warehouse; relative humidity should be kept low, and the product must be stored away from acids, alkalis, and corrosive gases, with original packaging intact and protected from heavy loads. Proper packaging not only ensures the stability of product performance during distribution and storage but also facilitates user traceability and ease of use; it is a crucial component of the quality assurance system for tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wire. title: Surface Quality of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires
text: The surface quality of tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires is a key indicator of their performance, directly affecting temperature measurement accuracy, service life, and stability. Strict technical requirements regarding surface quality are stipulated in standards such as GB/T 29822-2013, "Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires and Graduation Tables." I. Basic Requirements for Surface Quality According to national standards, the surface of qualified tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires must be smooth and clean, free from oxidation discoloration, folds, burrs, laminations, and splits. Furthermore, the wires must not exhibit welded joints, cracks, or kinks. Regarding permissible minor imperfections—such as dents, spots, or scratches—there are strict quantitative limits on depth or size; typically, these should not exceed 5% of the wire diameter. II. Common Surface Defects and Their Impact In actual production and application, the following types of surface defects may occur in tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires: Surface cracks and scratches: Cracks—particularly open cracks—are serious defects that significantly compromise the wire's mechanical strength. Research indicates that crack depths can reach 180 μm, making them a major cause of wire breakage. While minor scratches may fall within permissible limits, an excessive number or excessive depth can still impair performance. Oxidation and discoloration: Tungsten-rhenium alloys are highly susceptible to oxidation at high temperatures. Oxidation can be observed on these wires at temperatures as low as 873°C (for W-5%Re) or even 681°C (for W-26%Re). The resulting oxide layer not only affects appearance but—more critically—fails to form a protective film; instead, it tends to crack and become porous, causing abrupt changes in thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) and leading to thermocouple failure. Folds and burrs: These defects often arise during processing steps such as wire drawing, compromising the wire's surface finish and dimensional uniformity. III. Factors Affecting Surface Quality The surface quality of the wires is influenced by various factors. Raw material purity, parameters of the wire-drawing process, and the heat treatment environment (particularly atmosphere control) are all crucial. Furthermore, surface quality is closely linked to flexibility; the standard stipulates that when the thermocouple wire is wound five times around a mandrel with a diameter five times that of the wire itself, the surface must show no cracks. IV. Inspection of Surface Quality Surface quality is a mandatory inspection item for tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires prior to shipment. Inspections are typically conducted in accordance with the GB/T 29822-2013 standard, involving a comprehensive assessment of the wire's surface condition—using visual inspection or tools such as a magnifying glass or microscope—to ensure compliance with standard requirements. title: Quality Inspection of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire
text: Tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wire is a core temperature-sensing material used in high-temperature measurement, finding wide application in high-end sectors such as vacuum furnaces, metallurgy, aerospace, and scientific research. It consists of a matched pair comprising a low-rhenium positive wire and a high-rhenium negative wire; common types include Tungsten-Rhenium 3/Tungsten-Rhenium 25 (Type D), Tungsten-Rhenium 5/Tungsten-Rhenium 26 (Type C), and Tungsten-Rhenium 5/Tungsten-Rhenium 20 (Type A). A rigorous, standardized inspection process is crucial for ensuring product reliability. Given that these wires operate at temperatures up to 2300°C and require exceptional compositional uniformity and thermoelectric stability, quality inspection directly determines their temperature measurement accuracy and service life. I. Key Inspection Standards for Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire Quality inspection is primarily based on the national standard GB/T 29822-2013 "Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires And Temperature-Electromotive Force (EMF) Tables" It also references industry standards such as JB/T 5401-2013 "Expendable Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires" and JB/T 5402-2013 "Test Method for the Thermoelectric Force of Expendable Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires", as well as international specifications like ASTM E696 "Standard Specification for Tungsten-Rhenium Alloy Thermocouple Wire". II. Classification of Inspections Inspections are generally categorized into factory acceptance tests (routine inspections) and type tests. Factory acceptance tests are conducted on every coil (or spool) of product to ensure compliance regarding key indicators such as surface quality, dimensions, and thermoelectric properties. Type tests are performed during new product development, following significant process changes, or during periodic spot checks, covering a more comprehensive verification of performance characteristics. III. Appearance and Dimensional Inspection Regarding appearance, the surface of the thermocouple wire must be smooth and clean, free from obvious oxidation discoloration, kinks, burrs, laminations, or splitting. Minor scratches, indentations, and a limited number of spots are permissible, provided they do not impair the wire's functionality. Visual inspection is employed, supplemented by a magnifying glass when necessary. Regarding dimensions, the common diameter range is 0.1 mm to 0.5 mm, with allowable deviations generally controlled within ±0.01 mm. Measurements are taken using a micrometer with a precision of at least 0.001 mm; readings are recorded in two mutually perpendicular directions at the same cross-section. At least three different locations per coil are sampled, and the average value is used to determine conformity. Straightness and roundness must also meet relevant requirements to ensure stability during subsequent processing and use. IV. Chemical Composition Inspection Chemical composition directly determines thermoelectric properties. The rhenium content of positive wires (e.g., WRe3, WRe5) and negative wires (e.g., WRe25, WRe26) must be strictly controlled near nominal values; excessive deviation causes the thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) to deviate from the standard calibration table. Rhenium content is typically determined using Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy (ICP-OES) or dimethylglyoxime colorimetry, while impurity elements such as carbon, oxygen, and iron are also monitored to ensure purity meets standards. Compositional uniformity along the length of the wire is critical; sampling must cover the beginning, end, and middle sections. V. Thermoelectric Property Inspection This primarily covers two aspects: thermoelectric EMF (deviation from the standard calibration table) and thermoelectric EMF inhomogeneity. Thermoelectric EMF testing is usually conducted at multiple temperature points—such as 100°C, 1000°C, 1200°C, 1400°C, 1600°C, and 2000°C—or at points agreed upon with the customer. Testing methods follow JB/T 6820, utilizing the comparison method or the fuse method (suitable for testing fine wires at palladium or platinum melting points). Permissible error limits generally require deviations not to exceed ±4°C within the 0–400°C range, and not to exceed ±1.0%t (where t is the measured temperature) within the 400–2300°C range, with the larger of the two values applying. Thermoelectric EMF inhomogeneity reflects the consistency of the wire along its length. After sampling in accordance with regulations, measurements are taken at 1200°C using the homogeneous electrode method; the inhomogeneity of the thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) across the entire coil of positive or negative wire generally must not exceed 80 μV (referenced to 0°C). Variations between the ends and along continuous sections must be strictly controlled to ensure the repeatability and reliability of temperature measurements. VI. Inspection of Mechanical and Processing Properties Tungsten-rhenium wire is prone to embrittlement at high temperatures; therefore, its room-temperature mechanical properties and windability must be inspected. Tensile testing is conducted in accordance with GB/T 228.1-2021 "Metallic materials—Tensile testing—Part 1: Method of test at room temperature" to evaluate tensile strength and elongation. The windability test involves winding the wire five times around a mandrel with a diameter five times that of the wire itself at an ambient temperature of 20–30°C; the wire must show no surface cracks or breakage, thereby verifying its flexibility and suitability for processing. Additionally, certain applications require the assessment of parameters such as electrical resistivity and high-temperature stability. High-temperature stability is evaluated by measuring changes in thermoelectric EMF after holding the wire at a specified temperature, ensuring that performance does not drift significantly during long-term use. VII. Inspection Rules and Quality Control Factory inspections involve either 100% inspection or batch-based sampling, with non-conforming products strictly rejected. Type testing entails the random selection of at least three coils from the finished product for comprehensive testing. Upon passing inspection, products must be accompanied by a certificate of quality clearly stating the grade, diameter, batch number, and thermoelectric performance data. Packaging must provide protection against moisture and oxidation, and precautions must be taken to prevent mechanical damage and contamination during storage and transportation. title: Characteristics of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire
text: The core value of tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wire lies in its ability to provide an economical, reliable, and high-temperature-capable solution for contact-based temperature measurement, playing a pivotal role across numerous industrial sectors and cutting-edge technologies. The characteristics of tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wire can be summarized as follows: I. Exceptional Performance of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire (1) Ultra-high maximum operating temperature: This is the most outstanding feature of the tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wire produced by CTIA GROUP. Its long-term operating temperature can reach 2,000–2,400°C, while the short-term limit can soar to 2,800–3,000°C. This makes it one of the metal thermocouples capable of operating at the highest temperatures available today. (2) Excellent physical and chemical properties: High melting point: The material itself has an extremely high melting point, ranging from 3,120°C to 3,360°C. High mechanical strength: It maintains excellent mechanical strength and pressure resistance even at high temperatures. Good chemical stability: It exhibits high chemical stability in non-oxidizing atmospheres, such as vacuum, hydrogen, or inert gases. High sensitivity and thermoelectric potential: It generates a high absolute thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF)—2 to 3 times that of platinum-rhodium thermocouples—resulting in high sensitivity. (3) Outstanding thermoelectric properties: Precise and reliable measurement: Thermoelectric potential depends solely on the composition of the thermocouple wires and the temperature difference between the two ends—independent of shape or size—ensuring measurement accuracy. Fast response speed: It allows for direct contact with the object being measured and reacts very sensitively to temperature changes. Good linearity: There is a strong linear relationship between temperature and electromotive force. (4) Significant cost-effectiveness: Compared to expensive precious metal thermocouples (such as platinum-rhodium types), tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are much more affordable, offering a high cost-performance ratio for high-temperature measurement. II. Disadvantages of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire (1) Susceptibility to oxidation: In oxidizing atmospheres, tungsten-rhenium wire oxidizes rapidly, leading to failure. Therefore, it must be used in non-oxidizing atmospheres, such as vacuum, inert gas, or dry hydrogen. To operate in oxidizing environments, special protective measures—such as the use of protection tubes or surface coatings—are required. (2) Material brittleness: Tungsten-rhenium alloys are inherently brittle, which presents challenges for processing, installation, and usage. (3) Corrosion in specific atmospheres: In carbon-containing atmospheres (such as those involving hydrocarbons), carbide formation occurs at temperatures exceeding 1000°C, leading to brittle fracture and reduced sensitivity. (4) Data scatter at high temperatures: Measurement consistency deteriorates at temperatures above 2300°C; therefore, operation around 2000°C is recommended to ensure optimal performance. III. Applications of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire Metallurgical industry: Used for rapid temperature measurement of molten metals, such as molten steel and iron. Aerospace: Used to measure the temperature of ultra-high-temperature gas streams, such as rocket and aircraft engine exhaust plumes. Energy and nuclear industries: Applied in nuclear reactor core temperature monitoring and high-temperature, high-pressure environments like coal gasifiers. Scientific research and new materials: Used for temperature monitoring in equipment such as high-temperature furnaces and crystal growth furnaces (e.g., for sapphire). Other industries: Widely used in ultra-high-temperature processes within sectors such as chemicals, building materials, glass manufacturing, and heat treatment. title: Temperature Measurement Principle of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples
text: The tungsten-rhenium thermocouple is a temperature-sensing element designed specifically for ultra-high-temperature measurements, and its temperature measurement principle is based on the Seebeck effect (also known as thermoelectric effect). In 1821, Seebeck discovered that when two homogeneous conductors of different compositions (known as thermoelements) are connected to form a closed loop, a thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) is generated within the circuit if there is a temperature difference between the two junctions. The magnitude of this EMF depends on the properties of the conductor materials and the temperature difference between the two ends; by precisely measuring the EMF and referencing the established calibration curve, the temperature of the measured medium can be determined. The measuring junction (hot junction) is placed within the temperature field being measured, while the reference junction (cold junction) is maintained at a known, constant temperature—typically 0°C—or compensated to eliminate the effects of temperature fluctuations at the reference end. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are constructed from tungsten-rhenium alloy wires with varying rhenium contents. Common types include Tungsten-Rhenium 5/Tungsten-Rhenium 26 (Type C; positive electrode approx. W-5%Re, negative electrode approx. W-26%Re) and Tungsten-Rhenium 3/Tungsten-Rhenium 25 (Type D; positive electrode approx. W-3%Re, negative electrode approx. W-25%Re). Tungsten and rhenium have extremely high melting points—approximately 3300°C and 3180°C, respectively. While pure tungsten tends to become brittle due to recrystallization at high temperatures, alloying it with rhenium effectively improves the material's toughness and long-term stability. Tungsten-rhenium alloys exhibit excellent chemical stability and low vapor pressure in vacuum, inert gas, or dry hydrogen environments. They are suitable for long-term operation at temperatures around 2000°C and short-term operation up to approximately 2800°C—far exceeding the operating ranges of standard thermocouples or platinum-rhodium thermocouples. Additionally, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples offer advantages such as high thermoelectric output, high sensitivity, and a favorable linear relationship between temperature and electromotive force. However, tungsten-rhenium materials are highly susceptible to oxidation; in oxidizing atmospheres, they must be used in conjunction with protective sheaths (such as molybdenum, tungsten, or ceramic tubes) and insulating materials (e.g., alumina, magnesia, or boron nitride). In carbon-containing atmospheres, they are prone to carbide formation, which leads to performance degradation. In practical applications, the thermoelectric electromotive force is converted into a temperature reading by secondary instrumentation and calibrated against reference tables or standard curves. This principle enables tungsten-rhenium thermocouples to play an irreplaceable role in fields such as aero-engines, vacuum furnaces, the nuclear industry, and ultra-high-temperature metal smelting, serving as a vital tool for high-temperature measurement. title: Australia and Vietnam Deepen Critical Minerals Cooperation, Focusing on Tungsten and Rare Earth Industries
text: On 11 August 2026, Australia and Vietnam signed cooperation agreements covering defence, agriculture, border security and other areas to further deepen their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. According to foreign media reports, the two countries particularly emphasised in their joint statement the strengthening of cooperation on critical minerals, semiconductors and clean energy supply chains, while expressing concern over restrictive trade practices that disrupt global supply chains. Concurrently, the bilateral Energy and Minerals Ministerial Dialogue focused on promoting investment by enterprises of both countries in mineral exploration, extraction and deep processing, and stressed technology transfer, environmental protection and the application of ESG standards. In recent years, global energy transition and high-technology industries have driven sustained growth in demand for minerals such as rare earths, tungsten and molybdenum, making supply-chain security a focal concern for major economies. Australia defines critical minerals as those essential to modern technologies, the economy and national security, and whose supply chains are vulnerable to disruption. Its "Critical Minerals Strategy 2023–2030" and the associated "Australia’s Critical Minerals List and Strategic Materials List" cover 31 critical minerals, including antimony, arsenic, beryllium, bismuth, chromium, cobalt, fluorine, gallium, germanium, graphite, hafnium, high-purity alumina, indium, lithium, magnesium, manganese, molybdenum, nickel, niobium, platinum-group elements, rare earth elements, rhenium, scandium, selenium, silicon (high-purity), tantalum, tellurium, titanium, tungsten, vanadium and zirconium. Vietnam, in strategic plans such as "Decision No. 333/QD-TTg on Promulgating the Plan for Implementation of Planning for Exploration, Extraction, Processing and Use of Minerals for the 2021–2030 Period, with a Vision to 2050", designates rare earths as a mineral with large reserves and strategic importance. It emphasises the simultaneous development of deep processing, restrictions on the export of raw materials, and active promotion of foreign investment and international cooperation to introduce advanced technologies, thereby increasing the value-added of the industrial chain. Tungsten and other metals are also included in the plans, with priority targets for exploration and development. According to the U.S. Geological Survey’s "Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026", both Australia and Vietnam possess certain advantages in mineral resources, with particularly strong complementarity in the tungsten and rare earth sectors. Australia is a major global mining country, ranking among the world’s leaders in production or reserves of iron ore, coal, gold, lithium, and titanium-zirconium mineral sands. In rare earths, mine production in 2025 was approximately 29,000 tonnes (rare earth oxide equivalent), with reserves of about 6.3 million tonnes, ranking third globally. Economically recoverable tungsten resources stand at approximately 570,000 tonnes (second in the world), although production is only around 1,000 tonnes, with multiple projects currently being restarted or developed. Vietnam has a rich variety of mineral resources, with world-leading bauxite reserves and significant scale in coal, titanium and tin. Rare earth reserves are approximately 3.5 million tonnes (fifth globally), while production is only 150 tonnes. Tungsten reserves are about 170,000 tonnes, with annual production of around 3,000 tonnes, making Vietnam an important source of tungsten supply outside China. Against the backdrop of the increasingly urgent need for global supply-chain diversification, Australia–Vietnam cooperation is regarded as an important measure to enhance regional economic resilience. The two sides may engage in further exchanges and cooperation on extraction and processing technologies for key minerals such as tungsten and rare earths. However, analysts note that infrastructure, environmental regulation and transparency in mining governance remain the main challenges to the concrete implementation of subsequent projects.
