title: How Is the Arc Stability of Yttrium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes, as a type of rare earth tungsten electrode, exhibit arc stability in multiple industrial operation dimensions. In conventional welding and heat treatment processes, the arc of yttrium-tungsten electrodes shows relatively small swing amplitude and good concentration. When the current is within a specific range, the arc column is not prone to irregular wandering or intermittent phenomena, which is conducive to forming uniform penetration depth and weld bead appearance. The stability of its arc combustion process helps reduce spatter and maintain continuous energy input. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes image I. Dispersion distribution characteristics of rare earth yttrium oxide At the microstructure level, the distribution state of yttrium oxide particles inside the tungsten matrix plays a fundamental role in overall performance. In electrode materials prepared by powder metallurgy, the internal oxides generally exist in the form of dispersed particles. This uniformly distributed microstructure provides numerous electron emission sites inside the electrode. When local areas are excited by heat, the dispersed phase can continuously replenish active substances, slowing down local depletion, thereby providing internal material support for maintaining arc stability. II. Electron work function of yttrium-tungsten electrodes The electron emission capability is generally affected by the work function of the material. The surface work function of yttrium-tungsten electrodes shows a moderate numerical range, allowing the cathode to maintain a stable electron emission rate at relatively low temperatures. Compared with pure tungsten electrodes, the activation energy required for thermionic emission of yttrium-tungsten electrodes is lower, reducing voltage fluctuations caused by insufficient emission capability. This physical mechanism allows the arc to quickly transition to the steady-state combustion stage after arc initiation, reducing the probability of transient disturbances from the external power supply. III. Operating performance of yttrium-tungsten electrodes under medium to low current densities In practical applications, CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes show excellent operating performance within the medium to low current parameter range. In this current range, the temperature distribution at the electrode tip tends to be reasonable, maintaining the necessary electron emission activity without causing excessive tip melting or burning loss. This moderate thermal state keeps the arc axis highly symmetrical, with clear arc column edges, not prone to arc blow caused by thermal deformation, keeping the entire arc combustion process in a stable state. IV. Arc convergence and heat concentration of yttrium-tungsten electrodes The convergence characteristics of the arc determine the degree of heat concentration transmitted to the workpiece. During operation of yttrium-tungsten electrodes, due to the relatively small and concentrated cathode spot size, the arc produces a certain convergence effect toward the axial direction. This convergence characteristic brings relatively high heat density, making energy transmission more stable. Stable heat input helps control the size of the heat-affected zone, reducing cumulative deformation of the workpiece during operation, and improving the macroscopic quality of the processing area. CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes image V. Effect of shielding gas on arc column morphology The physical and chemical properties of the surrounding atmosphere have a synergistic effect on arc stability. Generally, when using inert gases such as argon for shielding, the shielding gas flow produces a mechanical compression effect on the arc column. The steady-state flow of this gas flow, combined with the electron emission characteristics of CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes, jointly maintains the conductive channel of the arc space. The uniformity of gas flow distribution reduces the stretching or distortion of the arc caused by external disturbances, protecting the integrity of the arc morphology. VI. Effect of yttrium-tungsten electrode shape on arc stability The geometric configuration of the electrode front end largely regulates the spatial distribution of the electric field. Standardized axisymmetric taper angles and appropriate top flat sizes help constrain the diffusion direction of electron emission. If the taper angle is reasonably designed, the electric field intensity maintains a uniform gradient at the tip, which prevents the arc root from climbing disorderly on the electrode side wall, thereby ensuring that the arc's spatial trajectory remains unchanged during long-term operation, maintaining a sustained arc morphology.

title: How Is the Thermal Conductivity of Yttrium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: Thermal conductivity, as a physical indicator for measuring the ability of a material to transfer heat, has reference significance for understanding the thermal balance mechanism of yttrium-tungsten electrodes under high-temperature conditions. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes image I. How is the thermal conductivity of yttrium-tungsten electrodes? For metals and alloys, heat conduction is mainly achieved through the migration of free electrons and lattice vibration (phonons). Pure tungsten has good thermal conductivity, with a thermal conductivity at room temperature of approximately 170–175 W/(m·K). When yttrium oxide is added to the tungsten matrix, since yttrium oxide particles are distributed as a dispersed phase at tungsten grain boundaries, these particles scatter the movement of free electrons and increase lattice defects, resulting in a slight decrease in the thermal conductivity of the material compared with pure tungsten. Studies have shown that the thermal conductivity of yttrium-tungsten electrodes (with yttrium oxide content generally between 1% and 2%) at room temperature is generally in the range of 150–165 W/(m·K). As temperature increases, the thermal conductivity of tungsten-based materials shows a decreasing trend due to enhanced lattice vibration scattering. Under high-temperature environments where the working temperature reaches above 1000°C, the thermal conductivity of yttrium-tungsten electrodes generally decreases to around 80 W/(m·K). This trajectory of thermal conductivity change reflects the energy transport characteristics of the material during heating. II. Mechanism of the effect of microstructure on the thermal conduction efficiency of yttrium-tungsten electrodes The thermal conductivity of CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes is not determined solely by material composition; the morphology of its microstructure plays a role in heat transfer: (1) Distribution morphology of the dispersed phase: The degree of dispersion of yttrium oxide particles in the tungsten matrix is key to affecting thermal conductivity. If the dispersed distribution is highly uniform and fine, it can reduce obstruction to electron transport, thereby maintaining relatively high thermal conductivity while strengthening the mechanical properties of the material. (2) Sintering density: The powder metallurgy process in manufacturing affects the density of the electrode. If micro-pores exist inside the electrode, these pores become barriers to heat transfer, significantly reducing the macroscopic thermal conductivity of the material. High-density processing is a technical guarantee for maintaining stable thermal conductivity. (3) Grain boundary thermal resistance: Interfaces between tungsten grains form thermal resistance. Through high-temperature sintering processes that tightly bond grains, the disturbance of grain boundaries to heat energy transfer can be reduced. CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes image III. Effect of thermal conductivity on the high-temperature stability of yttrium-tungsten electrodes During arc processing, the tip of CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrode withstands the impact of high-temperature plasma, and the level of thermal conductivity affects the efficiency of heat transfer from the tip to the electrode shaft. (1) Thermal stress management: Appropriate thermal conductivity can assist the electrode in transferring localized high temperature at the tip to cooler areas in time, thereby reducing the temperature gradient between the tip and the shaft, reducing thermal stress caused by uneven thermal expansion, and delaying crack formation. (2) Suppression of abnormal softening: If thermal conductivity is too low, heat at the tip is difficult to dissipate, causing the local temperature to rapidly rise above the recrystallization temperature of tungsten, leading to severe grain growth or softening deformation. Therefore, maintaining reasonable thermal conductivity in yttrium-tungsten electrodes helps maintain their geometric shape under continuous working conditions. (3) Thermal balance of the arc region: The efficient heat conduction of the electrode helps maintain stable anchoring of the arc root at the electrode end, reducing arc drift, thereby improving the continuity of the processing process.

title: How Is the Electron Work Function of Yttrium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: In modern industrial processing and gas discharge fields, tungsten electrodes have achieved performance optimization through the addition of rare earth oxides. Yttrium-tungsten electrodes, as one of the representatives, by adding an appropriate amount of yttrium oxide to the tungsten matrix, while maintaining the high melting point characteristics of tungsten, significantly improve their electron emission efficiency and welding process performance. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes image I. How is the electron work function of yttrium-tungsten electrodes? The electron work function is a physical indicator that measures the minimum energy required for electrons to escape from the material surface, and its magnitude reflects, to some extent, the difficulty of initiating the electron emission process of the material. For pure tungsten, its electron work function is generally around 4.5 eV. After adding yttrium oxide to the tungsten matrix, due to the dispersion effect of the rare earth oxide on the matrix surface and the change in charge distribution, the equivalent electron work function of the material changes. Studies have shown that the electron work function of tungsten electrodes with yttrium oxide added is generally lower than that of pure tungsten, generally in the range of 2.6 eV to 3.5 eV. This numerical fluctuation is mainly affected by yttrium oxide content, process parameters, and electrode surface treatment methods. The lower work function enables the electrode to produce thermionic emission more easily during operation, thereby reducing the arc starting voltage and improving the arc starting performance. II. Factors affecting the electron work function of yttrium-tungsten electrodes The electron work function of CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes is not a fixed constant, but a parameter affected by multiple factors. (1) Microscopic composition of the material: Yttrium oxide, as second-phase particles dispersed in tungsten grain boundaries, has its distribution density and particle size affecting the surface electron potential barrier. The more fine and uniform the particles, the more electron emission sites there are, which helps improve emission uniformity. (2) Temperature changes: Thermionic emission is a physical process that varies with temperature. When the electrode is in a high-temperature working state, the intensification of surface atomic vibrations and thermal excitation effects cause the effective work function of the material to show a certain degree of change with increasing temperature. (3) Surface state: The surface cleanliness of the tungsten electrode, surface crystal orientation, and physical evolution under arc working conditions (such as surface roughness, formation of active films, etc.) all adjust the energy barrier required for electron escape. (4) External environment: Under arc working conditions with inert gas shielding, the electrode surface maintains a relatively stable physicochemical state, which has reference significance for maintaining stable emission characteristics. CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes image III. Application advantages of yttrium-tungsten electrodes in welding processes Due to their unique physicochemical properties, yttrium-tungsten electrodes show three application advantages in industrial production: First, arc starting performance: Due to the reduction in work function, yttrium-tungsten electrodes can establish a stable arc under low current conditions, reducing energy loss and time fluctuation during the arc starting process. Second, arc beam concentration: The arc generated by yttrium-tungsten electrodes during operation is relatively concentrated, with a relatively small diffusion angle. This characteristic is conducive to heat convergence toward the base metal, improving the heat-affected zone control capability during welding. Third, high-temperature structural stability: Yttrium oxide can play a grain boundary pinning role at high temperatures, effectively inhibiting abnormal grain growth of tungsten at high temperatures, thereby maintaining the geometric shape of the electrode tip, and showing good ablation resistance in continuous welding operations.

title: What Role does Yttrium Oxide Play in Tungsten Electrodes?
text: In modern industrial manufacturing and gas discharge technology, tungsten-based materials are widely used due to their high melting point, high density, and good electrical conductivity. However, pure tungsten materials are often accompanied by physical characteristics such as low electron emission efficiency, easy arc divergence, and relatively fast burning rates under high-temperature working conditions. In order to improve these properties, a small amount of rare earth metal oxides such as yttrium oxide is usually introduced into the tungsten matrix in industry. CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes image CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. I. Development background of tungsten electrodes and principle of rare earth modification Tungsten has a relatively high melting point (approximately 3422°C), which makes it an ideal matrix material in the field of high-temperature arc and electron emission. However, pure tungsten is difficult to process at room temperature, and its electron work function is relatively high at high temperatures, resulting in high arc starting voltage and insufficient arc stability. In order to overcome the inherent limitations of pure tungsten, the concepts of dispersion strengthening and surface activation have been introduced in the field of materials engineering. By adding a small amount of rare earth metal oxides to tungsten powder and forming dispersed second-phase particles during powder metallurgy sintering, the electron emission capability, creep resistance, and high-temperature ablation resistance of tungsten materials can be significantly improved. This modification method not only broadens the application range of tungsten electrodes but also extends their working life under different operating conditions. II. What role does yttrium oxide play in tungsten electrodes? In the microscopic system of CTIA GROUP's tungsten electrodes, yttrium oxide is mainly distributed in the form of dispersed phase particles uniformly at tungsten grain boundaries and within grains. It mainly plays the following three roles during electrode operation: First, reducing the electron work function: The electron work function of pure tungsten is relatively high, and the introduction of yttrium oxide can reduce the electron work function on the electrode surface to a certain extent. When the electrode is heated, the dispersed yttrium oxide particles help electron emission, making the arc easier to ignite and maintain a stable combustion state at lower voltage levels. Second, refining the grain structure: During the high-temperature sintering and processing evolution of the electrode, the dispersed yttrium oxide particles can effectively hinder abnormal grain growth of tungsten. This grain refinement effect helps improve the high-temperature mechanical strength and creep resistance of the material, slowing down localized deformation and spalling of the electrode in high-temperature arc environments. Third, inhibiting high-temperature volatilization and burning loss: Under high-temperature working conditions, yttrium oxide and the tungsten matrix can maintain a relatively stable microstructure balance, reducing the volatilization rate of tungsten atoms, thereby extending the overall service life of the electrode. CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes image III. Microstructural characteristics and macroscopic physical performance of yttrium-tungsten electrodes The distribution state and dispersion degree of yttrium oxide in the tungsten matrix have a significant effect on the macroscopic physical performance of the electrode. Through powder metallurgy process control, yttrium oxide particles can be uniformly dispersed between tungsten grain boundaries. This microstructure not only affects the heat conduction path but also has an effect on arc convergence. Convergence of arc beam: Compared with some traditional electrodes, the arc beam of yttrium-tungsten electrodes generally shows better stability, with a smaller arc diffusion angle, making heat input more concentrated, suitable for processing links with control requirements for the heat-affected zone. Stability of thermionic emission: Yttrium oxide has good chemical stability at high temperatures and is not prone to decomposition or violent reactions, which enables the electrode to maintain relatively stable electron emission capability during long-term continuous operation.

title: Tungsten Prices Edge Down at the Start of September
text: Analysis of Latest Tungsten Market from Chinatungsten Online As September began, tungsten concentrate prices saw a modest pullback from the RMB 420,000/standard ton level. Industry sources note that this adjustment is more of a technical correction after earlier high quotes failed to materialize in actual transactions, rather than a substantive weakening of market conditions. Producer willingness to support prices remains firm. Nevertheless, the downward move has sparked concern among some market participants, who question whether the traditional “Golden September” peak season will materialize as expected. According to research by China Tungsten Online, while market participants often hold seasonal expectations, the fundamental drivers of tungsten prices remain supply-demand dynamics, policy measures, and cost support. Seasonal factors act primarily as catalysts for market sentiment and short-term trading rhythms, rather than as the decisive force determining price direction. Consequently, the actual delivery of the so-called “Golden September and Silver October” still needs to be verified against underlying fundamentals. Looking at current market performance, downstream procurement remains largely needs-based, with limited willingness to build inventories proactively. Most end-users are purchasing flexibly according to actual orders and, drawing on experience from the start of the year, are reluctant to lock in inventory early in order to manage risk. Overall transaction pace is slow and trading atmosphere relatively subdued. On the raw-material side, there is some pressure to digest inventories. Since March, stocks have gradually accumulated to relatively high levels amid soft demand; the temporary drawdown seen at the end of May proved limited in duration, and overall inventory pressure has not been effectively relieved. Combined with squeezed profit margins, smelters have reduced operating rates and shown stronger willingness to adjust supply. As of the time of writing, ammonium paratungstate (APT) stood at RMB 595,000/ton, down 11.2% from the beginning of the year; tungsten powder at RMB 920/kg, down 14.8%; tungsten carbide powder at RMB 870/kg, down 16.4%; and 70% ferro-tungsten at RMB 640,000/ton, down 1.5%. Scrap tungsten rod prices were at RMB 735/kg, up 8.3% year-to-date. China Tungsten Online believes the recent modest decline in tungsten prices reflects the combined effects of supply-demand mismatch and cautious market sentiment. In the near term, prices are likely to remain in a stable-to-weak range with sideways oscillation. Upside potential is constrained by the pace of downstream demand recovery, while downside room is relatively limited owing to active supply-side adjustments and cost support; expectations of either a sharp rally or a deep correction remain low. It is still premature to declare the “Golden September” a washout. Attention should be paid to the actual release of demand from end-use sectors, long-term contract quotations and procurement strategies of major tungsten producers, and marginal changes in the broader macro-political and economic environment. The interplay of these factors will determine the quality of the September market. Until then, the market is likely to remain dominated by wait-and-see positioning and tactical maneuvering, with a clear directional trend still requiring patience. title: NWF Backs £71M Restart of Hemerdon Tungsten and Tin Mine
text: On August 25, 2026, the UK’s National Wealth Fund (NWF) announced an investment of up to £71 million to support the restart of the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine, located near Plymouth, Devon. The investment comprises £36 million in equity (representing an approximately 7.42% stake) and up to £35 million in debt financing; these funds will cover mine construction, commissioning, and processing costs, as well as the repayment of prior short-term loans. Hemerdon Tungsten and Tin Mine, Tungsten West website The UK government will secure exclusive negotiation rights to purchase up to 50% of the tungsten output projected in the mine's 2025 feasibility study for use in sectors such as defense, aerospace, and next-generation energy. Chancellor John Healey stated that this move is a crucial step toward supporting British industry and ensuring sovereign access to critical minerals in an increasingly "dangerous world." Tungsten—a metal prized for its high hardness and heat resistance—is widely used in cemented carbides, armor-piercing munitions, high-temperature aerospace components, and advanced manufacturing tools. Global supply is highly concentrated, with China holding a dominant share of 53% of reserves and 79% of production. The UK’s recently published critical minerals strategy explicitly aims to meet 10% of domestic demand through local production and 20% through recycling by 2035, while limiting reliance on any single country to no more than 60% of supply, thereby enhancing economic resilience and national security. The restart of Hemerdon is viewed as a key implementation of this strategy, helping to build a more reliable alternative supply chain for the West amidst rising global geopolitical risks. Hemerdon Tungsten and Tin Mine, Tungsten West website The Hemerdon tungsten-tin mine is considered one of the UK's largest domestic tungsten resources. According to public reports from Tungsten West, the mine has already completed initial trial production; it is scheduled to commence formal production in the third quarter of 2026 and reach full capacity in the first quarter of 2027. At full capacity, it is expected to produce approximately 3,320 tonnes of tungsten concentrate and 462 tonnes of tin concentrate annually, accounting for 20% of the global supply outside of China. China Tungsten Online believes that, in terms of sheer volume, the restart of the Hemerdon tungsten-tin mine will not significantly impact China's export market share; however, the capital injection involving the local government and the secured production commitments reflect the West's long-term determination to achieve autonomous control over critical minerals. The Chinese tungsten industry needs to closely monitor trends toward supply substitution driven by overseas policy directives while leveraging its advantages in technology, cost, and the industrial supply chain to consolidate and enhance its competitiveness.

title: Is the Arc Beam of Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes Concentrated?
text: Whether the arc of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is concentrated is a core evaluation indicator affecting their ability to handle precision welding and plasma processing. Based on material properties and process performance, cerium-tungsten electrodes have significant arc beam concentration characteristics, which make them high in energy density, narrow in heat-affected zone, and vertical in cutting seam in scenarios such as low-current DC welding and plasma cutting. The physical root of their arc beam concentration can be attributed to the synergistic effects of cathode spot shrinkage, enhanced self-magnetic compression, and the material's dynamic self-sharpening characteristics. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Shrinkage of the cathode spot: a gift from work function reduction The primary physical mechanism for the arc beam concentration of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes originates from the reduction of their cathode spot. The cathode spot is the attachment area of the arc on the electrode surface, and its size affects the degree of arc root diffusion. Pure tungsten electrodes have a high work function of 4.5–4.6 eV, requiring a relatively high cathode voltage drop (approximately 13 V) during thermionic emission, and the cathode spot is relatively large and dispersed. Cerium-tungsten electrodes, by doping with cerium oxide, significantly reduce the work function to 2.7–2.8 eV, and the cathode voltage drop correspondingly decreases to approximately 12 V, about 1 V lower than thoriated tungsten electrodes. This seemingly small voltage drop difference brings substantial physical effects: a lower cathode voltage drop means that the electric field strength required to maintain thermionic emission is reduced, the attachment point of the arc on the electrode surface naturally shrinks, the cathode spot decreases, and electron emission becomes more concentrated. The process manifestation of cathode spot shrinkage is: the arc root is pinned at the tip center, avoiding disordered jumping of the arc on the electrode side wall, and the arc column directivity is significantly enhanced. II. Self-magnetic compression effect: arc self-focusing under high current When the welding current increases, the arc beam concentration characteristic of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is further enhanced, thanks to the self-magnetic compression effect of the arc itself. The arc current is essentially a directional moving charge flow, generating a circular magnetic field around the conductor. According to electromagnetic principles, this magnetic field produces a Lorentz force on the arc plasma directed toward the axis: the larger the current, the greater the magnetic field centripetal pressure, and the tighter the arc is compressed. Since cerium-tungsten electrodes have a lower cathode voltage drop and can carry higher current density at the same voltage, this self-magnetic compression effect is therefore more significant. In addition, during welding, the metal vapor generated by the arc heating the workpiece has the highest density at the center axis of the arc, with relatively large resistance. The arc current tends to conduct along the path with lower resistance, and this low-resistance trend further drives the arc to contract toward the axis. The superposition of the two mechanisms gives cerium-tungsten electrodes the typical characteristics of a narrow and bright arc column during welding, with more concentrated energy and higher thermal efficiency. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Natural sharpening effect: self-maintaining mechanism of tip shape Another unique aspect of the arc beam concentration characteristic of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is that the tip forms an adaptive geometric optimization during service: the natural sharpening characteristic. During welding, the cerium element migrates to the high-temperature zone of the electrode tip and enriches there, forming a low-work-function surface layer. Under plasma cutting or high-current conditions, the water-cooled anode simultaneously cools the electrode. This thermal equilibrium state brings the electrode tip to a dynamic balance of evaporation and condensation: excessive active substances are suppressed from evaporation, while the evaporated part may be attracted back by the electric field in the plasma. The final result is that the electrode tip spontaneously forms a relatively sharp geometric shape during operation, maintaining concentrated arc directivity without the need for frequent manual grinding. IV. Process boundary: applicable conditions for concentration characteristics It should be noted that the arc beam concentration advantage of cerium-tungsten electrodes has a clear current application range. In the medium to low current range, the arc beam concentration, arc starting sensitivity, and arc jitter control of cerium-tungsten electrodes are all excellent, especially suitable for thin plate stainless steel, titanium alloy welding, and miniature precision component welding. However, when the current exceeds the recommended upper limit, the strong heat flow brought by high current accelerates the evaporation loss of the cerium element, leading to damage to the surface active layer, and the arc may diverge or jitter again. In AC welding scenarios, cerium-tungsten electrodes are also prone to splitting, and the arc beam concentration deteriorates accordingly. External factors such as asymmetric tip grinding and turbulent shielding gas can also destroy their original concentration characteristics.

title: Can Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes Completely Replace Thoriated Tungsten Electrodes?
text: The original intention behind the development of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes was precisely to replace thoriated tungsten electrodes with radioactive risks. After decades of application verification, the answer is: in the field of medium and low current DC welding, cerium-tungsten electrodes have basically achieved the replacement of thoriated tungsten electrodes; however, in high-current, AC welding, and some special applications, they cannot yet be completely replaced. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Chemical basis for replacement: lower work function, significant safety advantages The first driving factor for CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes to replace thoriated tungsten electrodes is safety. Thoriated tungsten electrodes contain 1%–2% thorium oxide (ThO₂), and thorium is a radioactive element, posing occupational health risks and waste disposal problems during long-term use. With the tightening of environmental regulations such as the EU REACH, cerium-tungsten electrodes, containing no radioactive substances, have become a compliant preferred option. From the perspective of electron emission performance, cerium-tungsten electrodes even have certain advantages. Their electron work function is 2.4–2.8 eV, lower than the approximately 2.7 eV of thoriated tungsten electrodes. A lower work function means easier arc starting: the minimum arc starting voltage of cerium-tungsten electrodes can be as low as 12 V, while that of thoriated tungsten electrodes is approximately 30 V. II. Scenario boundaries for replacement: low-current DC is the main field, AC and high-current are shortcomings Although cerium-tungsten electrodes are superior to thoriated tungsten in arc starting performance, their applicable scenarios have clear boundaries. Cerium-tungsten electrodes are mainly suitable for DC negative electrode welding, especially in low-current scenarios such as pipe welding, stainless steel thin plates, and fine precision components, where they are the preferred replacement for thoriated tungsten electrodes. Cerium has the highest mobility and performs excellently in the initial stage of welding. However, cerium-tungsten electrodes have two significant performance shortcomings: First, they are not recommended for AC welding. Under AC TIG welding conditions, cerium-tungsten electrodes are prone to splitting, and arc stability is significantly inferior to that of thoriated tungsten electrodes. Therefore, when AC welding materials such as aluminum and magnesium alloys, zirconium-tungsten or lanthanum-tungsten electrodes are generally selected. Second, insufficient life under high-current conditions. Under high-current or long-term continuous operation, the service life of cerium-tungsten electrodes is significantly lower than that of thoriated tungsten electrodes. This is because the high mobility of cerium under high thermal loads destroys the uniform distribution of oxides, accelerating performance degradation. For high-current, high-voltage welding, thoriated tungsten or lanthanum-tungsten electrodes remain better choices. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Root of the difference: physicochemical essence of cerium and thorium The reason why CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes cannot completely replace thoriated tungsten electrodes lies in the intrinsic differences between the two elements cerium and thorium. Mobility and timeliness: Cerium has the highest mobility among rare earth elements, which gives it excellent performance in the initial arc starting stage. However, as service time extends and grain growth occurs, migration efficiency significantly decreases. Thorium is relatively stable, with more gradual performance degradation during long-term service. Vapor pressure and high-temperature stability: Cerium has a relatively high vapor pressure and is prone to volatilization at high temperatures, which leads to problems of fast decay and poor stability when cerium-tungsten electrodes are used as cathode materials in gas discharge light sources such as high-power xenon lamps. Thorium has a lower vapor pressure and better high-temperature stability, and to this day still cannot be replaced in certain fields. Thermal conductivity and ablation resistance: Thoriated tungsten electrodes have higher crystallization temperature and better electrical conductivity, are not easily deformed under high-current arc action, and have strong oxidation resistance. Cerium oxide and the tungstates formed at high temperatures have relatively low melting points, and excessive doping actually reduces ablation resistance.

title: What Role does Cerium Oxide Play in Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes are electrode materials with approximately 1.8%–2.2% cerium oxide incorporated into the tungsten matrix, identified by a gray tip color code. The introduction of cerium oxide fundamentally changes the electron emission characteristics and high-temperature service behavior of pure tungsten electrodes, serving as the core functional phase affecting the performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Electronic structure regulation: physicochemical essence of reducing the work function The most core contribution of cerium oxide to cerium-tungsten electrodes lies in its significant reduction of the electron work function of the electrode material. The electron work function of pure tungsten is approximately 4.5–4.9 eV, making it difficult for electrons to be effectively emitted at room temperature, relying on high-temperature thermionic emission mechanisms. After cerium oxide incorporation, the work function can be reduced to the range of approximately 2.4–2.8 eV. The chemical essence of this reduction lies in the mixed valence state characteristics of cerium ions. The outer electron structure of cerium is 4f¹5d¹6s², coexisting in cerium oxide as Ce³⁺ and Ce⁴⁺. The work function of Ce₂O₃, the compound of Ce³⁺, is only 2.3 eV, far lower than that of metallic tungsten. During the reduction sintering process of electrode preparation, Ce⁴⁺ is reduced to Ce³⁺, and this redox reaction simultaneously increases oxygen vacancies in the matrix, enhancing the ionic conductivity of the rare earth oxide. The higher the Ce³⁺ content, the stronger the electron emission capability of the electrode. II. Dynamic surface behavior: migration and enrichment under arc action Cerium oxide does not exist statically during the service of cerium-tungsten electrodes, but exhibits dynamic surface regulation behavior. Under the high-temperature action of the welding arc, cerium oxide particles migrate and enrich toward the electrode tip through grain boundary diffusion or surface diffusion mechanisms, accompanied by the continuous transformation of cerium ions from +4 to +3 valence, forming a low-work-function surface active layer at the tip. Cerium is one of the elements with the highest mobility among rare earth elements. This characteristic enables cerium-tungsten electrodes to quickly function in the initial stage of arc starting, with significantly superior arc starting sensitivity compared with other rare earth tungsten electrodes. This dynamic balance allows the electrode tip to always maintain a relatively low electron work function state during service, which is conducive to stable arc starting and maintenance at relatively low open-circuit voltages. However, this migration mechanism also has temporal limitations. As service time extends and grain growth occurs, migration efficiency gradually decreases. Therefore, CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes are suitable for short-cycle welding or automated welding scenarios with high requirements for arc starting frequency. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Dispersion strengthening effect: improving ablation resistance and service life Cerium oxide, as a dispersed phase distributed in the tungsten matrix, also functions as a structural strengthener. Cerium oxide particles produce a pinning effect on tungsten grain boundaries, inhibiting abnormal grain growth and recrystallization at high temperatures, thereby improving the high-temperature creep resistance and geometric stability of the electrode. In terms of ablation resistance, cerium-tungsten electrodes have lower melting and evaporation rates compared with pure tungsten electrodes, with ablation mainly concentrated at the tip rather than the entire matrix. It should be noted that higher cerium oxide content is not always better. Due to the relatively low melting point of cerium oxide and the tungstates formed at high temperatures, excessive doping actually reduces the ablation resistance and yield of the electrode. IV. Non-radioactive substitution value: safety and application boundaries Another significant significance of cerium oxide in cerium-tungsten electrodes is that it endows the material with the feasibility of replacing thoriated tungsten electrodes. Thoriated tungsten electrodes contain trace amounts of radioactive thorium, posing occupational health and environmental radiation risks during production and long-term use. In terms of service performance, cerium-tungsten electrodes have sensitive arc starting, concentrated arc, and low maintaining current in low-current DC welding, suitable for pipe welding, stainless steel thin plates, and fine precision component welding scenarios. However, under AC welding conditions, cerium-tungsten electrodes are prone to splitting, so other types of tungsten electrodes are recommended for AC conditions.

title: Does Yttrium-Tungsten Electrode Need Preheating Before Use?
text: For yttrium-tungsten electrodes, no dedicated preheating is required under conventional welding conditions, but exceptions exist in specific high-demand scenarios. This is essentially the result of the combined effect of the thermionic emission mechanism and the material's thermal conductivity—preheating is not a necessary condition for arc initiation, but under certain conditions, it can become an active technical means to protect the electrode and improve stability. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP’s yttrium-tungsten electrodes I. From the perspective of the electron emission mechanism: why preheating is not required under conventional conditions The core advantage of CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes lies in the significant reduction of the work function on the tungsten matrix surface by yttrium oxide (Y₂O₃). The electron work function of pure tungsten is approximately 4.5 eV, while that of yttrium-tungsten electrodes can be reduced to the range of 2.0–3.9 eV. This reduction means that electrons can be emitted in large quantities at relatively low electric field strengths even at room temperature, achieving rapid arc initiation. From a chemical thermodynamics perspective, the reduction in work function is essentially the result of the local dipole moment induced by Y₂O₃ at the W-Y₂O₃ interface changing the surface potential barrier distribution. Therefore, yttrium-tungsten electrodes can quickly establish a stable arc even under low-current conditions, generally without the need for high-frequency arc starting devices. This is fundamentally different from the mechanism of pure tungsten electrodes that rely on high-temperature thermionic emission: pure tungsten requires preheating to a certain temperature to obtain sufficient electron emission capability, while yttrium-tungsten electrodes can start working at room temperature by virtue of the electron-assisting emission function of yttrium oxide. II. Support from material thermophysical properties: high-temperature stability and thermal management capability Another basis for why CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes do not require preheating lies in their intrinsic thermal conductivity and high-temperature deformation resistance. Yttrium-tungsten electrodes have good thermal conductivity, capable of rapidly conducting localized high-temperature heat from the arc tip along the axial direction to the rear end, preventing tip melting or ablation; at the same time, it helps achieve uniform temperature distribution across the electrode, reducing thermal stress concentration and micro-crack initiation. This self-heat-dissipation characteristic means that even during cold start, tip thermal shock can be quickly dispersed, without the need to pre-establish a temperature gradient through preheating to avoid thermal stress damage. In addition, the pinning effect of yttrium oxide particles at tungsten grain boundaries effectively inhibits grain migration and coarsening at high temperatures, enabling yttrium-tungsten electrodes to maintain their original geometric shape even at arc temperatures above 2000°C. Therefore, the instantaneous thermal shock during cold start does not pose a substantial threat to the microstructure of yttrium-tungsten electrodes. This is the structural and chemical basis for their lack of need for preheating. Pictures of CTIA GROUP’s yttrium-tungsten electrodes III. Boundary conditions for preheating: when active preheating is required Although preheating is not required under conventional conditions, in the following specific conditions, preheating of yttrium-tungsten electrodes is a technical measure worth considering: Low ambient temperature: In cold environments, the initial temperature of the electrode matrix is too low, which may cause excessive thermal shock at the moment of arc initiation. Although the work function of yttrium-tungsten electrodes has been significantly reduced, electron emission efficiency under low-temperature conditions is still affected to a certain extent. High humidity environments or after long-term storage: If the electrode has been exposed to humid air for a long time, the tip surface may adsorb moisture or form a slight oxide layer. At this time, light preheating before arc initiation helps remove surface adsorbates, ensuring smooth arc initiation and arc stability. This is not because the material itself needs preheating, but a surface treatment measure taken to ensure the chemical purity of the tip surface. Ultra-high current or extreme thermal load conditions: In thick plate welding or plasma arc welding scenarios where the current exceeds 300 A, if the initial electrode temperature is too low and large current is loaded instantaneously, micro-crack initiation at the tip may occur due to superimposed thermal shock. At this time, gradually increasing the current to allow the electrode to warm up step by step is essentially an engineering extension of the preheating concept. IV. Precautions for preheating operations of yttrium-tungsten electrodes When it is determined that preheating of yttrium-tungsten electrodes is necessary, the following points should be noted: Preheating method: The most common method is to use the arc generated by the welding torch itself at a relatively low current for a short arc burn, allowing the tip to gradually warm up to near the working temperature. External heat sources such as open flames or resistance heating should be avoided to prevent contamination or localized overheating. Temperature control: The preheating temperature should not be too high. The recrystallization temperature of yttrium-tungsten electrodes has been increased through yttrium oxide dispersion strengthening, but excessive preheating may accelerate surface oxidation, which is not conducive to electrode life.

title: How High is the Current-Carrying Capacity of Yttrium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: The current-carrying capacity of CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes is essentially the result of the synergistic effect of their material characteristics, geometric dimensions, and process environment. Compared with pure tungsten electrodes and thoriated tungsten electrodes, yttrium-tungsten electrodes, with the dispersion strengthening and electron emission optimization of yttrium oxide, exhibit higher tolerance limits and lower burning rates under high-current-density conditions. Their current-carrying capacity is not a fixed value, but a parameter system that dynamically changes with electrode diameter, current polarity, shielding atmosphere, and tip shape. Current-carrying capacity of yttrium-tungsten electrodes under DC positive polarity conditions DC positive polarity (DCEN, electrode connected to negative) is the standard mode for yttrium-tungsten electrodes to exert their current-carrying advantages. Under this polarity, electrons are emitted from the electrode to the workpiece, and the tip mainly bears the combined effect of the cooling effect from thermionic emission and ion bombardment, with a relatively moderate thermal load, allowing higher current input. According to application data, the typical current ranges for yttrium-tungsten electrodes of different diameters under DCEN conditions are: diameter 1.6 mm: 60–150 A; diameter 2.4 mm: 150–250 A; diameter 3.2 mm: 150–300 A; diameter 4.0 mm and above: up to 400 A or more. In welding of zirconium alloy fuel rods for the nuclear industry, the current can reach 300–500 A; in plasma spraying of nickel-based alloy turbine blades in the aerospace field, the current can be increased to 400–600 A. This is得益于 the higher yttrium oxide content, which further increases the recrystallization temperature of the electrode and significantly enhances the resistance to tip erosion. II. Current-carrying capacity of yttrium-tungsten electrodes under AC and DC reverse polarity conditions In AC welding, the electrode bears the thermal load of electron bombardment during the positive half-cycle, and its current-carrying capacity is generally lower than that of DC positive polarity. Taking a 3.2 mm diameter electrode as an example, under balanced wave AC conditions, the typical current-carrying capacity is approximately 120–200 A. If there is a DC bias component in the AC waveform, the thermal load of the electrode will further increase, requiring appropriate derating. Under DC reverse polarity (DCEP, electrode connected to positive) conditions, the tip serves as the anode receiving high-speed electron bombardment, and the thermal load increases sharply. Its current-carrying capacity does not have a clear critical value, but is determined by weighing according to actual application requirements. Since the electrode burning rate is significantly accelerated in this mode, it is generally only used briefly for welding the oxide film on the surface of aluminum and magnesium alloys in engineering, or operated at relatively low currents to extend electrode life. title: Will Yttrium-Tungsten Electrodes Produce Arc Drift?
text: In the tungsten inert gas shielded welding process, the directivity and stability of the arc are core factors affecting weld formation quality. Arc drift is manifested as irregular swinging or deviation of the arc axis, leading to uneven heat input, penetration fluctuation, and weld appearance defects. Whether CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes are prone to arc drift needs to be examined from three aspects: their intrinsic material characteristics, actual performance under working conditions, and process matching. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP’s yttrium-tungsten electrodes I. Structural design of yttrium-tungsten electrodes: intrinsic mechanism for suppressing arc drift Within the range of standard process parameters, yttrium-tungsten electrodes are not prone to obvious arc drift. This advantage is rooted in their unique microstructure. Yttrium-tungsten electrodes use high-purity tungsten as the matrix, with an appropriate amount of yttrium oxide added through powder metallurgy, and the oxide particles uniformly distributed in a dispersed state at tungsten grain boundaries. This microstructure plays two key roles: First, the emission point fixation effect. The dispersed yttrium oxide particles form numerous uniform low-work-function emission centers on the electrode surface, reducing the potential barrier for electron emission. After arc ignition, thermoelectrons tend to emit from the tip center where the electromagnetic field and temperature field are most concentrated, and the cathode spot is stably anchored in the core area of the tip, reducing the probability of random jumping on the electrode surface. Second, the high-temperature deformation resistance. The dispersion strengthening and Zener pinning effect of yttrium oxide effectively inhibit the migration and recrystallization of tungsten grain boundaries at high temperatures, raising the recrystallization temperature from approximately 1250°C for pure tungsten to above 1650°C. Under continuous arc thermal load, the electrode tip is not prone to asymmetric melting, collapse, or spalling, and the symmetry of the tip geometric shape is maintained, thereby ensuring the constancy of the arc path. In addition, the arc column formed by CTIA GROUP's yttrium-tungsten electrodes at high currents has good convergence, with the arc axis maintaining high symmetry and a relatively small arc column diffusion range, conducive to reducing drift caused by arc divergence. II. Influence of process conditions: how external factors induce arc drift Although yttrium-tungsten electrodes have good anti-drift characteristics, in actual welding operations, if affected by adverse external factors, significant arc deflection may still be induced. The geometric shape of the tungsten electrode tip affects the spatial distribution of the electric field. If the taper angle is asymmetric, the tip is eccentric, or the grinding texture is not parallel to the axis during manual grinding, it will cause uneven current density distribution, inducing the arc to deflect to one side. Standard tip grinding should be an axisymmetric taper angle, ensuring a uniform electric field gradient and preventing the arc root from climbing disorderly on the electrode side wall. Abnormal fluctuations in shielding gas flow rate, damaged nozzles, or strong airflow disturbances in the surrounding environment change the air pressure and thermal equilibrium state around the arc, causing mechanical stretching or distortion of the arc column. Too low gas flow cannot effectively shield the arc, while too high flow may form turbulence, both of which can cause arc jitter. In high-current welding circuits, if the workpiece wiring position is improper or there is a residual magnetic field, the generated electromagnetic force acts on the arc current, causing the arc to deviate from the center axis. This is one of the common causes of arc drift in high-current DC welding. Pictures of CTIA GROUP’s yttrium-tungsten electrodes III. Influence of material purity: threat of impurities to arc stability The chemical purity of the yttrium-tungsten electrode matrix is a prerequisite for ensuring its anti-drift capability. The presence of trace impurity elements can destroy the arc stability of the electrode. Relevant technical standards have limits on impurity content: iron is generally required to be below 50 ppm, silicon below 20 ppm, and carbon below 10 ppm. When impurity content exceeds the standard, on the one hand it increases the resistivity of the electrode, causing uneven heating at the tip; on the other hand, impurity elements may form low-melting-point eutectic phases at high temperatures or segregate at grain boundaries, becoming preferential initiation points for arc drift and localized burning loss. If there are cracks, delamination, micro-cracks, or non-uniform grain structure inside the electrode, the arc starting process will be unstable, making it more prone to arc interruption, arc bursting, and drift.

title: Mt Mulgine Tungsten Project Scheduled for Production in 2029
text: Recently, Tungsten Mining NL released the results of the Pre-Feasibility Study (PFS) for its Mt Mulgine Tungsten Project in Western Australia, concluding that the project has the potential to become one of the world’s largest and lowest-cost tungsten developments. The Mt Mulgine Project is located in the Murchison region of Western Australia, approximately 330–350 km northeast of Perth, in a well-recognised low-risk mining jurisdiction with established infrastructure. It is an Archaean porphyry-style tungsten-molybdenum-gold-silver polymetallic deposit. The main mineralised zone is hosted in the Mulgine Trench, which is 150–260 m thick and extends more than 1.5 km along strike. Under the JORC 2012 Code, the Mulgine Trench deposit contains approximately 247 million tonnes of resources hosting about 270,000 tonnes of tungsten (as scheelite) and 69,000 tonnes of molybdenum. The Mulgine Hill deposit contains approximately 12.3 million tonnes at an average grade of about 0.16% WO₃. Overall, the Mt Mulgine Project hosts approximately 259 million tonnes of resources at an average grade of 0.11% WO₃, with associated molybdenum, copper, gold and silver. Tungsten Resources Across Mt Mulgine Tenure According to the PFS, the base-case scenario is designed for an annual processing rate of 8 million tonnes of ore, with an initial capital expenditure of approximately A$870 million and a mine life of about 21.9 years. Using a forecast APT price of US$1,509/mtu, the project delivers a pre-tax net present value (NPV) of A$6.823 billion (at an 8% discount rate) and an internal rate of return (IRR) of 55%. Under a spot APT price scenario of US$3,088/mtu, the pre-tax NPV rises to A$15.553 billion with an IRR of 113%. The project is scheduled to commence production in the second quarter of 2029. A second stage expansion, planned for 2034, would increase the processing rate to 16 million tonnes per annum and require additional capital of approximately A$420 million, extending the remaining mine life to 14 years. Under the expansion scenario, the forecast-price case yields a pre-tax NPV of approximately A$8.195 billion and an IRR of about 57%; at spot prices the pre-tax NPV is approximately A$18.351 billion with an IRR of about 113%. On a contained-metal basis, the Mt Mulgine Project is planned to produce a total of 123,796 tonnes of tungsten, 67.6 million pounds of molybdenum, 43.08 million pounds of copper, 180,966 ounces of gold and 9.94 million ounces of silver over its life. Under the base-case design, average annual production is approximately 5,653 tonnes of tungsten, 3.09 million pounds of molybdenum, 1.97 million pounds of copper, 8,263 ounces of gold and 453,872 ounces of silver, with a by-product credit WO₃ cost of US$127/mtu. After the expansion, average annual production rises to 8,843 tonnes of tungsten, 4.83 million pounds of molybdenum, 3.08 million pounds of copper, 13,000 ounces of gold and 709,985 ounces of silver, with a by-product credit WO₃ cost of US$103/mtu.
