title: Is the Arc Starting Voltage of Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes High?
text: Arc starting voltage is a core electrical parameter for measuring the ease of arc initiation of electrodes, affecting the start-up efficiency of welding processes and the reliability of automated welding. Due to the functional doping of cerium oxide, CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes exhibit clear advantages and boundary conditions in arc starting performance. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Numerical positioning and reference system of the arc starting voltage of cerium-tungsten electrodes The typical arc starting voltage of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes (WC20 grade, CeO₂ content 1.8%–2.2%) is 12 V, which can be obtained under DC positive polarity (DCEN) conditions, placing it at a relatively low level among rare earth tungsten electrodes. Placing this value in a reference system makes its performance advantages clearer: the arc starting voltage of pure tungsten electrodes is significantly higher than that of rare earth-doped electrodes, making it difficult to start an arc at room temperature without high-frequency auxiliary devices. The arc starting voltage of thoriated tungsten electrodes is approximately 30 V, about 2.5 times that of cerium-tungsten electrodes. II. Physicochemical mechanism of the reduction of arc starting voltage of cerium-tungsten electrodes The significant reduction in arc starting voltage of cerium-tungsten electrodes originates from the electronic structure modification caused by cerium oxide doping, which can be attributed to the following two pathways: Direct effect of work function reduction. The electron work function is positively correlated with arc starting voltage: the lower the work function, the smaller the potential barrier for electrons to escape from the electrode surface, and the correspondingly lower the applied voltage required for arc starting. The electron work function of cerium-tungsten electrodes is 2.4–2.8 eV, significantly lower than the 4.5–4.55 eV of pure tungsten. The reduction in work function allows cerium-tungsten electrodes to obtain sufficient thermionic emission current under relatively low open-circuit voltage, achieving rapid arc starting. Simultaneous decrease in cathode voltage drop. The cathode voltage drop is the potential difference required to maintain electron emission in the cathode region of the arc, and its value is closely related to the emission efficiency of the electrode material. The cathode voltage drop of cerium-tungsten electrodes is approximately 12.0 V, about 1 V lower than that of thoriated tungsten electrodes (13.0 V). This difference is particularly critical during the arc starting stage: the lower cathode voltage drop means that cerium-tungsten electrodes can cross the emission threshold more quickly after voltage application and enter a stable arc discharge state. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Dependence of the arc starting voltage of cerium-tungsten electrodes on operating conditions The arc starting voltage value of 12 V for CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is not a fixed constant, but a parameter that changes dynamically with current polarity, electrode diameter, and welding mode. DC positive polarity mode is the optimal operating condition for the arc starting performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes. Under this polarity, the electrode serves as the cathode receiving positive ion bombardment, with the highest thermionic emission efficiency, and the minimum arc starting voltage of 12 V is measured under this mode. This characteristic gives cerium-tungsten electrodes outstanding arc starting sensitivity in low-current DC welding (5–20 A range), capable of arc initiation without high-frequency arc starting assistance, with a re-arc starting success rate also at a relatively high level. Under DC reverse polarity (DCEP) and AC modes, the arc starting voltage shows an increasing trend. In DCEP mode, the electrode serves as the anode receiving electron bombardment, the thermal load mechanism reverses, and the arc starting voltage rises to the 15–20 V range. In AC mode, due to the periodic reversal of current polarity, the electrode bears the anode thermal load during the positive half-cycle, and the arc starting voltage further rises to 15–25 V, slightly higher than the 12–20 V of thoriated tungsten electrodes in AC mode. This difference indicates that the arc starting advantage of cerium-tungsten electrodes narrows in AC welding scenarios. The influence of electrode diameter should also not be ignored. Experiments show that under large diameter (≥2.4 mm) conditions, the minimum stable arc starting current of cerium-tungsten and thoriated tungsten electrodes tends to converge; as the diameter decreases (≤2.0 mm), the arc starting performance advantage of cerium-tungsten electrodes gradually appears. This phenomenon is closely related to the high mobility of cerium: the smaller the diameter, the shorter the diffusion path of cerium atoms to the tip surface, and the higher the formation efficiency of the low-work-function surface layer.

title: Are Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes Suitable for AC Welding?
text: Compared with DC welding, the current direction changes periodically during AC TIG welding, and the cerium-tungsten electrode and workpiece bear thermal loads at different stages, thus imposing certain requirements on the heat resistance, electron emission capability, and tip stability of the electrode material. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Application of cerium-tungsten electrodes in AC welding CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes have good electron emission characteristics and can participate in periodic arc discharge under AC TIG welding conditions. During AC TIG welding, the current direction changes periodically between positive and negative half-cycles. When the tungsten electrode is in the cathode state, the electrode needs to emit electrons; when the tungsten electrode is in the anode state, the thermal load on the electrode increases significantly. Since cerium-tungsten electrodes contain cerium oxide, they have good electron emission capability, thus offering certain advantages in the establishment and maintenance of AC arcs. However, there are obvious differences between AC welding and DC welding. Under DC positive polarity conditions, the tungsten electrode mainly serves as the cathode, and the electrode thermal load is relatively low; during AC welding, the polarity of the tungsten electrode changes continuously, and its temperature variation and thermal load distribution are more complex. Therefore, the same specification of cerium-tungsten electrode may show different working states under AC and DC conditions. For materials such as aluminum and aluminum alloys, magnesium and magnesium alloys, AC TIG welding has relatively important application value. These materials usually have oxide films with relatively high melting points on their surfaces, and the cathode cleaning effect of the AC arc can help remove or weaken the influence of the oxide film on the welding process. Therefore, cerium-tungsten electrodes have a certain application basis in related AC welding scenarios. However, if the welding current is relatively high and the continuous working time is long, the thermal load at the tungsten electrode tip will increase significantly. At this time, more attention should be paid to the electrode diameter, tip shape, and high-temperature stability of the material. II. Arc shape and cerium-tungsten electrode characteristics in AC welding When CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes are used for AC TIG welding, the arc shape is affected by the change in current direction. The AC arc does not always maintain the same discharge state, but changes with the AC cycle. When the tungsten electrode is in the cathode state, electrons are emitted from the tungsten electrode surface and enter the arc region. Cerium oxide can improve the electron emission conditions, giving cerium-tungsten electrodes good arc starting and arc maintaining capability. For AC welding, this electron emission characteristic helps maintain arc continuity. When the current direction changes and the tungsten electrode enters the anode state, the heat absorbed by the electrode increases. Since AC welding has periodic thermal load changes, the electrode tip temperature changes with the current waveform. If the welding current is relatively high, the electrode tip may experience significant temperature rise, thereby affecting the shape stability of the tungsten electrode tip. The arc of cerium-tungsten electrodes generally has good stability, but the actual arc column shape is also related to AC frequency, current waveform, peak current, and arc length. Increasing the AC frequency can change the contraction and diffusion state of the arc; changing the AC waveform changes the heat distribution between the tungsten electrode and the workpiece in different half-cycles. Therefore, the arc performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes in AC welding cannot be attributed solely to cerium oxide. The electrode material, power source parameters, shielding gas, and electrode tip geometry together constitute the actual arc working conditions. For precision AC TIG welding requiring a relatively stable arc, reasonable control of the electrode tip shape and arc length can improve the degree of arc concentration. An excessively long arc may cause arc column diffusion, while overheating at the electrode tip may cause tip shape changes, causing the arc root position to fluctuate. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Thermal load issues of cerium-tungsten electrodes during AC welding Compared with DC positive polarity, cerium-tungsten electrodes need to withstand more complex thermal load changes during AC welding, which is an important issue to consider when selecting electrodes. Under DC positive polarity conditions, the tungsten electrode is connected to the negative terminal and the workpiece to the positive terminal, with a relatively large proportion of heat acting on the workpiece, and the thermal load at the tungsten electrode tip is relatively low. During AC welding, the tungsten electrode and workpiece change polarity periodically, so the tungsten electrode bears a relatively high thermal load during part of the AC cycle. When the current is relatively high, the electrode tip temperature may rise significantly. If the electrode diameter is too small, the current load per unit cross-sectional area is relatively high, easily causing tip overheating. Long-term continuous welding may also produce heat accumulation, gradually blunting or causing localized deformation of the tungsten electrode tip. Therefore, when cerium-tungsten electrodes are used for AC welding, it is generally necessary to select an electrode diameter that matches the welding current. Relatively smaller diameter electrodes can be chosen for lower currents, while under higher current conditions, the electrode size should be appropriately increased according to the equipment and welding material. The electrode tip shape also needs to be adjusted according to AC welding conditions. DC TIG welding generally uses a tungsten electrode tip with a certain taper angle, while during AC welding, the stability of the electrode tip under high-temperature conditions needs to be considered. If the electrode tip becomes significantly rounded, the arc may diffuse, and the heat distribution in the welding area will also change. In addition, waveform control of the AC power source also has an effect. Modern TIG welding machines can usually adjust AC frequency, AC balance, and waveform parameters, thereby changing the heat distribution between the electrode and the workpiece. By reasonably adjusting these parameters, the tungsten electrode thermal load can be controlled while meeting the oxide film cleaning requirements. IV. Applicable scope and selection recommendations for cerium-tungsten electrodes in AC welding CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes can be used for AC TIG welding, especially in applications with medium to low currents and requirements for arc starting and arc maintaining performance. For thin-plate aluminum alloys, magnesium alloys, and other materials suitable for AC TIG welding, cerium-tungsten electrodes can be selected according to actual process conditions. However, from a professional selection perspective, "can be used for AC welding" should not be equated with "most suitable for all AC welding conditions." AC welding has relatively high requirements for the heat resistance of the tungsten electrode, especially under high-current conditions, where the electrode tip needs to withstand significant thermal loads. Therefore, in high-current, long-duration continuous AC welding, the performance characteristics of different electrode materials such as cerium-tungsten and lanthanum-tungsten should be comprehensively compared. For cerium-tungsten electrodes, their advantages mainly come from the electron emission performance brought by cerium oxide. Under low to medium current conditions, this characteristic helps improve arc establishment and stable maintenance. For AC TIG applications requiring frequent start-stop, fine control, and relatively low welding currents, cerium-tungsten electrodes have certain applicability.

title: Are Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes Suitable for DC Welding?
text: CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes are mainly used in tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding. From the perspective of current form, TIG welding can generally be divided into DC welding and AC welding. DC welding also involves different connection methods such as DC positive polarity (DCEN) and DC reverse polarity (DCEP). Among these, cerium-tungsten electrodes are more commonly used under DC positive polarity conditions. In this connection mode, the tungsten electrode serves as the cathode, electrons mainly move from the tungsten electrode toward the workpiece, and the electrode bears a relatively moderate thermal load, which is conducive to maintaining the tungsten electrode tip shape and arc stability. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Therefore, from the perspective of common welding applications, cerium-tungsten electrodes are suitable for DC welding, especially for DC positive polarity TIG welding. However, the specific use effect still depends on process conditions such as welding current, electrode diameter, tip grinding method, shielding gas, and the material being welded. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Why are cerium-tungsten electrodes suitable for DC welding? CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes are suitable for DC welding due to their material composition and electron emission characteristics. Tungsten itself has a high melting point and good high-temperature stability, capable of withstanding the high-temperature arc action during TIG welding; cerium oxide can improve the electron emission capability of the electrode. During DC TIG welding, the establishment and maintenance of the arc are closely related to cathode electron emission. When the cerium-tungsten electrode serves as the cathode, cerium oxide can reduce the difficulty for electrons to escape from the electrode surface, making the electron emission process easier. Therefore, compared with pure tungsten electrodes, cerium-tungsten electrodes generally have better arc starting and arc maintaining performance under lower current conditions. This characteristic makes cerium-tungsten electrodes particularly suitable for low-current and medium-to-low-current DC welding. For example, during TIG welding of thin plates, precision parts, and small metal components, the welding current generally needs to be controlled at a relatively low level, at which time the electrode's electron emission performance has more obvious process value. At the same time, under DC positive polarity conditions, the arc can maintain good directionality. With a reasonably ground cerium-tungsten electrode, the arc root is generally concentrated near the tungsten electrode tip, conducive to forming a relatively stable arc column. For welding processes that require control of weld width and heat input, this arc characteristic has certain advantages. II. DC positive polarity is a common working mode for cerium-tungsten electrodes In DC positive polarity (DCEN) TIG welding, the cerium-tungsten electrode is connected to the negative terminal of the power source, and the workpiece is connected to the positive terminal. Electrons mainly move from the tungsten electrode toward the workpiece, the electrode receives relatively low heat, while the workpiece receives a relatively high proportion of heat. This heat distribution is more suitable for tungsten electrode operation. On the one hand, tungsten has a high melting point and can remain stable in the high-temperature arc environment; on the other hand, the lower electrode thermal load is conducive to reducing electrode tip overheating, deformation, and burning loss. CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes themselves have good electron emission capability, so they can more easily form a stable arc under DC positive polarity conditions. Especially in the low-current range, the electron emission characteristics brought by cerium oxide can be more fully utilized. In terms of arc shape, DC positive polarity generally forms an arc column with good directionality. Current passes through the tungsten electrode tip concentratedly into the arc space, forms a plasma conductive channel through shielding gases such as argon, and finally acts on the workpiece surface. For materials that can use DC TIG welding, such as stainless steel, carbon steel, nickel-based alloys, and titanium alloys, cerium-tungsten electrodes can be selected according to specific current ranges and welding requirements. Especially in applications requiring more concentrated arcs and smaller heat-affected zones, DC positive polarity has good process adaptability. However, electrode diameter and welding current must be reasonably matched. When the current is too high, even with DC positive polarity, the electrode tip may still experience temperature rise, tip deformation, or increased tungsten electrode consumption. Therefore, current selection cannot be determined independently of electrode specifications. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. What are the differences between DC welding and AC welding of cerium-tungsten electrodes? There are obvious differences between DC and AC TIG welding in current direction and electrode thermal load, so the working state of cerium-tungsten electrodes under the two conditions also differs. During DC welding, the current direction remains relatively stable, the arc state is generally more continuous, and the thermal state at the electrode tip is also easier to control. For cerium-tungsten electrodes, this working condition is conducive to exerting their electron emission characteristics and maintaining a relatively stable arc column. AC TIG welding has periodic current direction changes. During part of the AC cycle, the tungsten electrode is in the cathode state; during another part, it is in the anode state. Because the current direction changes, the heat distribution between the electrode and the workpiece also changes accordingly. Therefore, it cannot be simply said that DC is more suitable for cerium-tungsten electrodes than AC. The two correspond to different welding materials and process requirements. For DC TIG welding where arc concentration, low-current stability, and relatively high thermal efficiency are the main requirements, cerium-tungsten electrodes have good applicability; for materials such as aluminum and magnesium that require cathode cleaning action, AC mode should be selected according to welding equipment and process requirements. IV. How to select parameters when performing DC welding with cerium-tungsten electrodes? When performing DC welding with CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes, reasonable electrode specifications and welding parameters play an important role in exerting their performance. First, the electrode diameter should be selected according to the welding current. Small-diameter electrodes are suitable for lower-current welding, conducive to forming a concentrated arc; as the welding current increases, the electrode diameter should be correspondingly increased to reduce the current load per unit cross-sectional area. Second is electrode tip grinding. DC TIG welding generally uses a tapered tip so that the arc can be stably drawn from the tungsten electrode tip area. The tip angle affects the degree of arc concentration and the heat distribution on the workpiece surface, so it needs to be adjusted according to the welding current and weld requirements. Shielding gas should also not be overlooked. Argon is a commonly used shielding gas in TIG welding. An appropriate gas flow rate can maintain a stable shielding layer and reduce air entry into the arc area. Too low a gas flow rate may result in insufficient shielding, while too high a flow rate may form turbulence, affecting arc stability. Arc length also needs reasonable control. When the arc length is short, the arc is generally more concentrated; when the arc length is too long, the arc column diffusion may increase and the arc's concentrated effect on the welding area may decrease.

title: How Is the High-Temperature Creep Resistance of Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: The so-called high-temperature creep refers to the slow, continuous plastic deformation of a material over time under relatively high temperatures and sustained stress. For cerium-tungsten electrodes, this deformation is mainly manifested as gradual changes in the electrode tip shape under high-temperature working conditions. If the electrode is subjected to excessively high thermal loads for extended periods, tip blunting, bending, localized deformation, or burning loss may occur, thereby changing the arc shape. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes' creep resistance is mainly built upon the high-temperature performance of the tungsten matrix, while also being affected by factors such as cerium oxide addition, grain structure, manufacturing process, electrode dimensions, and actual welding parameters. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. The tungsten matrix endows cerium-tungsten electrodes with good high-temperature stability Tungsten is the main constituent material of cerium-tungsten electrodes and the basis of their high-temperature performance. Tungsten has a melting point of approximately 3422°C, making it a high-melting-point material among metals, while also having good high-temperature strength retention capability. These characteristics enable tungsten electrodes to adapt to the relatively high electrode working temperatures during TIG welding. It should be noted that high melting point and creep resistance are not completely identical concepts. The melting point of a material reflects the temperature at which it transitions from solid to liquid, while creep is a time-dependent deformation of the material under sustained stress in a high-temperature environment below the melting point. Even if the material is still far from its melting point, different degrees of creep may occur. For cerium-tungsten electrodes, the arc heat is concentrated at the electrode tip during welding, making the tip temperature significantly higher than other areas of the electrode. At relatively low or appropriate welding currents, the tungsten matrix can maintain relatively stable structure and shape, and the electrode tip is not prone to obvious deformation due to continuous thermal effects. As the temperature further increases, the plastic deformation capability of tungsten material gradually increases, and the creep rate is also affected. Therefore, the actual creep resistance of the electrode is closely related to the working temperature. For the same cerium-tungsten electrode, under different welding currents and continuous working times, the degree of high-temperature deformation may vary significantly. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes II. Effect of welding temperature and current on the creep resistance of cerium-tungsten electrodes The high-temperature creep resistance of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes has distinct operating condition characteristics, among which temperature is an important factor affecting creep behavior. Under otherwise similar conditions, the higher the electrode working temperature, the greater the likelihood of deformation under long-term high-temperature effects. Welding current affects the thermal load at the electrode tip. Under low-current conditions, the heat input to the electrode is relatively low, and the tungsten matrix can maintain good shape stability. Cerium-tungsten electrodes have good application adaptability in this working range. When the welding current continuously increases, the electrode tip temperature rises, and the high-temperature deformation mechanisms inside the material become more active. If the electrode diameter is too small while the welding current is relatively high, the current load per unit cross-sectional area increases, and the electrode tip is more prone to overheating. After prolonged operation, tip rounding, localized deformation, or even burning loss may occur. The matching between electrode diameter and welding current is therefore very important. Reasonable electrode specifications can keep the current load within an appropriate range, helping to control electrode temperature rise. At the same time, the grinding angle and blunt end size of the electrode tip also change the thermal interaction area between the arc and the electrode, thereby affecting local temperature distribution. Current polarity also affects the thermal load on the electrode. Under different current modes, the heat distribution between the electrode and the workpiece differs, so the actual working temperature of cerium-tungsten electrodes also changes. The thermal state of the electrode under AC welding and DC welding conditions is not exactly the same, and the specific power source mode should be considered when selecting electrode specifications. In addition to current, welding time and duty cycle also have effects. During short-time welding, the heat accumulation on the electrode is limited; continuous long-time welding may form more significant heat accumulation, keeping the electrode in a high-temperature state for extended periods. Therefore, for applications such as continuous automated welding and high-current welding, more attention should be paid to the long-term thermal stability of the electrode.

title: How Is the Thermal Conductivity of Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes are non-radioactive rare earth tungsten electrodes made by incorporating 1.8%–2.2% cerium oxide into a high-purity tungsten matrix through powder metallurgy, high-temperature sintering, and swaging and drawing processes. They are widely used in industrial scenarios such as tungsten inert gas welding and plasma welding. Thermal conductivity is a core thermal parameter of cerium-tungsten electrodes, affecting electrode heat transport, tip temperature distribution, burning rate, current-carrying upper limit, arc shape, and weld formation quality. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Basic thermal conductivity parameters and temperature dependence of cerium-tungsten electrodes The room-temperature thermal conductivity of the pure tungsten matrix is approximately 170 W/(m·K). As a body-centered cubic refractory metal, it relies on free electrons and lattice vibration to complete heat transfer, possessing a relatively prominent thermal conductivity level among refractory metals. The cerium oxide dispersed in cerium-tungsten electrodes is a ceramic phase with thermal conductivity much lower than that of metallic tungsten. The second-phase particles dispersed at tungsten grain boundaries and within grains hinder phonon scattering, causing the overall thermal conductivity of cerium-tungsten electrodes to decrease slightly compared with pure tungsten, with a typical room-temperature thermal conductivity range of 145–158 W/(m·K). CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes exhibit significant temperature dependence of thermal conductivity. As temperature increases, metal lattice thermal vibration intensifies, electron scattering effects increase, and thermal conductivity gradually decreases. In the welding arc operating range of 1000–2500°C, the thermal conductivity of cerium-tungsten electrodes continues to decay. At high temperatures, lattice scattering dominates, and the scattering effect caused by cerium oxide particles is further amplified. In the tip working area approaching the tungsten melting point of 3410°C, the material's thermal conductivity significantly decreases, heat transfer efficiency to the electrode tail declines, and a large amount of heat accumulates in the tip cathode spot area. This thermal characteristic, combined with the low work function characteristic of cerium-tungsten electrodes, ensures continuous electron emission under low-current conditions. At the same time, the coefficient of thermal expansion of cerium-tungsten electrodes is maintained at 4.5×10⁻⁶/K, which is a low thermal expansion level. During thermal conduction and temperature transfer, thermal stress remains within a controllable range, reducing the risk of cracking failure under thermal cycling. II. Microscopic mechanism of thermal conductivity performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes The heat conduction of cerium-tungsten electrodes is mainly carried by free electrons in the tungsten matrix. The dispersed cerium oxide second phase, grain boundaries, and internal pores are the three major microscopic factors affecting thermal conductivity. Cerium oxide particles, distributed at tungsten grain boundaries and within grains at nano- to micron-scale, form phonon scattering interfaces at the ceramic-metal interface, hindering the heat transfer path of lattice vibration. This is the core reason why the thermal conductivity of cerium-tungsten is lower than that of pure tungsten. The doping amount of cerium oxide has a certain effect on thermal conductivity: the higher the cerium oxide proportion, the greater the number of second-phase interfaces, and the greater the decrease in thermal conductivity. During high-temperature welding cycles, heat conduction behavior undergoes dynamic changes accompanying structural evolution. Under long-term high-temperature service, cerium oxide undergoes directional migration, gradually enriching toward the cathode spot area at the electrode tip. The local proportion of cerium oxide in the tip area increases, local thermal conductivity further decreases, intensifying the heat storage effect at the tip, which is conducive to maintaining arc ignition. However, excessive local heat storage also increases the probability of tip burning loss and nodulation, causing arc drift. At the same time, tungsten grain growth at high temperatures reduces the number of grain boundaries, which to some extent weakens the grain boundary scattering effect and provides a small compensatory effect on thermal conductivity. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Effect of thermal conductivity performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes on welding engineering applications The thermal conductivity performance of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes affects electrode current-carrying capacity, tip temperature field distribution, burning rate, and arc stability, serving as an important underlying basis for process selection and parameter formulation. Thermal conductivity affects the heat dissipation efficiency of the electrode. When welding current increases, arc heat input increases, and heat is conducted to the electrode clamping end through heat conduction, combined with water cooling or air cooling of the welding torch for heat dissipation. Under limited thermal conductivity conditions, when the current exceeds the electrode's allowable threshold, the tip temperature rises rapidly, causing tip melting, balling, and flowering failure. Good thermal conductivity can reduce the overall electrode temperature, slow down tungsten matrix evaporation loss, and extend electrode service life; however, the relatively low thermal conductivity of cerium-tungsten electrodes keeps the tip at a higher temperature, obtaining lower arc starting voltage and excellent re-arc starting performance, which is also an important reason why cerium-tungsten electrodes are widely used in thin plate precision welding and pipe welding scenarios. In engineering applications, thermal conductivity constrains electrode diameter selection. Small-diameter cerium-tungsten electrodes have limited heat dissipation cross-sections and short heat conduction paths, making them more suitable for low-current welding; large-diameter electrodes have larger heat conduction cross-sections, lower heat flux density, and can withstand larger welding currents. At the same time, thermal conductivity characteristics also impose requirements on welding torch cooling. Insufficient cooling conditions cause heat accumulation, and even with reasonable electrode specification selection, rapid tip burning loss still occurs.

title: How Is the Electrical Conductivity of Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: Due to tungsten's high melting point, good high-temperature strength, and certain electrical conductivity, CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes can maintain good working stability in high-temperature arc environments. Evaluating the electrical conductivity of cerium-tungsten electrodes requires distinguishing between the material's own electrical conductivity and the conductive, arc starting, and arc maintaining performance during the welding process. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes Cerium-tungsten electrodes do not achieve good welding performance by improving material electrical conductivity, but rather use cerium oxide to improve the electron emission characteristics of the tungsten electrode, allowing the electrode to more easily establish and maintain an arc even under lower current conditions. Therefore, the electrical conductivity of cerium-tungsten electrodes should be analyzed in combination with material composition, electrode temperature, current density, and actual welding conditions. I. The electrical conductivity of cerium-tungsten electrodes mainly comes from the tungsten matrix The main material of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is metallic tungsten. Tungsten is a metal with good electrical conductivity, and its resistivity is significantly lower than that of insulating or semiconducting materials such as ceramics and oxides. Therefore, cerium-tungsten electrodes can carry welding current and concentrate the current delivery to the electrode tip to form an arc. However, cerium-tungsten electrodes are not pure tungsten material. A certain proportion of cerium oxide is added during production, and cerium oxide itself is not a highly conductive metal material. Therefore, from a material composition perspective, adding cerium oxide is not for improving the overall electrical conductivity of cerium-tungsten electrodes. The main role of cerium oxide in cerium-tungsten electrodes is to improve the electron emission characteristics of the electrode. During welding, the temperature at the tungsten electrode tip rises, and electron emission occurs under the action of the electric field and high temperature. The electrons enter the shielding gas and participate in arc discharge. Cerium oxide can reduce the difficulty for electrons to escape from the electrode surface, allowing the electrode to have good electron emission capability even under lower working currents. Therefore, from a materials science perspective, cerium-tungsten electrodes can be understood as composite electrodes where tungsten carries current conduction and cerium oxide improves electron emission. The functions of the two are not completely identical. In actual welding, current first enters the cerium-tungsten electrode through the welding torch and electrode holder, then transmits along the tungsten matrix to the electrode tip. When the electrode tip reaches an appropriate temperature and meets the discharge conditions, electrons enter the arc space from the electrode, forming a stable plasma conductive channel. Therefore, when discussing the electrical conductivity of cerium-tungsten electrodes, it is not appropriate to judge their welding performance solely based on metal resistivity; attention should also be paid to their electron emission capability and working performance at high temperatures. II. The conductive performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes is closely related to arc starting performance In TIG welding, electrode conductivity and arc starting performance are two related but different concepts. Conductivity mainly describes the material's ability to transmit current, while arc starting performance is more related to electron emission on the electrode surface, ionization process, electric field strength, and welding power source characteristics. A typical characteristic of cerium-tungsten electrodes is that cerium oxide improves electron emission, giving them good arc starting and arc maintaining capability under lower current conditions. When the welding current is small, the thermal state at the electrode tip is relatively low. For pure tungsten electrodes, the electron emission conditions may be more stringent, while the cerium oxide in cerium-tungsten electrodes can improve this process, making it easier for electrons to escape from the electrode surface. It should be noted that this advantage of cerium-tungsten electrodes does not mean their material conductivity is necessarily higher than that of pure tungsten. In fact, cerium oxide is an added phase, and its existence mainly changes the electron emission behavior of the electrode, rather than simply improving the current transmission capability of the tungsten matrix. During the actual welding process, if there is poor contact between the electrode and the torch holder, or if the electrode surface has obvious contamination, oxides, or mechanical damage, even if the electrode itself has good conductivity, problems with unstable current transmission may occur. Therefore, when evaluating the conductive performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes, the internal conductive path of the material, the contact state between the electrode and the clamping system, and the arc formation process should all be considered simultaneously. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Current, electrode size, and temperature affect the working state of cerium-tungsten electrodes The actual conductive performance of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is not fixed, but is affected by factors such as current, electrode diameter, working temperature, and tip shape. First is the welding current. As the welding current increases, the current density through the electrode increases, and the electrode tip temperature also rises accordingly. At high temperatures, electron emission is more sufficient, and the arc can obtain higher energy input. If the current exceeds the range adapted to the electrode diameter and tip shape, it may cause electrode overheating, tip deformation, or even tungsten material loss. Second is the electrode diameter. Under the same welding current, the smaller the electrode diameter, the higher the current density per unit cross-sectional area generally; as the electrode diameter increases, the distribution conditions of current on the electrode cross-section change. Therefore, the electrode diameter needs to be reasonably matched with the welding current. The electrode tip shape also has an effect. TIG welding generally requires grinding the tungsten electrode to form a geometry suitable for arc establishment at the tip. The tip angle, blunt end size, and surface grinding quality all change the degree of current concentration in the tip area and further affect the arc shape. In addition, electrode temperature also plays an important role. The cerium oxide in cerium-tungsten electrodes participates in the electron emission process during welding, so its performance is related to the thermal state of the electrode. At appropriate working temperatures, electron emission is more sufficient, conducive to maintaining a stable arc. Shielding gas conditions also need to be comprehensively considered. TIG welding generally uses inert gases such as argon or helium as shielding media. The gas type, flow rate, and nozzle structure affect the arc state, thereby affecting the actual working performance of the electrode. IV. What welding scenarios are the conductive characteristics of cerium-tungsten electrodes suitable for? With the good high-temperature conductivity of the tungsten matrix and the electron emission characteristics brought by cerium oxide, CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes have good application adaptability in low-current TIG welding. In thin plate welding, the welding current generally needs to be controlled in a relatively low range to reduce excessive heat input. At this time, the electrode's ability to stably start and maintain the arc is relatively high. The good electron emission capability of cerium-tungsten electrodes is conducive to establishing stable discharge under low-current conditions. In precision welding and small part processing, the arc needs to have good stability and controllability. Cerium-tungsten electrodes can select appropriate specifications according to welding materials, current ranges, and equipment conditions, and improve the arc state through reasonable grinding of the electrode tip.

title: How Is the Arc Shape of Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes are non-consumable electrodes made with tungsten as the matrix and a certain proportion of cerium oxide added, commonly used in welding processes such as TIG/GTAW. Their arc shape is not determined solely by the electrode material, but is affected by multiple factors including welding current, current polarity, shielding gas, electrode tip geometry, arc length, and workpiece material. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. With reasonable parameter matching, the arc generated by cerium-tungsten electrodes generally exhibits characteristics of relatively stable arc column, concentrated arc root, and good directionality, particularly suitable for thin plates, low currents, and welding scenarios with high requirements for arc control. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. How is the arc shape of cerium-tungsten electrodes? The arc of cerium-tungsten electrodes consists of the cathode region, arc column region, and anode region. During TIG welding, current passes through the shielding gas to form a high-temperature plasma, establishing a continuous conductive channel between the electrode and the workpiece. When observed with the naked eye, a bright arc column extending from the tungsten electrode tip toward the workpiece can usually be seen. One of the more obvious characteristics of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is the ability to maintain a relatively concentrated arc column under appropriate current conditions. Especially in DC TIG welding, when the electrode uses a suitable tip angle and blunt size, the arc is generally concentrated near the tungsten electrode tip and extends along the electrode axis toward the workpiece. Its shape is not completely fixed but changes with welding parameters. Visually, a stable cerium-tungsten arc generally presents a relatively continuous conical or columnar luminous region. The arc root near the electrode tip is relatively concentrated, and the arc column gradually expands toward the workpiece. As current increases, the heat input and plasma density of the arc increase, and the brightness, width, and action area on the workpiece surface of the arc column also change. It should be noted that arc concentration does not mean the arc always remains straight or fixed. The arc itself is a high-temperature plasma, and its shape is affected by factors such as argon flow field, electromagnetic forces, arc length, and workpiece temperature. Therefore, judgment of the cerium-tungsten arc shape should be analyzed in combination with specific welding conditions. II. Arc column stability and arc root shape of cerium-tungsten electrodes Arc stability is one of the important indicators for evaluating tungsten electrode performance. For cerium-tungsten electrodes, stable electron emission is conducive to maintaining a continuous discharge process, allowing the arc to remain relatively stable within normal welding parameter ranges. In DC positive polarity (DCEN) TIG welding, cerium-tungsten electrodes serve as the cathode, and electrons mainly move from the tungsten electrode to the workpiece. Since cerium can improve the electron emission characteristics of the tungsten electrode, cerium-tungsten electrodes generally have good arc starting and arc maintaining performance in low-current ranges. A stable arc root can reduce irregular arc swinging, allowing heat to act more concentratedly on the welding area. The state of the electrode tip has a significant effect on the arc root shape. For example, when the tip grinding is standardized, the arc generally forms a relatively concentrated discharge area along the electrode axis. If the tip angle changes significantly, the degree of arc column diffusion and heat distribution may also change accordingly. In actual welding, a sharper electrode tip does not necessarily mean a more stable arc. An overly sharp tungsten electrode may experience tip overheating, burning loss, or even end deformation under higher current conditions, causing the arc root position to change. Therefore, cerium-tungsten electrodes need to select appropriate tip geometry according to the current range. In addition, arc length is also an important factor affecting the shape. When the arc length is short, the arc is generally more concentrated, and the welding heat action area is relatively small; when the arc length increases, the arc column shows a more obvious diffusion trend, and arc stability may also be affected by shielding gas flow and external disturbances. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. How current, polarity, and shielding gas change the cerium-tungsten arc shape The arc shape of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is closely related to welding current. Under lower current conditions, cerium-tungsten electrodes have good electron emission capability and can establish a stable arc relatively easily. At this time, the arc column is generally thinner, and the heat-affected zone is relatively limited, making it suitable for thin plate and precision welding. As current increases, arc energy increases, and the arc column generally becomes brighter and thicker, while the action area on the workpiece surface also expands. If the electrode diameter, tip shape, and welding current are not reasonably matched, phenomena such as arc root expansion and increased electrode tip temperature may occur. Current polarity also significantly changes the arc shape. Under DC positive polarity conditions, the tungsten electrode acts as the cathode, and cerium-tungsten electrodes have good electron emission characteristics, thus obtaining relatively stable DC arcs. For welding scenarios requiring higher arc concentration, DC positive polarity generally has good adaptability. In AC TIG welding, the current direction changes periodically, and the thermal load on the electrode also changes accordingly. The arc shape at this time differs from DC conditions. Although cerium-tungsten electrodes can be used in some AC welding scenarios, the actual selection also needs to comprehensively consider factors such as current magnitude, power source waveform, workpiece material, and electrode diameter. Shielding gas mainly affects the stability and diffusion state of the arc column. Argon has a low ionization voltage and good shielding effect, making it a commonly used shielding gas in TIG welding. With appropriate gas flow rate, a relatively stable shielding atmosphere can be formed, allowing the arc column to remain relatively uniform. If the argon flow rate is too low, the welding area is susceptible to air interference, possibly causing arc instability; if the flow rate is too high, strong turbulence may be generated, causing disturbance to the arc column. Therefore, higher shielding gas flow is not always better; it should be matched with nozzle size, electrode extension length, and welding current. It can be seen that the cerium-tungsten electrode itself is only one factor affecting the arc shape. Only when electrode material, current parameters, power source polarity, shielding gas, and tip processing state are all matched can a relatively ideal arc state be formed. IV. What effect does the arc shape of cerium-tungsten electrodes have on welding results? The arc shape of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes ultimately affects heat input, molten pool size, and weld formation during the welding process. A relatively stable and concentrated arc can focus heat more effectively on the welding area, helping to control molten pool size during thin plate welding. In low-current TIG welding, if the arc frequently drifts or shows obvious fluctuation, the molten pool will be subjected to uneven heat, increasing welding difficulty. The good electron emission capability of cerium-tungsten electrodes improves arc starting and arc maintaining performance in low-current ranges, thus having certain application value in fine welding.

title: Is It Easy to Strike an Arc With Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: The ease of arc starting is an important indicator for measuring the engineering applicability of tungsten electrodes, relating to welding start-up efficiency, automated production tempo, and welding quality consistency. As a typical representative of rare earth tungsten electrodes, how is the arc starting capability of cerium-tungsten electrodes? CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Physicochemical basis of the arc starting performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes: low work function and low cathode voltage drop The essential root cause of the easy arc starting of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes lies in the deep modification of the electronic structure of the tungsten matrix by cerium oxide doping. The significant reduction in electron work function is the primary driving factor. The electron work function of pure tungsten is approximately 4.5–4.55 eV, making it difficult for electrons to be effectively emitted at room temperature, relying on high-temperature thermionic emission mechanisms to establish an arc. The typical electron work function of cerium-tungsten electrodes (WC20) is 2.4–2.8 eV, significantly lower than that of pure tungsten. The reduction in work function reduces the surface potential barrier that electrons need to overcome for escape, allowing sufficient thermionic emission current to be obtained under relatively low open-circuit voltage conditions, thereby achieving rapid arc starting. The simultaneous decrease in cathode voltage drop further reinforces this advantage. It has been determined that the cathode voltage drop of cerium-tungsten electrodes is 12.0 V. The cathode voltage drop is the potential difference required to maintain electron emission in the cathode region of the arc; the lower this value, the smaller the excitation voltage required for arc starting. Low work function and low cathode voltage drop together constitute the electrical basis for the easy arc starting of cerium-tungsten electrodes. In addition, under the high temperature of the arc, cerium elements migrate along grain boundaries to the tip surface and enrich there, forming a low-work-function chemically active surface layer, allowing the electrode to quickly enter a high-efficiency emission state in the initial stage of arc loading. This dynamic surface behavior gives cerium-tungsten electrodes excellent arc starting sensitivity in the initial stage of arc initiation. II. Quantitative evaluation of arc starting performance: comparison of minimum stable arc starting current The quantitative indicator of the ease of arc starting is the minimum stable arc starting current: the lower this value, the lower the current condition under which the electrode can establish and maintain a stable arc. Studies show that under the condition of an electrode diameter of 2.0 mm, the minimum stable arc starting current of thoriated tungsten electrodes is 6.0 A, while that of cerium-tungsten electrodes can be as low as 2.0 A. Under smaller diameter (1.0 mm) conditions, the minimum stable arc starting current of cerium-tungsten electrodes further decreases to 1.0 A, while thoriated tungsten electrodes remain at a relatively high level. Studies show that the arc starting performance of cerium-tungsten electrodes under small-diameter specifications is significantly superior to that of thoriated tungsten electrodes, with a higher arc starting success rate in the low-current range. However, this advantage has significant size dependence. When the electrode diameter increases to 5.0 mm, the minimum stable arc starting current of cerium-tungsten and thoriated tungsten electrodes tends to converge (100 A). This phenomenon is closely related to the high mobility characteristic of cerium: the smaller the diameter, the shorter the diffusion path of cerium atoms along grain boundaries to the tip surface, the higher the formation efficiency of the low-work-function surface layer, and the more fully the arc starting advantage is manifested. In terms of arc starting voltage, the minimum arc starting voltage of cerium-tungsten electrodes is 12 V, while that of thoriated tungsten electrodes is 30 V. The significant difference in arc starting voltage further verifies the advantageous position of cerium-tungsten electrodes in terms of ease of arc starting. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Process boundaries of arc starting performance: applicable scenarios and constrained conditions The arc starting advantage of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is not universally applicable to all welding conditions, but has clear process boundaries. Applicable scenarios: low-current DC positive polarity welding. In DC positive polarity mode, cerium-tungsten electrodes exhibit optimal arc starting performance, especially in low-current scenarios such as thin-plate stainless steel, titanium alloy welding, and fine precision components, with high arc starting sensitivity and high re-arc starting success rate, capable of arc initiation without high-frequency auxiliary devices. In situations requiring frequent arc starting and extinguishing such as automated welding and robotic welding, the low-current arc starting characteristic of cerium-tungsten electrodes significantly reduces the arc starting failure rate. Constrained conditions: AC welding and high-current conditions. Under AC TIG welding conditions, cerium-tungsten electrodes have a problem of being prone to splitting, and their arc starting performance and arc stability are inferior to thoriated tungsten or lanthanum-tungsten electrodes, so they are not recommended for AC welding of aluminum and magnesium alloys. Under high-current or long-term continuous operation conditions, the high mobility of cerium causes excessive enrichment of cerium oxide at the tip, the uniformity of active substances is destroyed, the electrode performance undergoes irreversible degradation, and the arc starting performance deteriorates accordingly.

title: How Is the Ablation Resistance of Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: The ablation resistance of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes is a core indicator for evaluating their engineering applicability, affecting electrode service life and welding process stability. Compared with pure tungsten electrodes and thoriated tungsten electrodes, cerium-tungsten electrodes, with the functional doping of cerium oxide (CeO₂), exhibit significantly optimized ablation resistance under suitable operating conditions. However, their ablation behavior is synergistically regulated by multiple factors and needs to be analyzed from dimensions such as material composition, operating conditions, and service environment. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Dose-effect relationship of cerium oxide content on the ablation resistance of cerium-tungsten electrodes Cerium oxide, as the core modifier of cerium-tungsten electrodes, has its doping concentration playing an important role in ablation resistance. However, this effect has a significant bidirectional nature, with an optimal concentration window matching specific operating conditions. Studies show that the melting point of cerium oxide (approximately 2673 K) is lower than that of tungsten trioxide, and tungstate low-melting-point phases may be formed in the high-temperature arc environment, and such compounds significantly reduce the heat resistance of the material. Production practice confirms that excessively high cerium oxide content reduces the ablation resistance and yield of the electrode at high temperatures. Through systematic comparative testing, cerium-tungsten electrodes with a mass fraction of 1% CeO₂ performed better in overall ablation resistance than products with 2% CeO₂. This counterintuitive phenomenon is attributed to the precipitation of low-melting-point eutectic phases by excessive cerium oxide at high temperatures, accelerating tip melting loss. However, in high-current plasma spraying comparison tests, the burning loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes with 4% CeO₂ was significantly better than that of the 2% specification, and the arc current fluctuation rate was one order of magnitude lower than that of 2% thoriated tungsten electrodes. The above results indicate that the optimal doping concentration varies with service current level, cooling conditions, and arc chamber atmosphere, and needs to be matched according to specific operating conditions. II. Mediating effect of shielding atmosphere and temperature field on burning loss The service environment has a significant mediating effect on the burning rate of cerium-tungsten electrodes. High-temperature oxidation is one of the main chemical paths leading to accelerated burning loss. Under argon shielding, CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes exhibit ablation resistance superior to pure tungsten, thoriated tungsten, and lanthanum-tungsten electrodes. However, in atmospheres with higher partial pressures of oxygen or water vapor, the high-temperature tungsten surface undergoes oxidation reactions, generating volatile WO₃, leading to continuous mass loss at the tip. Burning loss experiments show that cerium-tungsten electrodes show slight oxidation ring characteristics after arc burning, and the degree of oxidation deepens with extended burning time, indicating that the erosion of the electrode surface structure by oxidizing atmospheres has a time-accumulative effect. The distribution of the tip temperature field is equally critical. Along the axial direction of the tip, it can be divided into an evaporation zone, an enrichment protective layer zone, and a uniform doping reservoir zone. When the tip temperature exceeds 4000 K, the evaporation rate of cerium breaks through the supply limit of bulk diffusion, causing a decline in the surface active layer concentration and subsequent deterioration of ablation resistance. Therefore, maintaining high purity and an appropriate flow rate range of the shielding atmosphere is a necessary prerequisite for suppressing oxidative burning loss. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Dynamic supply mechanism and service life boundary The maintenance of the ablation resistance of cerium-tungsten electrodes relies on the dynamic supply mechanism of the cerium element during service, that is, the competitive process between the evaporation escape rate and the bulk diffusion supply rate. Under the high temperature of the arc, cerium atoms migrate along grain boundaries to the tip surface and enrich there, forming a low-work-function chemical barrier layer, which plays a key role in inhibiting further ablation of the matrix. After continuous operation, the evaporation and diffusion of cerium can reach a dynamic balance, and the burning rate tends to stabilize. However, as service time extends and grain growth occurs, migration efficiency significantly decreases. In terms of arc starting repetition count, CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes have a reference arc starting count of 1000–2500 times under normal conditions (DC/low-current welding), with sensitive arc starting, suitable for automated welding scenarios. Beyond this frequency, the surface active layer continues to thin, and ablation resistance undergoes irreversible degradation. Therefore, cerium-tungsten electrodes are suitable for short-cycle welding or automated welding scenarios with high requirements for arc starting frequency, while under high-current, long-term continuous service conditions, the sustainability of their performance advantages faces challenges.

title: What Factors Affect the Loss of Cerium-Tungsten Electrodes?
text: The loss rate of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes during service directly affects welding quality and production tempo. Compared with pure tungsten or thoriated tungsten electrodes, cerium-tungsten electrodes, with the modification effect of cerium oxide (CeO₂), exhibit excellent ablation resistance under most operating conditions. However, their loss behavior is not determined by a single factor, but is the result of the coupling of multiple variables including current parameters, material composition, atmosphere environment, and cooling conditions. CTIA GROUP and its parent company, CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, have been dedicated to the tungsten-molybdenum products industry for nearly 30 years. They specialize in providing flexible, customized global services for tungsten-molybdenum products, designing, manufacturing, and precisely processing various standard specifications, grades, and dimensional precision according to customer requirements, suitable for a wide range of applications. For more information on tungsten electrodes, please visit the website: http://www.tungsten.com.cn/tungsten-electrodes.html. If you require tungsten electrodes, please contact CTIA GROUP: sales@chinatungsten.com, 0592-5129595. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes I. Effect of current parameters and polarity on the loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes Current intensity is one of the electrical factors affecting the loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes. In the cathode region of the arc, the temperature can exceed 4000 K, and the evaporation and ablation rate at the electrode tip increases exponentially with current density. Studies show that for a 2.4 mm diameter cerium-tungsten electrode, below the critical current of 230 A, its burning loss is lower than that of lanthanum-tungsten and yttrium-tungsten electrodes; when the current exceeds this threshold, the loss disadvantage gradually becomes apparent. This indicates that under high-current conditions, the thermal load of cerium-tungsten electrodes has approached the limit of the dynamic balance of their active substances. Current polarity is equally critical. Under DC positive polarity (DCEN, electrode connected to negative), the tip mainly bears the combined effect of the cooling effect from thermionic emission and ion bombardment, with relatively moderate burning loss; DC reverse polarity (DCEP) makes the electrode serve as the anode receiving high-speed electron bombardment, the thermal load increases sharply, and the loss rate significantly accelerates. High-frequency arc starting has less impact on the electrode, while contact arc starting causes more severe mechanical wear. II. Effect of cerium oxide content and its distribution on the loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes Cerium oxide, as the core functional phase, has its content and distribution state as the chemical basis affecting the loss resistance of cerium-tungsten electrodes. However, this factor has the characteristic of "too much is as bad as too little." Excessive cerium oxide actually aggravates loss. The melting point of CeO₂ (approximately 2673 K) is lower than that of WO₃, and the tungstates that may be formed at arc high temperatures have even lower melting points. The Ce₂O₃ formed during hydrogen sintering also has the problem of insufficient high-temperature resistance. Production practice shows that excessively high cerium oxide content reduces the ablation resistance and yield of the electrode at high temperatures. In high-current plasma spraying comparison tests, the burning loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes with 4% CeO₂ was significantly better than that of the 2% specification, and the arc current fluctuation rate was 10 times lower than that of 2% tungsten-thorium electrodes. This shows that cerium oxide content is not lower the better, but there is an optimal window matching specific operating conditions (current level, cooling conditions). Too low doping results in insufficient active substance supply, while too high doping accelerates loss due to precipitation of low-melting-point phases. Pictures of CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes III. Effect of atmosphere environment and temperature field on the loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes The chemical activity of the service atmosphere has a direct effect on the loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes. Under argon shielding, CTIA GROUP's cerium-tungsten electrodes exhibit excellent ablation resistance, with a loss rate lower than that of pure tungsten, thoriated tungsten, lanthanum-tungsten, and neodymium-tungsten electrodes. However, when the atmosphere switches to nitrogen, Nd₂O₃ and La₂O₃ accelerate decomposition due to the strong oxidizing effect of nitrogen radicals, and the loss rate surpasses that of thoriated tungsten; cerium-tungsten electrodes still maintain the lowest loss rate under nitrogen, attributed to the higher chemical stability of CeO₂. The distribution of the temperature field is equally critical. Studies show that after operation under a 200 A DC arc, three functionally distinct temperature zones are formed along the axial direction of the cerium-tungsten electrode tip: Zone I (0-500 μm from the tip) is the Ce evaporation zone, where active substances volatilize in large quantities; Zone II (500-750 μm) is the Ce enrichment protective layer zone, forming a low-work-function barrier; Zone III (>750 μm) is the uniform doping reservoir zone, continuously supplying cerium to the high-temperature zone. When the tip temperature exceeds 4000 K, the evaporation rate breaks through the dynamic balance limit, causing the protective layer to fail. IV. Effect of cooling conditions on the loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes The heat dissipation conditions of the electrode and the supply-volatilization dynamic balance of cerium are the deep mechanisms affecting the long-term service loss of cerium-tungsten electrodes. Efficient cooling is an effective strategy to reduce loss. In plasma cutting, the water-cooled anode cools the cathode, on the one hand suppressing excessive evaporation and diffusion of active substances, and on the other hand causing the electrode tip to reach a dynamic balance of evaporation and condensation, forming a unique natural sharpening characteristic, thereby extending life. Conversely, when cooling is insufficient, the burning loss of bare tungsten electrodes is relatively large, attributed to the combined effect of cylindrical surface oxidation and tungsten oxide sublimation. The migration and valence transformation of cerium constitute the self-healing capability of loss. Under arc action, cerium undergoes a four-stage migration process of "rear-end supply → grain boundary diffusion → tip enrichment → surface volatilization."

title: Zimbabwe Bans Exports of Antimony and Tungsten
text: According to foreign media reports, Zimbabwe’s Ministry of Mines and Mining Development wrote to the state-owned Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe (MMCZ) on 21 July 2026, instructing it to “suspend, with immediate effect and until further notice, all exports of antimony and tungsten in any form, including ores and concentrates.” MMCZ is responsible for the marketing, sale and export of all minerals produced in Zimbabwe except gold and silver. No individual or company may export minerals independently without MMCZ authorisation or through its channels. MMCZ handles the full process, including contract negotiation, export clearance, logistics arrangements and inventory monitoring, and charges a commission for its services. Zimbabwe is richly endowed with mineral resources but has long relied mainly on the export of raw ores or concentrates, which generate relatively low added value. The export ban is reportedly intended to promote domestic value-added processing of the country’s mineral resources and to encourage mining companies to establish smelting and refining facilities locally in order to capture higher economic returns. Antimony and tungsten are both critical raw materials for industry and high-tech applications. Antimony is primarily used in flame retardants, lead-acid battery alloys, semiconductor materials and specialty glass. Tungsten, owing to its high melting point, high hardness and excellent wear resistance, is widely used in cemented carbide tools, high-temperature alloys, electronic components, military armour and armour-piercing materials, as well as in the nuclear industry and specialty steels. It is an indispensable strategic metal for modern manufacturing and defence industries. On 22 May 2026, Zimbabwe’s Ministry of Mines issued the Mineral Classification and Declaration, formally designating 14 minerals as critical minerals. These include lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, copper, rare earth elements, chromium, platinum group metals (PGMs), manganese, antimony, uranium, ruthenium, tungsten and niobium. The declaration requires that, without an approved transitional deep-processing plan and a clear domestic processing timeline authorised by the Minister, these minerals may not be exported in raw or unprocessed form. The state will also exercise mandatory minimum equity holdings through special-purpose vehicles (SPVs). China Tungsten Online notes that although Zimbabwe’s production of antimony and tungsten accounts for a relatively small share of global output and the direct impact on China’s raw-material supply is limited, the ban may cause short-term disruption to supply expectations and further reinforce the signal that African resource-rich countries are prioritising domestic processing. Tightening controls on tungsten resources worldwide are intensifying supply tightness in the global tungsten products market outside China and will also exert reverse pressure and provide support to the domestic market. According to data compiled by China Tungsten Online from the General Administration of Customs, in the first seven months of 2026 China imported 156.91 tonnes of tungsten ores and concentrates from Zimbabwe, accounting for 0.82% of total imports, and 54.87 tonnes of other antimony ores and concentrates, accounting for 0.08% of total imports.

title: What's Tungsten Alloy Radiation Shield?
text: Tungsten alloy radiation shield is manufactured through powder metallurgy using tungsten as base material, with nickel, iron, or copper serving as binder phases. Tungsten content generally ranges from 80% to 97%, with density typically ranging from 16.5–19.0 g/cm³, about 1.5 times that of lead. Tungsten’s high atomic number and high density strongly attenuate X-rays and gamma rays. Compared with lead, tungsten alloy enables thinner, more compact, stronger, corrosion-resistant, and stable structures without toxicity concerns.
