title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Threaded-Mount Thermocouples
text: Threaded-mount thermocouples (also known as fixed-thread or screw-in thermocouples) are a common type of assembled temperature sensor used in industrial applications. They are securely mounted and sealed by screwing a standard external thread—located at the end of the protective tube or on the connection head (e.g., M27×2, M33×2, G1/2, NPT)—into a pre-threaded hole on the equipment or piping. Tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) wire is frequently used as the thermoelement (thermocouple wire) for these sensors, making them particularly suitable for ultra-high-temperature operating conditions. Thanks to their extremely high melting points, favorable thermoelectric properties, and relatively low cost, tungsten-rhenium wires from CTIA GROUP serve as a key alternative to platinum-rhodium (noble metal) thermocouples and are widely used in vacuum furnaces, metallurgy, aerospace, and high-temperature industrial processes. 1. Basic Characteristics and Classification of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires Tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires consist of a matched pair of alloy wires made from tungsten (W) and rhenium (Re) in varying proportions; they generate thermoelectric potential based on the Seebeck effect. Common combinations include: Type C (WRe5/26): Positive leg approx. 95% W + 5% Re; negative leg approx. 74% W + 26% Re. Type D (WRe3/25): Positive leg approx. 97% W + 3% Re; negative leg approx. 75% W + 25% Re. Type A (WRe5/20): Positive leg approx. 95% W + 5% Re; negative leg approx. 80% W + 20% Re. These tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires all possess melting points exceeding 3000°C. Their theoretical upper temperature limit reaches 2500–2800°C, with a common industrial operating range of 0–2300°C and an optimal stability range of approximately 1300–2000°C. Their thermoelectric output is significantly higher than that of Type S or Type B platinum-rhodium thermocouples (approximately twice that of Type S and three times that of Type B), resulting in high sensitivity. The permissible deviation is typically ±4.0°C within the 0–400°C range, and ±0.25%t or ±0.5%t above 400°C (where *t* is the measured temperature). Common wire diameters range from 0.08 mm to 0.5 mm; thinner wires offer faster response times, while thicker wires provide greater durability. The material exhibits excellent chemical stability in vacuum, hydrogen, nitrogen, and inert atmospheres; however, in air or oxidizing atmospheres at high temperatures, it is highly susceptible to oxidation, grain growth, and failure, necessitating strict protective measures. 2. Structure of Thread-Mounted Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples The typical structure of a thread-mounted thermocouple comprises tungsten-rhenium thermoelements (with the measuring ends welded to form a hot junction), a protective tube, insulating materials, and a threaded mounting fitting. Protective tubes are commonly made from high-temperature materials such as molybdenum, tantalum, tungsten, corundum ceramics, or cermets; the interior is filled with highly insulating powders (e.g., beryllium oxide or aluminum oxide) and sealed to exclude air. The threaded section provides mechanical fixation and sealing (often utilizing asbestos rope or high-temperature refractory cement; standard PTFE tape is prohibited). The insertion depth is generally required to be 8–15 times the outer diameter of the protective tube to ensure the measuring junction is positioned within the main flow of the medium. 3. Application Advantages of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Ultra-high temperature capability: Capable of operating in ranges above 2000°C, where platinum-rhodium thermocouples struggle to maintain stability. Cost-effectiveness: Priced at approximately one-third of platinum-rhodium thermocouples; my country’s abundant tungsten resources ensure a high price-to-performance ratio. Response and strength: Thin wires offer rapid response; the alloy exhibits better ductility than pure tungsten and possesses high mechanical strength. Threaded mounting compatibility: Available in armored or assembled configurations, supporting mounting methods such as fixed threads or adjustable compression fittings. This facilitates easy installation, removal, and sealing, making them suitable for fixed measurement points in pipelines, reaction vessels, and high-temperature furnace bodies. 4. Applications of Thread-Mounted Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples Thread-mounted tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are secured to equipment or pipelines via standard threads, facilitating easy installation, removal, and sealing, and are widely used in ultra-high-temperature measurement applications. Primarily used in vacuum heat treatment furnaces, monocrystalline silicon growth furnaces, and high-temperature sintering equipment, it enables precise temperature monitoring above 2000°C. In the metallurgical industry, it is employed for the rapid measurement of molten steel and iron temperatures and for monitoring high-temperature smelting processes. In the aerospace sector, it monitors thermal environments such as rocket engines and combustion chambers. It is also suitable for applications in the nuclear industry and chemical kilns involving inert, reducing, or vacuum atmospheres. With oxidation-resistant protection, it can partially replace platinum-rhodium thermocouples, offering a balance of high-temperature performance and cost-effectiveness while enhancing the precision and safety of industrial process control. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires for Engine Exhaust Plume Temperature Measurement
text: During the development and testing of aero-engines, rocket engines, and hypersonic propulsion systems, the temperature of the exhaust plume is a critical parameter for evaluating combustion efficiency, thermal protection design, thrust performance, and structural safety. Exhaust plume temperatures often reach 1500–3000 K and are accompanied by high-speed gas flow erosion, intense vibration, corrosion from oxidizing combustion products, and drastic transient fluctuations, placing extremely high demands on temperature sensors. Traditional platinum-rhodium thermocouples have limited upper temperature ranges and high costs. While infrared optical thermometry offers non-contact measurement, its accuracy is often compromised by factors such as radiation characteristics, soot/particulates, and medium transparency. CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) thermocouple wires have become the preferred sensing material for contact-based engine exhaust plume temperature measurement due to their ultra-high melting points, high thermoelectric output, excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, and relatively low cost. my country has established the industry standard JB/T 14355-2023, "Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire for Engine Exhaust Plume Temperature Measurement," which standardizes product classifications (such as W-Re5/W-Re20), technical requirements, and inspection methods, thereby further promoting their engineering application in propulsion system testing. 1. Characteristics and Advantages of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire Tungsten (W) has a melting point of approximately 3422°C, and Rhenium (Re) has a melting point of approximately 3186°C. Thermocouple wires made from these alloys can operate for extended periods at temperatures between 2000°C and 2300°C—and even approach 3000°C for short durations—in vacuum, inert, or reducing atmospheres. Common pairings include W-5%Re/W-26%Re (Type C), W-3%Re/W-25%Re (Type D), and W-5%Re/W-20%Re (Type A). The addition of an appropriate amount of rhenium significantly mitigates the brittleness of pure tungsten wire while enhancing ductility, creep resistance, and the recrystallization temperature, thereby making the wire easier to draw, weld, and install. The tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires produced by CTIA GROUP exhibit a thermoelectric output significantly higher than that of platinum-rhodium series thermocouples. They offer sensitivity typically in the range of 15–20 μV/°C (in medium-to-high temperature zones) and rapid response times, making them ideal for capturing transient temperature fluctuations in engine exhaust plumes. Wires with diameters of 0.02 mm or less possess low thermal inertia, enabling response times ranging from milliseconds to microseconds—capabilities that meet the testing requirements for rapid processes such as ignition and acceleration. Compared to noble metal thermocouples, tungsten-rhenium wires offer lower costs and superior cost-performance ratios, making them suitable for use as disposable or expendable exhaust plume probes. 2. Application of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wires in Engine Exhaust Plume Temperature Measurement Engine exhaust plumes present extreme operating environments characterized by high-temperature, high-velocity gas flows, strong oxidizing conditions, particle erosion, and vibration. CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires are suitable for the following applications: (1) Single-point and multi-point contact temperature measurement: Probes fabricated from fine tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires are positioned along the plume's central axis and in the peripheral flame zones to directly measure local, actual temperatures. When paired with protective housings made of stainless steel or high-temperature alloys—featuring a constricted-opening design and ceramicized silicone rubber filling—these probes can withstand airflow impact and prevent short circuits. In practice, they are often used in conjunction with two-color infrared pyrometers to cover a broader temperature range (approximately 300–3300 K) and facilitate temperature field reconstruction. (2) Solid and liquid rocket engine testing: These wires are used for measuring gas temperatures and diagnosing conditions at the nozzle exit and within the plume. Armored or embedded tungsten-rhenium thermocouples can measure temperatures near the inner wall or within the flow field, providing data for ablation assessment and thermal protection system design. Enhanced thermocouples featuring multi-layer anti-oxidation coatings (such as a WSi₂ transition layer combined with a ZrO₂-Al₂O₃-SiO₂ ceramic barrier) can achieve a service life dozens of times longer than standard versions when operating in oxidizing environments at temperatures between 2000 K and 2700 K. (3) Aero-engines and scramjets: Used for temperature measurement at the combustor exit, downstream of the turbine, and at the exhaust nozzle. Thin-film or coaxial tungsten-rhenium thermocouples can further minimize flow field interference, enabling temperature monitoring at or near the wall surface. These applications directly support combustion efficiency assessment, thermal load calculation, and structural optimization, serving as vital tools for both ground-based engine testing and flight trials. The primary drawback of tungsten-rhenium wire is its susceptibility to oxidation. In air or oxidizing exhaust plumes, rapid formation of volatile oxides at high temperatures leads to failure. Engineering solutions typically include inert gas shielding, vacuum encapsulation, anti-oxidation coatings, ceramic protection tubes, double-layer sealed structures with oxygen-absorbing fillers, and specialized protective housing designs (featuring constricted inlets and exhaust vents) to reduce local oxygen partial pressure and flow impingement. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Surface Temperature Measurement Thermocouples
text: In modern high-temperature industrial processes and extreme-environment temperature measurement, accurate acquisition of surface temperature is critical for process control, equipment safety, and material performance evaluation. Conventional noble-metal thermocouples (such as platinum-rhodium types) offer good stability, yet their upper temperature limit is typically restricted to about 1800 °C and their cost is high. Tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) wire, as the key electrode material for refractory-metal thermocouples, has become the preferred solution for surface temperature measurement thermocouples operating in vacuum, inert, or reducing atmospheres. It combines an ultra-high melting point, excellent thermoelectric properties, and favorable cost-performance. Based on tungsten alloys with controlled rhenium additions that improve ductility and high-temperature stability, W-Re thermocouple wires are widely used in rapid steel-melt temperature measurement, vacuum-furnace monitoring, aero-engine exhaust-plume sensing, and spacecraft thermal testing. 1. Material Characteristics of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires are alloys of tungsten (W) and rhenium (Re). Common compositions use a positive leg containing 3 % or 5 % Re and a negative leg containing 25 % or 26 % Re, corresponding to types such as WRe3/25 (Type D) and WRe5/26 (Type C). Their melting points range from 3120 °C to 3360 °C. Long-term service temperatures extend from 0 °C to 2300 °C, with short-term capability exceeding this range. The material combines high mechanical strength, good ductility, and stable electrical performance: the Seebeck coefficient is approximately twice that of platinum-rhodium thermocouples, yielding high sensitivity; thermoelectric force deviation at 1200 °C can be kept to a low level. Wire diameters are typically 0.1–0.5 mm (tolerance ±0.02 mm), facilitating fine-diameter processing for rapid response and intimate surface contact. Pure tungsten wire is relatively brittle; the addition of rhenium markedly improves workability and resistance to recrystallization. However, W-Re wire oxidizes rapidly in oxidizing atmospheres and therefore must be used with protective sheaths or specialized coatings. 2. Advantages of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire in Surface Temperature Measurement Thermocouples Surface temperature measurement thermocouples require fast response, reliable contact with the measured surface, and stability under dynamic high-temperature conditions. Because of its low thermal mass, fine diameter, and high thermoelectric power, W-Re wire is particularly well suited to thin-film, coaxial, or rapidly consumable surface temperature measurement thermocouples. Response times are short, enabling capture of transient temperature changes. In vacuum or inert environments the material exhibits good chemical stability and strong thermal-shock resistance. Compared with non-contact infrared pyrometry, contact-type W-Re thermocouples measure true surface temperature directly, reducing errors arising from uncertain emissivity. With protective tubes (molybdenum, tantalum, silicon carbide, or molybdenum disilicide) or anti-oxidation coatings, selected products can be extended to short-term or moderate-temperature use in oxidizing atmospheres, further broadening the application range of surface temperature measurement. 3. Applications of Surface Temperature Measurement Thermocouples Using Tungsten-Rhenium Wire In the metallurgical industry, rapid-response thermocouples made from tungsten-rhenium wire produced by CTIA GROUP are widely employed for surface or liquid-level temperature measurement of molten steel and iron. Response times are only a few seconds, accuracy reaches the ±0.25 %t level, and cost is substantially lower than platinum-rhodium alternatives. In vacuum furnaces, high-temperature sintering furnaces, and silicon-carbide crystal-growth equipment, W-Re thermocouples directly monitor furnace-wall or workpiece surface temperatures, meeting the requirements of vacuum or reducing atmospheres up to 2300 °C. In aerospace applications they are used for surface-temperature acquisition on engine exhaust plumes, combustor walls, and spacecraft vacuum thermal tests under extreme conditions above 1600 °C. In nuclear and plasma devices, W-Re surface temperature measurement thermocouples measure high-heat-flux surfaces such as divertor target plates, offering erosion resistance and rapid response. In recent years, thin-film and coaxial W-Re thermocouples have advanced further; micro-pillar array gas-film structures or protective coatings enhance anti-adhesion and anti-oxidation performance, making them suitable for continuous steel-melt temperature measurement and high-heat-flux environments. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Assembled Thermocouples
text: Assembled thermocouples are widely used temperature sensors in industrial applications. They consist of a sensing element (such as tungsten-rhenium wire), an insulating sleeve, a protective tube, a terminal box, and mounting hardware. Capable of directly measuring the temperature of gases, liquids, or solid surfaces, they are typically used in conjunction with display instruments, recorders, or controllers. Tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) wire serves as the sensing element for high-temperature measurement; due to advantages such as a high melting point, high thermoelectric potential, high sensitivity, and relatively low cost, it is a critical material for measuring ultra-high temperatures (especially those exceeding 1500°C). It finds extensive application in metallurgy, vacuum furnaces, aerospace, refractory materials, and special atmospheric environments. 1. Basic Characteristics and Classification of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium wire is an alloy wire produced by adding rhenium (Re) to tungsten (W). The addition of rhenium creates the "rhenium effect," which significantly mitigates the brittleness of pure tungsten while enhancing ductility, recrystallization temperature, high-temperature strength, and thermoelectric properties. Common compositions include low-rhenium alloys (W-3%Re, W-5%Re) and high-rhenium alloys (W-25%Re, W-26%Re). Typical thermocouple pairings include: WRe3/25 (Type D): Positive electrode W-3%Re, negative electrode W-25%Re. WRe5/26 (Type C): Positive electrode W-5%Re, negative electrode W-26%Re. WRe5/20 (Type A): Positive electrode W-5%Re, negative electrode W-20%Re. The tungsten-rhenium wires produced by CTIA GROUP generally feature melting points exceeding 3000°C. They are suitable for long-term use at temperatures up to approximately 2300°C in vacuum, inert gas (argon, helium, etc.), or dry hydrogen environments, and can withstand even higher temperatures for short durations. They exhibit a high thermoelectric power rate (in the order of 15–20 μV/℃) and superior sensitivity compared to some platinum-rhodium thermocouples; furthermore, their cost is only one-half to one-quarter that of platinum-rhodium wire, offering a significant economic advantage. Wire diameters and dimensions can be customized to meet specific customer requirements or application scenarios. 2. Applications of Assembled Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples In the metallurgical industry, assembled tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are widely used in high-temperature smelting furnaces, molten steel temperature measurement, powder metallurgy sintering, and non-ferrous metal smelting processes. Tungsten-rhenium wires from CTIA GROUP offer rapid response times, enabling the quick capture of instantaneous temperature fluctuations in molten steel or high-temperature melts; this helps optimize smelting processes, improve product quality, and reduce energy consumption. Offering a clear cost advantage over traditional platinum-rhodium thermocouples, they have become a common alternative in vacuum induction furnaces and controlled-atmosphere furnaces. In the fields of aerospace and specialty materials—such as rocket engine nozzles, thermal protection systems for re-entry vehicles, plasma wind tunnels, and high-temperature structural material testing—monitoring temperatures exceeding 2000℃ is often required. Their assembled structure facilitates easy installation and mounting; when paired with protection tubes made of refractory metals (like molybdenum or tantalum) or composite ceramics, they operate stably in vacuum or inert atmospheres, providing reliable data for engine performance verification and material evaluation. In equipment for refractory materials, ceramic sintering, and crystal growth—including high-temperature kilns, single-crystal silicon/sapphire growth furnaces, and sintering furnaces for advanced ceramics like silicon carbide—vacuum or hydrogen-protected atmospheres are commonly used. CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wires withstand high thermal loads over long periods; designs incorporating solid-fill sealing or double-layer protection tubes effectively extend service life and reduce replacement frequency. Certain products treated for oxidation resistance (e.g., via coatings or airtight composite protection tubes) can even replace expensive dual platinum-rhodium thermocouples in mildly oxidizing atmospheres, such as those found in chrome-corundum production lines and other industrial kilns. Additionally, assembled tungsten-rhenium thermocouples find applications in the nuclear industry, high-temperature chemical reactors, vacuum heat-treatment furnaces, and high-temperature experimental apparatuses for scientific research. It features high mechanical strength and good thermal shock resistance; when paired with various mounting methods (such as threaded connections or flanges), it is suitable for applications involving high pressure, vibration, or complex spatial constraints. 3. Precautions for the Use of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium wire is highly susceptible to oxidative failure in high-temperature oxidizing atmospheres; therefore, strict isolation from oxygen is essential. It should be used in vacuum, reducing, or inert atmospheres. In oxidizing environments, protective measures such as dense, gas-tight protection tubes (e.g., molybdenum disilicide-corundum composite tubes), coatings, or sealing with insulating materials are required. At high temperatures, grain growth occurs; if the grain size approaches the wire diameter, the wire becomes brittle and prone to fracture. Consequently, operating temperatures and durations must be controlled, and annealed wire should be selected to enhance initial stability and toughness. Exposure to carbon-containing atmospheres at high temperatures causes corrosion and must be avoided. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Heating Furnace Thermocouples
text: Tungsten-rhenium wire from CTIA GROUP is a critical material in the field of high-temperature thermometry. Thermocouples made from this wire are widely used for temperature monitoring in various types of heating furnaces, vacuum furnaces, sintering furnaces, and ultra-high-temperature industrial kilns. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples demonstrate unique adaptability and economic efficiency, particularly in vacuum, reducing, or inert atmosphere environments. 1. Material Composition and Main Types of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire Tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires are made from tungsten (W) and rhenium (Re) alloys, typically paired with a low-rhenium alloy as the positive leg and a high-rhenium alloy as the negative leg. WRe3-WRe25 (corresponds to Type D): The positive leg contains 3% rhenium and the negative leg contains 25% rhenium. Early applications also included a combination of pure tungsten and WRe26 (Type G); however, the pure tungsten positive leg is relatively brittle, so this type is now rarely used. CTIA GROUP manufactures tungsten-rhenium wire using powder metallurgy, sintering, swaging, and wire-drawing processes. Specifications such as diameter and length can be customized to meet client needs. The wire is characterized by a high melting point (over 3000°C), high strength at elevated temperatures, and low vapor pressure. Adding an appropriate amount of rhenium significantly improves the brittleness and recrystallization behavior of pure tungsten, thereby enhancing the material's toughness and thermal stability. 2. Advantages of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Heating Furnace Thermocouples Exceptional temperature measurement capability: Capable of long-term operation between 0°C and 2300°C—and higher temperatures for short durations—in vacuum, dry hydrogen, or inert atmospheres, meeting the requirements of ultra-high-temperature heating furnaces, crystal growth furnaces, hot isostatic pressing (HIP) furnaces, and more. Excellent thermoelectric properties: The thermoelectric output is approximately twice that of Type S platinum-rhodium thermocouples; the material offers high sensitivity, good linearity between temperature and electromotive force (EMF), and rapid response times. In air or oxidizing atmospheres, it oxidizes rapidly and fails at temperatures above 300–500°C; furthermore, grain growth at high temperatures leads to embrittlement. Consequently, the operating environment must be strictly controlled, or special protective measures must be implemented. 3. Applications of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Heating Furnace Thermocouples In the field of heating furnaces, CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wire thermocouples are primarily used in: ultra-high-temperature equipment such as vacuum heat treatment furnaces, molybdenum wire furnaces, and tungsten wire furnaces; powder metallurgy sintering furnaces and silicon carbide crystal growth furnaces; furnaces operating in reducing or alternating atmospheres, such as gasifiers and sulfur recovery units; and applications involving rapid temperature measurement of molten steel and continuous temperature monitoring in certain metallurgical furnaces. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Flange-Mounted Thermocouples
text: In industrial sectors such as petrochemicals, coal gasification, metallurgical smelting, high-temperature vacuum furnaces, and nuclear energy, reaction vessels often operate in environments characterized by extreme temperatures, high pressures, and complex media that are highly corrosive, flammable, or explosive. As critical temperature-sensing components in these demanding conditions, flange-mounted thermocouples require a flange structure to ensure highly reliable physical isolation and pressure sealing, while relying on internal sensing elements to provide accurate and rapid temperature feedback. In the ultra-high temperature range exceeding 1300°C—or even 2000°C—tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) thermocouple wire has become the material of choice for the vast majority of extreme temperature-sensing applications in flange-mounted thermocouples, thanks to its irreplaceable high-temperature thermoelectric properties. I. High-Temperature Thermoelectric Properties of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium alloy wire from CTIA GROUP is a solid-solution material composed of tungsten (W) and rhenium (Re); common pairings include WRe3-WRe25 and WRe5-WRe26. In the field of high-temperature thermoelectric measurement, tungsten-rhenium wire demonstrates outstanding overall performance. Ultra-high temperature measurement limit and high thermoelectric potential. Tungsten has a melting point of 3410°C, and rhenium melts at 3180°C. When alloyed with rhenium, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples exhibit extremely high thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) and excellent sensitivity across a broad temperature range of 0–2300°C; their thermoelectric output is significantly higher than that of noble-metal platinum-rhodium thermocouples. In vacuum, hydrogen, or inert atmospheres, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples can withstand temperatures above 2000°C for extended periods, and even up to 3000°C for short durations. Breakthroughs in mechanical properties driven by the "rhenium effect." Pure tungsten wire tends to become brittle and fracture easily after undergoing recrystallization at high temperatures. Adding 3% to 25% rhenium to tungsten promotes the formation of extensive twin structures at grain boundaries; this increases ductility by approximately 300% while maintaining high strength, effectively resolving the inherent brittleness of tungsten. This modification endows tungsten-rhenium wire with a combination of advantages, including high strength at both room and elevated temperatures, good plasticity following recrystallization, and excellent resistance to vibration fatigue. Excellent thermoelectric properties and cost-effectiveness. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples feature a linear relationship between temperature and electromotive force (EMF) and offer reliable thermal stability. The magnitude of the thermoelectric potential depends solely on the alloy composition and the temperature difference between the two ends, remaining independent of the thermocouple's shape, length, or diameter. At 1200°C, the deviation in non-uniform thermal EMF across a full coil of wire can be controlled within 40–80 μV, achieving a temperature measurement accuracy of ±0.5%. Furthermore, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are significantly less expensive than platinum-rhodium counterparts; this cost-performance advantage has led to their widespread adoption in industrial temperature measurement. II. Compatibility of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire with Flange Sealing Structures The core design of flange-mounted thermocouples involves using a flange plate and a metal gasket or flexible graphite seal to tightly secure the temperature-sensing probe to the reactor wall, ensuring zero leakage of high-pressure or hazardous media. Tungsten-rhenium wire serves as an ideal sensing material for such structures because its material properties align exceptionally well with the mechanical, physical, and environmental requirements of the flange assembly and the internal chamber. Environmental compatibility within the sealed protective chamber. Tungsten-rhenium wire oxidizes rapidly in air at temperatures above 400°C, which is the primary limitation on its application. Flange sealing structures provide a reliable seal for the interior of the protective sheath, facilitating evacuation or the introduction of high-purity inert gas. In a pure vacuum or a reducing/inert protective atmosphere, tungsten-rhenium wire exhibits exceptional chemical stability; this synergy with the sealed flange chamber effectively overcomes the material's susceptibility to oxidation. Structural compatibility with flange mechanical stress and vibration environments. Flange connections are often zones where thermal expansion stress, medium pulsation, and mechanical vibration concentrate on pressure vessels. Tungsten-rhenium wires modified with the element rhenium exhibit excellent toughness and elongation; they effectively withstand the bending and tensile stresses encountered as the thermocouple passes through the flange neck and terminal box, preventing brittle fracture caused by stress concentration during prolonged vibration and thermal cycling. Compatibility with thermal expansion of insulating seals. Within the flange sealing assembly, the thermocouple wires must pass through rigid insulating beads—typically made of high-purity alumina or magnesium oxide—and connect to glass or ceramic seals at the terminal. Tungsten-rhenium alloys possess a low and stable coefficient of thermal expansion (approximately 4.3 × 10⁻⁶/K), matching well with corundum insulating tubes and high-temperature sealing materials. This significantly reduces the risk of insulating beads crushing the wires or seal failure caused by uneven thermal expansion and contraction. III. Application Scenarios for Flange-Mounted Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples Flange-mounted thermocouples equipped with CTIA GROUP tungsten-rhenium wires feature an ultra-high temperature measurement limit, excellent thermoelectric stability, and superior mechanical toughness, making them suitable for a wide range of critical industrial sectors. Coal chemical processing and gasification units represent typical application scenarios for tungsten-rhenium flange thermocouples. In core equipment such as coal-water slurry gasifiers and pulverized coal gasifiers, reaction temperatures often reach 1300–1600°C, accompanied by high internal pressures and the presence of reducing synthesis gases (e.g., CO, H₂). The flange sealing structure prevents the leakage of highly toxic, high-pressure gases, while the internal tungsten-rhenium wires—housed within an inert-gas-purged thermowell—provide continuous, high-precision temperature measurement. In the metallurgical industry, high-precision tungsten-rhenium thermocouples can replace Type S platinum-rhodium thermocouples within the 1000–1600°C range; while platinum-rhodium thermocouples have a service life of only about two weeks in extremely harsh environments, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples not only serve as a substitute for these expensive units but also offer a significantly longer service life. Furthermore, in the aerospace and nuclear industries, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are suitable for measuring temperatures in exhaust plume gas flows and play a critical role in ultra-high-temperature measurement scenarios, such as within nuclear reactors. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Gas-Filled Thermocouples
text: In the field of ultra-high-temperature measurement, traditional platinum-rhodium thermocouples are limited by melting points and costs, making it difficult for them to operate stably for long periods in environments exceeding 2000°C. Thanks to their extremely high melting points, good thermoelectric linearity, and relatively low cost, tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires have become the core material for ultra-high-temperature measurement in vacuum, reducing, and inert atmospheres. Gas-filled thermocouples were developed specifically to address the high susceptibility of tungsten-rhenium wire to oxidation: the tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires are encapsulated within a high-melting-point protective tube, which is evacuated and then filled with an inert gas (such as argon or nitrogen) and sealed. This creates a positive-pressure protective atmosphere that isolates the wires from external oxygen and corrosive media, thereby significantly extending their service life. 1. Characteristics of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten has a melting point of approximately 3422°C, but pure tungsten wire is brittle and prone to breakage after recrystallization. Adding 3%–26% rhenium produces a significant "rhenium effect," markedly improving room-temperature ductility, resistance to recrystallization, and high-temperature strength, while maintaining low vapor pressure and excellent chemical stability. Common pairings include WRe5/WRe26 (Type C, with the positive electrode containing ~5% Re and the negative ~26% Re) and WRe3/WRe25 (Type D). They cover a temperature measurement range of 0–2300°C, with short-term capability reaching 3000°C. In vacuum, hydrogen, or inert atmospheres, they exhibit high thermoelectric output, high sensitivity, and good linearity, with tolerances reaching ±0.5%t or ±1%t. Compared to platinum-rhodium thermocouples, CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wires offer superior stability in non-oxidizing atmospheres and serve as a cost-effective alternative to precious metal thermocouples. The critical weakness of tungsten-rhenium wire is its poor high-temperature oxidation resistance; it oxidizes and fails rapidly in oxygen-containing environments at temperatures above 300°C. Therefore, a protective structure is essential. The gas-filled design capitalizes on this requirement: protective tubes—such as those made of molybdenum, tungsten, or corundum—are evacuated and then backfilled with an inert gas to create a positive-pressure sealed chamber. This prevents the ingress of external oxidizing or corrosive gases and inhibits reactions between the thermoelement wires and the protective tube material, thereby ensuring long-term stability of thermoelectric performance. 2. Mechanism of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire in Gas-Filled Structures Gas-filled tungsten-rhenium thermocouples typically feature a non-detachable structure. During manufacturing, the paired tungsten-rhenium wires are inserted into the protective tube; the assembly is evacuated using vacuum technology and backfilled with high-purity argon or nitrogen, with the cold end hermetically sealed using a plug and sealant. The internal positive pressure effectively blocks the ingress of reducing or corrosive gases generated during sintering or smelting processes, preventing oxidation, carburization, or embrittlement of the tungsten-rhenium wires. Tungsten protective tubes can withstand temperatures exceeding 2200°C; when combined with inert gas, they maintain seal integrity under extreme heat. Compared to solid-filled types, gas-filled thermocouples offer faster response times and superior resistance to thermal shock and vibration, making them ideal for applications requiring rapid temperature measurement. Additionally, equipment investment costs are relatively manageable, and production yields are high. In this structure, the tungsten-rhenium wire supplied by CTIA GROUP serves as both the temperature-sensing core and the critical factor determining service life and accuracy. Customizable fine-diameter wires accelerate thermal response, while thicker wires enhance mechanical strength and longevity. 3. Application Fields of Gas-Filled Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples Gas-filled tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are widely used in industrial and scientific research settings requiring precise measurement at ultra-high temperatures. In vacuum furnaces, controlled-atmosphere furnaces, monocrystalline silicon growth furnaces, and high-temperature sintering furnaces, they operate stably for extended periods at temperatures around 2000°C, offering a service life several times longer than that of platinum-rhodium thermocouples. In the metallurgical industry, they are used for rapid temperature measurement of molten steel, cemented carbides, and powder metallurgy products. In the chemical and coal-chemical sectors, they serve as cost-effective, operationally simpler alternatives to platinum-rhodium thermocouples that otherwise require gas-purge protection. In the aerospace and nuclear engineering sectors, gas-filled tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are utilized for temperature monitoring in rocket engines, hot-section components of scramjet engines, and the cores of high-temperature gas-cooled reactors. When paired with specialized protective tubes and gas-tight sealing, they enable long-term temperature measurement exceeding 1600°C in environments characterized by strong oxidation or alternating atmospheres, such as refractory kilns and sulfur recovery units. Furthermore, gas-filled tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are the preferred choice for laboratory-scale ultra-high-temperature research, hot isostatic pressing equipment, and high-temperature semiconductor processing due to their low contamination levels and high stability. Their cost-effectiveness offers significant economic advantages for large-scale industrial adoption. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Stepped-Tube Encapsulated Thermocouples
text: In the field of high-temperature industrial temperature measurement, traditional noble metal thermocouples (such as the platinum-rhodium series) struggle to meet the demands for precision measurement in ultra-high-temperature and complex atmospheric environments due to high costs and limited upper temperature ranges (typically ≤1800°C). CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) wire has become the core temperature-sensing material for stepped-tube encapsulated thermocouples, thanks to its ultra-high melting point, high thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF), excellent high-temperature strength, and cost-effectiveness. Stepped tubes (featuring a stepped protective sheath or nested structure) utilize a variable-diameter design to balance rapid response at the sensing tip with mechanical strength at the cold end; they are widely used in vacuum furnaces, sintering furnaces, molten steel temperature measurement, and the monitoring of high-temperature aerospace components. The use of tungsten-rhenium wire enables these thermocouples to operate stably within a range of 0–2300°C (with short-term capability for even higher temperatures), significantly expanding the application boundaries of contact-based temperature measurement. 1. Characteristics and Advantages of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium wire is a fine wire produced by alloying tungsten (W) and rhenium (Re) in specific proportions and processing the material through powder metallurgy, swaging, and drawing; the addition of rhenium significantly improves the inherent brittleness of tungsten. Common pairings for tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires include WRe3/25 (positive electrode ~3% Re, negative electrode ~25% Re; Type D) and WRe5/26 (positive electrode ~5% Re, negative electrode ~26% Re; Type C). Key features include: A melting point exceeding 3300°C, allowing for long-term use at 2000–2300°C and short-term use above 2800°C in non-oxidizing atmospheres—far surpassing the capabilities of platinum-rhodium thermocouples. High thermoelectric EMF—approximately 2 to 3 times that of platinum-rhodium thermocouples—resulting in excellent sensitivity and good linearity, which facilitates precise conversion. It possesses high mechanical strength and good ductility, retaining excellent toughness even when processed into diameters of 0.08–0.5 mm or finer, making it suitable for encapsulation within small-diameter stepped tubes. It exhibits outstanding chemical stability in vacuum, dry hydrogen, or inert atmospheres, features low vapor pressure, and does not readily volatilize at high temperatures. Furthermore, it offers a favorable cost-performance ratio. It should be noted that tungsten-rhenium wire is highly susceptible to oxidation, and grain growth occurring above 1500°C leads to embrittlement; therefore, strict isolation from air and carbon-containing atmospheres is essential—a critical consideration in the design of the stepped tube encapsulation and protective structure. 2. Application of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire in Stepped Tube Encapsulation Thermocouples encapsulated in stepped tubes typically employ armored or solid-state structures: the tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires are sealed alongside high-purity insulating materials (such as magnesium oxide [MgO], boron nitride [BN], or corundum powder) within a metal or ceramic protective tube, forming a solid, airtight assembly through repeated drawing or filling processes. The stepped design features a small diameter at the temperature-sensing end (to accelerate thermal response) and a thicker diameter at the transition and cold ends (to enhance strength and vibration resistance); flexible installation is often achieved through the use of springs and connecting sleeves. Tungsten-rhenium wire offers distinct advantages in this configuration: the fine-diameter wire can easily be inserted into narrow stepped tubes, ensuring a compact sensing junction; its high mechanical strength withstands repeated bending and vibration; and its high thermoelectric output minimizes signal attenuation during transmission over long leads. Special attention to oxidation prevention is required during encapsulation: filling is performed in a vacuum or inert atmosphere, followed by backfilling with high-purity argon or nitrogen; the cold end is sealed with high-temperature inorganic adhesive or a metal seal, and some products incorporate oxygen scavengers to further reduce residual oxygen. For applications involving oxidizing atmospheres, multi-layer composite protection (using corundum and molybdenum tubes) or solid-state anti-oxidation filling processes are employed to ensure the tungsten-rhenium wire operates in an isolated environment. The stepped tube structure also facilitates reliable connections to compensation leads and terminal boxes, making cold-junction temperature compensation easier to implement. This encapsulation design endows the thermocouple with advantages such as rapid response (due to the low thermal mass of the small-diameter tip), resistance to pressure and vibration, flexibility, and a long service life; it is particularly well-suited for high-temperature applications involving space constraints or frequent installation and removal. 3. Applications of Stepped-Tube Encapsulated Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples In the fields of metallurgy and powder metallurgy, they are used for temperature measurement in vacuum furnaces, hydrogen sintering furnaces, and molten steel (both intermittent and continuous processes), serving as a replacement for expensive platinum-rhodium thermocouples while offering a significantly longer service life. In refractory material processing and chemical industry kilns, when paired with oxidation-resistant composite tubes, they can operate continuously at temperatures exceeding 1600°C in strongly oxidizing or reducing atmospheres. In aerospace and specialized equipment sectors, they monitor extreme thermal environments, such as those found in scramjet engines and combustion chambers. In the nuclear industry and scientific research, they are suitable for temperature measurement under conditions of high temperature, high pressure, or corrosive media. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Handheld Thermocouples
text: In industrial sectors such as metallurgy, casting, and aerospace, measuring the temperature of molten metals and high-temperature furnace interiors has long faced the challenge of material temperature limits. As temperature requirements exceed 1800°C, platinum-rhodium thermocouples struggle to meet the demand; in contrast, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples—thanks to their exceptional high-temperature resistance—stand out as one of the few viable contact-based temperature measurement solutions for this range. For handheld thermocouples, which serve as convenient tools for rapid on-site temperature measurement, the core sensing element is a thermoelement made of tungsten-rhenium alloy wire. The performance of this wire directly determines the handheld device's upper temperature limit, response speed, and measurement accuracy. I. Material Properties and Temperature Measurement Principles of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium wire from CTIA GROUP is an alloy composed of a tungsten (W) matrix with added rhenium (Re). Common rhenium contents include 3%, 5%, 25%, and 26%, with typical grades being WRe3/25 and WRe5/26. The temperature measurement principle relies on the Seebeck effect: two tungsten-rhenium alloy wires of different compositions form a closed circuit. When a temperature gradient exists between the measuring junction and the reference junction, a thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) is generated; the temperature can be determined by measuring this EMF and referencing a standard calibration table. The most significant advantage of tungsten-rhenium wire is its extremely high melting point. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any elemental metal, and tungsten-rhenium alloy wires typically melt between 3120°C and 3360°C. Thermocouples made from these wires operate stably within the 0–2300°C range and can withstand temperatures exceeding 2800°C during short-term use. However, pure tungsten is highly brittle at room temperature, making it difficult to process into fine wire. The addition of rhenium effectively resolves this issue. Rhenium atoms promote the formation of extensive twin structures at grain boundaries, increasing the material's ductility by approximately 300% while maintaining high strength, thereby endowing the wire with excellent drawability and weldability. In terms of thermoelectric performance, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples exhibit a favorable linear relationship between temperature and electromotive force (EMF), reliable thermal stability, and high sensitivity. Taking the WRe3/25 type as an example, the nominal composition of the positive leg is 97% tungsten and 3% rhenium, while the negative leg consists of 75% tungsten and 25% rhenium. For a full spool of tungsten-rhenium wire, the deviation in thermoelectric EMF inhomogeneity at 1200°C is typically controlled within the range of 40–80 μV, ensuring consistency and reliability in temperature measurement. II. Special Requirements for Tungsten-Rhenium Wire in Handheld Temperature Measurement There are significant differences in operating modes between handheld thermocouples and fixed-installation thermocouples. Handheld temperature measuring instruments must perform rapid, accurate, single-point measurements in harsh on-site environments, which imposes specific requirements on the tungsten-rhenium wire. Rapid Response Capability. Handheld temperature measurements are typically completed within 3 to 5 seconds, requiring the thermocouple wire to have minimal thermal inertia. Tungsten-rhenium wires from CTIA GROUP are generally produced as fine filaments with diameters of 0.1–0.5 mm (customizable to client specifications). When paired with the structural design of a consumable rapid-response probe tip, they can quickly reach thermal equilibrium upon contact with molten metal, enabling response times on the order of seconds. Protection Tube and Oxidation Resistance Design. The primary limitation of tungsten-rhenium wire is its susceptibility to failure in oxidizing atmospheres; oxidation begins at temperatures as low as approximately 300°C. When handheld instruments measure molten steel or iron, effective protection measures are required during the few seconds the probe is immersed in the melt, even though the probe tip itself is a disposable consumable. In practice, cermet tubes or recrystallized silicon carbide tubes are typically used as outer protection tubes, filled with oxygen scavengers and high-temperature insulating materials to shield the tungsten-rhenium wire from oxidative corrosion during the brief measurement period. Signal Processing and Nonlinearity Compensation. Although tungsten-rhenium thermocouples exhibit good linearity between output EMF and temperature, a certain degree of nonlinearity remains. Handheld temperature measuring instruments require built-in compensation algorithms tailored to the specific calibration grades, such as WRe3/25 or WRe5/26. Existing patented technology demonstrates that nonlinear compensation can be effectively achieved using simple circuitry, keeping the maximum error within ±2°C (plus or minus one digit) across the 400–1900°C range. III. Applications of Handheld Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples Applications for handheld tungsten-rhenium thermocouples include, but are not limited to: rapid on-site temperature measurement of molten metals (such as molten steel and iron) in metallurgy and casting operations—including converters, electric arc furnaces, and medium- or power-frequency induction furnaces; intermittent temperature monitoring and troubleshooting in high-temperature industrial furnaces and kilns, such as coking ovens, chemical processing kilns, and glass melting furnaces; monitoring of ultra-high temperatures in aerospace and nuclear industries, such as engine exhaust plumes, rocket engine gas flow fields, and nuclear reactor cores; periodic calibration, multi-point temperature monitoring, and fault diagnosis for vacuum furnaces, powder metallurgy sintering furnaces, heat treatment furnaces, and high-temperature thermocouple calibration systems; and on-site spot-checking of temperatures up to 1600°C in oxidizing atmospheres within the chemical and building materials industries, when equipped with protective sheaths. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Screw-Mount Thermocouples
text: In the field of modern industrial high-temperature measurement, thermocouples are among the most widely used temperature sensors; their performance directly determines the precision of process control and the safety of equipment operation. While common base-metal thermocouples (such as types K, E, and J) typically have an upper temperature limit of 1,000–1,300°C, and noble-metal platinum-rhodium thermocouples can extend this range to 1,600–1,800°C, the latter are costly and still fall short in ultra-high-temperature applications. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples effectively bridge this gap. Utilizing tungsten-rhenium alloy wire as the thermoelement, they can operate reliably over the long term within a range of 0–2,300°C—and even approach 2,800°C for short durations—in vacuum, reducing, or inert atmospheres, making them core components for ultra-high-temperature measurement. Screw-mount thermocouples feature an assembly design that utilizes a threaded connection (commonly M6, M8, etc.) for mounting. Offering convenient installation and reliable thermal contact, they are particularly well-suited for applications involving equipment walls, heat sinks, mold surfaces, furnace linings, and scenarios requiring rapid installation or removal. Combining tungsten-rhenium wire with a screw-mount structure leverages the material's advantages—namely, ultra-high-temperature capability and high sensitivity—alongside the flexibility and excellent thermal contact characteristics of the screw-mounting method. The result is a specialized temperature sensor that balances high-temperature performance with ease of installation. These sensors are invaluable in applications such as vacuum furnaces, high-temperature sintering, metal smelting, aerospace thermal testing, and scientific research involving ultra-high temperatures. 1. Material Properties and Calibration Grades of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires consist of paired tungsten alloys with varying rhenium content; common combinations include: WRe5-WRe26 (positive electrode: 95% tungsten, 5% rhenium; negative electrode: 74% tungsten, 26% rhenium), corresponding to Type C calibration; WRe3-WRe25 (positive electrode: 97% tungsten, 3% rhenium; negative electrode: 75% tungsten, 25% rhenium), corresponding to Type D calibration; WRe5-WRe20 (positive electrode: 95% tungsten, 5% rhenium; negative electrode: 80% tungsten, 20% rhenium), corresponding to Type A calibration. Tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires exhibit a high thermoelectric potential rate—approximately twice the sensitivity of platinum-rhodium thermocouples—and offer rapid response times. Tungsten has a melting point of approximately 3410°C; the addition of rhenium significantly improves high-temperature ductility and resistance to recrystallization, allowing the wire to retain toughness at high temperatures and facilitating processing and use. They feature a wide operating temperature range, with standard calibration tables covering 0–2315°C and permissible deviations typically ranging from ±0.5% to ±1% of the temperature value (depending on specific standards and wire diameters; CTOMS offers flexible customization based on customer needs and application scenarios). It must be emphasized that tungsten-rhenium wire is highly susceptible to oxidation; direct exposure to air or oxidizing atmospheres is strictly prohibited. Contact with oxygen at high temperatures leads to rapid failure. Consequently, practical applications require the use of airtight protective tubes—such as molybdenum, tantalum, silicon carbide, or molybdenum disilicide composite tubes—and operation within vacuum, hydrogen, or inert gas environments. Compared to platinum-rhodium thermocouples, tungsten-rhenium wire costs only 30%–50% as much, offering a distinct economic advantage in scenarios where budgets are constrained and atmospheric control is available. 2. Structural Features and Working Principle of Screw-Type Thermocouples The core structure of a screw-type thermocouple comprises a temperature-sensing element (tungsten-rhenium thermoelements), an insulating sleeve, a protective tube (or an exposed sensing tip), a threaded mounting sleeve, a locking ferrule, and compensation lead wires or terminals. Common configurations include fixed-thread types and types with sliding/rotating threaded sleeves. During installation, the threaded sleeve is screwed into a pre-drilled hole in the object being measured; the sensing tip is then pressed firmly against the surface—ensuring good thermal contact via a ferrule and spring or locking mechanism—and the compensation leads are secured. Its working principle is based on the Seebeck effect: two wires of different compositions (a tungsten-rhenium alloy pair) are welded together at one end to form the measuring junction, while the other ends serve as the reference junction. When a temperature difference exists between the measuring and reference junctions, a thermoelectric potential is generated in the circuit; the magnitude of this potential depends solely on the material properties and the temperature difference between the two ends, independent of wire diameter or length. Temperature values can be read directly using compatible display instruments. The screw-type design ensures tight contact between the sensing tip and the measured surface, resulting in a short thermal response time (some designs achieve response times in the order of seconds), making it particularly suitable for surface temperature measurement. Thread specifications typically include options such as M6×1 and M8×1.25; probe diameters range from approximately 4 to 8 mm, and insertion depths can be customized. Some products feature shielding or aviation-grade connectors to facilitate use in industrial settings. It should be noted that standard screw-type structures are generally not waterproof and are unsuitable for measuring liquid media in pipelines; they are primarily used for solid surfaces or gaseous environments. 3. Applications of Screw-Type Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples (1) Temperature measurement of furnace walls and workpieces in high-temperature vacuum furnaces, molybdenum-wire furnaces, and tungsten-wire furnaces; (2) Ultra-high-temperature processes such as powder metallurgy, ceramic sintering, and silicon carbide crystal growth; (3) Rapid temperature measurement of molten metals like molten steel and iron; (4) High-temperature monitoring for aerospace engine thermal testing, plasma equipment, and the nuclear industry; (5) Laboratory testing of ultra-high-temperature material properties. Strict atmospheric control is required during operation; the protective tube must be airtight to prevent oxygen ingress. After prolonged exposure to high temperatures, tungsten-rhenium wire may undergo recrystallization and become brittle; therefore, regular inspection and replacement are required. During installation, ensure that threaded connections are secure and the temperature-sensing tip makes firm contact to prevent measurement errors caused by poor connections. Compensation lead wires must match the specific tungsten-rhenium calibration grade, and accurate reference-junction temperature compensation must be ensured. Calibration should ideally be performed under conditions that closely resemble the actual operating environment. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Industrial Thermocouples
text: CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wire (tungsten-rhenium alloy wire) is a critical temperature-sensing material used in industrial thermocouples for ultra-high-temperature measurement. Produced by adding an appropriate amount of rhenium (Re) to a tungsten (W) base and processing the mixture through powder metallurgy, swaging, and drawing, these fine wires serve as the positive and negative elements of a thermocouple pair. Key advantages include an extremely high melting point (approx. 3120–3350°C), good high-temperature strength, excellent thermoelectric output, and high cost-effectiveness. These properties make it a vital choice for measuring temperatures above 1600°C, and especially those exceeding 2000°C. Compared to noble metal thermocouples (such as platinum-rhodium), tungsten-rhenium wire costs only one-third to one-half as much while offering a higher maximum operating temperature, greater thermoelectric output, and superior sensitivity. Consequently, it is widely used in fields such as metallurgy, aerospace, nuclear energy, vacuum furnace operations, and the production of high-temperature materials. It is important to note that tungsten-rhenium wire oxidizes rapidly at high temperatures in air; therefore, it must be used in a vacuum, hydrogen, or inert atmosphere, or paired with special anti-oxidation protective structures to function effectively—whether for short-term or long-term applications—in oxidizing environments. 1. Main Types and Compositions of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouple Wire WRe5/WRe26 (corresponds to Type C calibration): Nominal composition is 95% W + 5% Re for the positive leg and 74% W + 26% Re for the negative leg. This is the most widely used type, featuring stable thermoelectric output and well-established calibration tables. WRe3/WRe25 (corresponds to Type D calibration): Positive leg is 97% W + 3% Re; negative leg is 75% W + 25% Re. It offers a higher thermoelectric output rate and superior stability in certain high-temperature applications. Other variants include W/W-26Re (corresponds to Type G calibration) and WRe5/WRe20 (corresponds to Type A calibration). 2. Properties of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire Tungsten-rhenium wire produced by CTIA GROUP features a high melting point (tungsten is approx. 3422°C and rhenium approx. 3186°C; while the alloy's melting point is lower, it still far exceeds that of most metals), low vapor pressure, and excellent high-temperature strength. The addition of rhenium significantly improves the room-temperature brittleness of pure tungsten, enhancing ductility, recrystallization temperature, and thermal shock resistance; this facilitates wire drawing and ensures the wire retains a degree of toughness after high-temperature service. Regarding thermoelectric properties, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples exhibit a thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) rate of approximately 15–16 μV/°C in the 1000–2000°C range—higher than that of Type S (Pt-Rh10/Pt) and Type B thermocouples—resulting in high sensitivity and strong signals. The relationship between temperature and thermoelectric EMF is relatively linear. The recommended long-term operating temperature is 0–2300°C (in vacuum, reducing, or inert atmospheres), with short-term capability reaching 2800–3000°C; however, data scatter increases above 2300°C, so industrial applications typically limit operation to below 2000°C. Permissible deviations are generally ±4.0°C for the 0–400°C range and ±0.25%t or ±0.5%t for the 400–2300°C range (where t is the measured temperature). Non-uniformity of thermoelectric EMF across the entire coil of wire at 1200°C is typically required to be no more than 40–80 μV. The density is approximately 19.2–19.7 g/cm³, and electrical resistivity increases with rhenium content. Mechanically, the tensile strength in the annealed state is significantly higher than that of pure tungsten, and the material maintains high strength at elevated temperatures. 3. Applications of Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Industrial Thermocouples CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium thermocouple wires are widely used for ultra-high-temperature measurement in vacuum furnaces, hydrogen furnaces, and inert-atmosphere sintering furnaces; for rapid temperature measurement of molten steel and iron; in extreme thermal environments such as aerospace engines, rocket nozzles, and plasma equipment; and in nuclear reactors, high-temperature materials research, and single-crystal growth furnaces. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Extra-Long Thermocouples
text: Tungsten-rhenium wire for extra-long thermocouples is a specialized material designed for applications requiring ultra-high temperatures, deep insertion, or long-distance temperature measurement. Utilizing tungsten-rhenium (W-Re) alloys as the thermoelement material—and incorporating specialized processing and structural designs—these wires enable stable, reliable contact-based temperature measurement in ultra-high temperature ranges (often exceeding 2000°C) where conventional thermocouples struggle to perform. Compared to standard short thermocouples, these extra-long products demand higher specifications regarding protection tube length, insulation filling, sealing techniques, and wire ductility. They are widely used in vacuum furnaces, high-temperature sintering furnaces, aerospace propulsion systems, nuclear reactors, and specialized metallurgical equipment. 1. Material Properties and Calibration Grades Tungsten has a melting point of approximately 3422°C, and rhenium approximately 3186°C; the resulting alloy retains an exceptionally high melting point while significantly improving upon the brittleness and workability of pure tungsten. Common thermocouple pairings include WRe3-WRe25, WRe5-WRe26, and W-WRe26, where the numbers indicate the rhenium content by mass percentage. These pairings can operate continuously within the 0–2300°C range in vacuum, reducing, or inert atmospheres, and can withstand even higher temperatures for short durations. Compared to platinum-rhodium thermocouples, CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium wires offer a higher thermoelectric electromotive force (EMF) rate—with sensitivity approximately double that of platinum-rhodium types—at a cost that is only one-half to one-quarter (or less) of the latter, while also providing excellent high-temperature strength and thermal shock resistance. It is important to note that tungsten-rhenium wire oxidizes rapidly in air or oxygen-containing atmospheres, showing significant reaction starting at approximately 300°C. Consequently, they must be used under the protection of a vacuum, hydrogen, or inert gas, or be equipped with specialized oxidation-resistant protection tubes and sealing structures. At temperatures exceeding 1500°C, grain growth occurs; when grain size approaches the wire diameter, the thermocouple wires become brittle, thereby reducing service life. This is a critical factor to control regarding wire material selection and heat treatment for extra-long products. 2. Structure and Manufacturing Essentials of Extra-Long Thermocouples The core challenge in producing extra-long tungsten-rhenium thermocouples lies in balancing length with high-temperature sealing requirements. While the thermocouple wires themselves are typically fine in diameter (commonly φ0.1–0.5 mm), the protective tube for the entire assembly can range from several hundred millimeters to over a meter in length, with some specifications reaching 1100 mm or more. The structure typically comprises: (1) Thermoelements: A matched pair of tungsten-rhenium wires joined by precision welding to form the measuring junction. (2) Insulation materials: High-temperature ceramics—such as corundum, beryllium oxide, or specialized ultra-high-temperature insulating materials—packed inside the protective tube to prevent short circuits and minimize thermoelectric potential shunting. (3) Protective tube: Materials are selected based on the operating atmosphere, including molybdenum, tungsten, corundum, cermet, or composite tubes. Molybdenum and tungsten tubes are suitable for vacuum or reducing atmospheres, while ceramic tubes offer an expanded application range under specific conditions. (4) Cold-end sealing and compensation: A vacuum-sealing process is employed at the cold end to ensure an oxygen-free interior; connections are made via compensation lead wires and a terminal box. Manufacturing requires strict control over the compositional uniformity of the thermocouple wires, the consistency of thermoelectric potential, and the airtightness of the protective tube. The extra-long configuration places higher demands on the ductility and recrystallization resistance of the wires; otherwise, they are prone to fracture at high temperatures due to grain growth. Some advanced products utilize solid-state anti-oxidation structures or protective coatings, enabling operation at temperatures up to approximately 1600–1700°C in alternating oxidizing and reducing atmospheres. 3. Applications of Extra-Long Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples Extra-long tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are particularly well-suited for ultra-high-temperature applications requiring deep insertion or remote temperature measurement. Examples include vacuum induction melting, powder metallurgy sintering furnaces, and heat treatment of high-temperature materials; aerospace and aviation engine testing, as well as temperature monitoring for rocket engine nozzles and combustion chambers; high-temperature testing related to nuclear reactors and the melting of specialty alloys; environments involving high corrosion or special atmospheres—such as refractory material processing, silicon carbide crystal growth, and coal gasification furnaces; and laboratory-based ultra-high-temperature research and calibration systems. In these scenarios, the extra-long design allows the measuring tip to reach deep into furnace chambers or pipelines while keeping the cold junction in a safe zone, effectively overcoming the measurement challenges that conventional short thermocouples cannot address. title: Tungsten-Rhenium Wire for Adjustable Threaded Compression-Fitting Thermocouples
text: The adjustable threaded compression-fitting tungsten-rhenium thermocouple is a temperature sensor specifically designed for environments involving ultra-high temperatures, vacuums, or inert atmospheres. By combining the exceptional high-temperature performance of tungsten-rhenium wire with the flexibility and sealing capabilities of an adjustable compression-fitting mounting structure, these thermocouples are widely used in vacuum furnaces, high-temperature sintering furnaces, crystal growth equipment, aerospace testing, and specialized metallurgy. I. Working Principle of Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples Thermocouples operate based on the Seebeck effect: a circuit is formed by welding together two conductors (or alloys) of different compositions. When a temperature difference exists between the measuring junction and the reference junction, a thermoelectric potential is generated in the circuit. This potential corresponds to the temperature, which can be displayed via secondary instrumentation. While common base-metal thermocouples (such as Type K or N) typically have a long-term operating limit of 1200°C, and noble-metal thermocouples (Types S, R, and B) peak at around 1600–1700°C, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples can operate continuously at 2000–2300°C in vacuum, dry hydrogen, or inert atmospheres—and even higher for short durations. They are currently among the highest-temperature contact-based temperature sensing elements practical for industrial and scientific applications. The adjustable threaded compression-fitting design is a common mounting configuration for both sheathed and assembled thermocouples. A compression fitting (ferrule) secures the protective tube via a threaded connection, ensuring both a seal and mechanical stability. The adjustable design allows for the regulation of insertion depth within a specific range and enables fine-tuning of the position after installation, accommodating various equipment port configurations and depth requirements. Compared to fixed threads or flanges, this mounting method offers ease of installation, reliable sealing, and convenient replacement, making it particularly suitable for high-temperature applications requiring frequent adjustments or on-site calibration. CTIA GROUP utilizes tungsten-rhenium wire combinations—typically WRe5/WRe26 (positive: tungsten-5% rhenium; negative: tungsten-26% rhenium) or WRe3/WRe25 (positive: tungsten-3% rhenium; negative: tungsten-25% rhenium)—as temperature-sensing elements. The addition of rhenium significantly enhances tungsten's ductility and recrystallization temperature while reducing high-temperature brittleness, ensuring the thermocouple wires maintain excellent mechanical properties and thermoelectric stability even after repeated thermal cycling. II. Performance Advantages of Adjustable Threaded Compression-Fitting Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples CTIA GROUP’s tungsten-rhenium thermocouples exhibit a high thermoelectric output rate—approximately 16 μV/°C within the 1000–2000°C range—providing a strong signal suitable for long-distance transmission and processing. Permissible error is typically ±1% of the measured temperature (or stricter, depending on wire diameter and calibration standards). The long-term operating temperature range is approximately 300–2000°C, with higher temperatures permissible for short-term use. Response time depends on wire and protection tube diameters; configurations using fine wires or thin-walled structures can achieve response times in the second range or faster. Compared to platinum-rhodium thermocouples, tungsten-rhenium wires offer significantly lower costs; my country’s relatively abundant tungsten and rhenium resources provide a distinct advantage for domestic production. These thermocouples feature high mechanical strength and excellent thermal shock resistance, making them suitable for applications involving rapid temperature fluctuations. The adjustable threaded compression-fitting structure offers several benefits: flexible installation without the need for precise pre-determination of insertion depth; reliable sealing capable of withstanding specific pressure levels; and ease of assembly and disassembly, facilitating maintenance and calibration. III. Applications of Adjustable Threaded Compression-Fitting Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples These products are widely used in vacuum heat treatment furnaces, high-temperature sintering furnaces, monocrystalline silicon and sapphire growth furnaces, powder metallurgy, aerospace engine component testing, high-temperature nuclear reactor experiments, and specialty metal smelting. In these applications, where traditional thermocouples cannot cover the ultra-high temperature range and optical temperature measurement is susceptible to factors such as window contamination and emissivity fluctuations, tungsten-rhenium thermocouples with adjustable threaded compression fittings offer a reliable, direct-contact temperature measurement solution. IV. Usage Considerations for Tungsten-Rhenium Thermocouples with Adjustable Threaded Compression Fittings Tungsten-rhenium thermocouples are extremely sensitive to oxidizing atmospheres; they will rapidly oxidize and fail in air or oxygen-containing environments and must be used in a vacuum, pure hydrogen, or inert gas (such as argon or helium). Caution should also be exercised regarding wet hydrogen or reducing carbon-containing atmospheres. Since the resistivity of insulating materials decreases at high temperatures—potentially affecting measurement accuracy—appropriate insulation materials must be selected, and operating temperature limits strictly observed. During installation, ensure the compression fitting is tightened with moderate torque to avoid crushing or damaging the protective sheath. Cold-junction compensation requires the use of matching compensation lead wires or a constant-temperature cold-junction arrangement. Periodic calibration is necessary during long-term use to monitor for thermoelectric potential drift. For applications such as vacuum furnaces, these thermocouples are often paired with specialized tungsten-rhenium connectors and high-vacuum sealing assemblies.
