title: CME Group to Launch Tungsten Futures
text: Changes in Global Tungsten Market Pricing Mechanisms & Implications for China’s Tungsten Industry Chain A comprehensive analysis by CHINATUNGSTEN ONLINE, based on exchange announcements, international financial media reports, and tungsten industry market data. On October 19, 2026, CME Group (Chicago Mercantile Exchange Group, hereinafter referred to as CME) officially announced plans to launch tungsten futures contracts, with trading expected to begin in early Q1 2027, subject to the completion of relevant regulatory reviews. This represents an important development in the international tungsten market. Tungsten prices have historically been determined primarily through spot transactions, trader quotations, and industry price assessments, with no standardized futures contract having achieved broad international influence. The new contract is expected to provide overseas tungsten raw material traders, processors, and downstream manufacturers with a tool for managing price risk. It could also change quotation practices, hedging strategies, and supply chain negotiations across the global tungsten market. However, this announcement should not be interpreted as meaning that international tungsten prices will henceforth be determined by a US exchange, nor does it necessarily imply that China’s influence over tungsten pricing will be displaced. Assessing the actual implications requires distinguishing among three factors: the design of the futures contract, the formation of prices in the international tungsten raw material market, and any changes in China’s industrial competitiveness across mining, smelting, powder production, cemented carbide manufacturing, and precision processing. I. Key Arrangements for CME Tungsten Futures 1. Expected Listing Date: Early Q1 2027 CME Group announced its plans on October 19, 2026. The commencement of trading remains subject to the relevant regulatory reviews. The announcement does not mean that the contract has already begun trading. 2. Settlement Method: Cash Settlement Rather Than Physical Delivery The contract will not provide for the direct delivery of tungsten metal through futures transactions. Under cash settlement, traders settle gains and losses based on the difference between the contract price and the final settlement benchmark, rather than taking physical delivery of tungsten concentrate, ammonium paratungstate, or tungsten metal upon expiry. 3. Risk Management: A Pricing Reference for Raw Material Traders and Industrial Consumers CME’s principal objective in launching tungsten futures is to serve raw material traders and industrial users. The exchange aims to provide traders, raw material purchasers, and manufacturing companies with a more transparent forward price reference, helping them manage risks associated with rising or falling prices and fluctuations in procurement costs. 4. Pricing Benchmark: Ammonium Paratungstate (APT) CME plans to use ammonium paratungstate (APT) as the underlying pricing benchmark for tungsten futures. The contract will be cash-settled against Fastmarkets’ APT price assessment, with the benchmark covering the Rotterdam and Baltimore markets on a duty-unpaid, cost, insurance and freight (CIF) basis. 5. Why Was APT Selected as the Pricing Benchmark? The tungsten industry chain includes tungsten concentrate, ammonium paratungstate, tungsten oxides, tungsten powder, tungsten carbide powder, tungsten materials, cemented carbides, and a wide range of downstream processed products. These products differ significantly in purity, processing costs, supply and demand conditions, transportation requirements, and contractual structures. It is therefore difficult for a single price to accurately represent all tungsten products. APT is a key intermediate product in the tungsten smelting industry chain, positioned between mineral feedstock and subsequent oxide, powder, and materials manufacturing. Selecting an APT price assessment as the futures settlement benchmark indicates that the new contract initially targets the internationally traded tungsten raw material market, rather than directly pricing finished products such as golf club weights, cemented carbide cutting tools, or tungsten alloy shielding components. This choice also means that the contract’s initial impact is likely to be concentrated in overseas raw material procurement, trade inventories, and long-term supply agreements, before potentially being transmitted downstream to materials and finished products. CTIA GROUP's Ammonium Paratungstate (APT) II. Drivers Behind CME’s Decision to Launch Tungsten Futures China Tungsten Online believes that CME’s planned launch is not an isolated financial innovation, but rather a response to changes in global tungsten supply and demand, geopolitics, and raw material trading patterns. 1. China’s Dominant Supply Position Has Made Overseas Markets More Sensitive to Disruptions Reports from international financial media and industry organizations indicate that China occupies a dominant position in global tungsten mining and APT smelting supply. Figures vary by year and statistical methodology, but market sources generally estimate that China accounts for approximately 80% of global tungsten mine production, while its share of APT processing capacity is also substantial. China’s competitive advantage extends beyond mineral resources to an integrated industrial cluster encompassing mining and beneficiation, smelting, tungsten powder, tungsten carbide powder, cemented carbides, and advanced processing. This comprehensive supply system gives China significant influence in the global tungsten market. For import-dependent markets such as Europe, the United States, and Japan, however, heavy reliance on a major supply source also means that export controls, logistics disruptions, mine production cuts, or trade policy changes can quickly translate into raw material shortages and price volatility. Since 2025, China has introduced export controls on certain tungsten-related items, increasing international supply tightness and prompting companies to seek alternative sources. 2. Greater Price Volatility Has Increased Business Operating Challenges According to China Tungsten Online’s market data analysis, Chinese tungsten product prices rose sharply in 2025. By March this year, prices of major tungsten products had increased by more than 600%, before subsequently falling rapidly by over 70% from their peaks amid profit-taking and panic-driven selling. During the same period, the international APT market continued to experience price increases amid tight supply, competition for procurement, and geopolitical factors. Although buyer resistance, delayed purchases, and market corrections also emerged during the year, cumulative price gains remain above 700% to date. For the tungsten industry chain, rising prices do not necessarily translate into higher profits for every company. Mining companies may benefit from higher raw material prices, but smelters must absorb increased concentrate procurement costs. Cemented carbide manufacturers may face higher inventory costs, pressure from customers to reduce prices, and difficulties fulfilling orders. Rapid raw material price movements can also exacerbate pricing mismatches in long-term procurement contracts. The significance of a futures market lies in providing a tradable tool for managing price risk in advance. Instead of bearing the full impact of price changes only when spot purchases or product sales occur, companies can establish futures positions that correspond to their physical market exposure, potentially offsetting part of the impact of price fluctuations. 3. Alternative Supply Chains Are Being Developed Outside China The reconstruction of international supply chains outside China is another important factor behind the planned launch. The United States, the United Kingdom, and other economies are supporting the development of tungsten mining, smelting, and materials manufacturing capacity outside China through policy incentives, capital investment, strategic procurement, and new projects. Meanwhile, the international market is exploring tungsten raw material price assessments based on different sources and delivery locations. For example, Platts, part of S&P Global, proposed in August 2026 a framework for tungsten concentrate and APT price assessments based on delivery to US ports, with a focus on materials originating from Australia, Brazil, Bolivia, Europe, South Korea, the United Kingdom, and Vietnam. This indicates that overseas markets are seeking not only futures instruments but also independent spot price indicators capable of reflecting the costs of non-Chinese supply. CME tungsten futures can therefore be viewed as part of the development of global tungsten market infrastructure, aiming to transform fragmented spot price information into instruments that are more suitable for trading, hedging, and risk assessment. Tungsten Price Statistics from China Tungsten Online III. Operating Design of the CME Tungsten Futures Contract Based on the currently available announcement, the contract will use APT price assessments as its cash settlement benchmark, with the underlying prices linked to international trading markets in Rotterdam and Baltimore. Three technical issues warrant particular attention. First, a futures contract is not a physical procurement agreement. Even if a company locks in a price level through futures, it must still enter into a separate physical purchase contract with a supplier and remain responsible for transportation, quality inspection and acceptance, payment, delivery schedules, and trade compliance. Second, futures prices may not exactly match a company’s actual procurement prices. For example, a company purchasing APT within China, or buying tungsten powder or tungsten carbide powder of a specific purity, may face additional regional price differentials, processing fees, freight costs, taxes, quality premiums, and contractual variations. Futures hedging can reduce related price volatility, but it cannot automatically eliminate all cost risks. Third, the price assessment agency remains a critical component of the contract. Fastmarkets, an international commodity price reporting and market information agency, will provide the APT price assessment used for settlement, while CME will be responsible for contract trading, rules, and clearing arrangements. Whether the contract becomes a reliable international benchmark will depend not only on the exchange’s reputation, but also on the market representativeness, transparency, and verifiability of the underlying price assessment. Fastmarkets has long monitored the tungsten market, publishing price assessments, market analysis, and historical data for products such as ammonium paratungstate, tungsten concentrate, and ferrotungsten. It assesses prices separately according to product specifications, trading regions, and delivery terms, rather than using a single price to represent all tungsten products worldwide. For example, its tungsten price assessments include China free on board (FOB) prices, as well as cost, insurance and freight (CIF) prices for relevant ports in Europe and the United States. These assessments can serve as references for commercial negotiations, long-term supply contracts, market trend analysis, and price risk management. The information currently available is insufficient to confirm the contract’s complete specifications, including contract size, minimum price fluctuation, specific expiry months, position limits, margin requirements, and detailed final settlement calculations. These details should be verified against the formal contract rules and regulatory filings rather than inferred from the announcement alone. Tungsten Ore for Producing APT, CTIA GROUP IV. Implications for the Global Tungsten Industry Chain: From Raw Material Trading to End-Product Manufacturing 1. Greater Transparency in International Tungsten Raw Material Prices APT traders, importers, and processors will gain a new forward price reference. If the contract achieves sufficient trading volume, market participants will be better able to compare spot procurement prices, future purchasing costs, and inventory valuations, reducing their reliance on quotations from individual traders. However, greater price transparency does not necessarily mean that prices will fall. 2. Improved Corporate Risk Management Companies purchasing APT, tungsten powder, or tungsten carbide powder may evaluate hedging strategies based on their actual procurement plans. Mining and smelting companies may also use futures to manage the risk of future selling prices. The effectiveness of such strategies depends on a sufficiently strong correlation between physical market prices and the futures settlement benchmark, as well as the company’s ability to manage margin requirements, liquidity, and basis risk. 3. Clearer Pricing References for Overseas Supply Chain Investment New mines, smelters, and powder production lines often require several years to develop. If the tungsten market establishes a reliable forward price reference, project investors will be better positioned to conduct revenue sensitivity analyses, negotiate long-term supply agreements, and assess financing risks. Nevertheless, futures trading cannot resolve issues involving ore grades, environmental approvals, construction schedules, or actual production capacity. 4. Potential Changes in Profit Distribution Across the Industry Chain With a clearer price curve, companies in mining, smelting, powder production, cemented carbide manufacturing, and downstream manufacturing may adopt price-linked contracts more frequently. Changes in raw material prices may be transmitted more readily into processing fees, product quotations, and inventory valuations, potentially altering the basis for negotiations between companies. (1) Upstream Mining: Clearer Price Signals, but Not All Mines Will Benefit For overseas tungsten mine developers, futures prices can help estimate future sales revenue and assess project economics under different price scenarios. If the futures market achieves sufficient liquidity, mining companies may also find it easier to discuss mechanisms for sharing price risk with banks, investors, and downstream customers. However, the CME contract is based on APT rather than tungsten concentrate from all producing regions. Mining companies must still account for concentrate grade, impurities, beneficiation recovery rates, transportation costs, smelting fees, and the price differential between concentrate and APT. Futures prices can provide a reference, but they cannot directly replace the actual settlement price for a mine’s concentrate. (2) Smelting and Powder Manufacturing: Basis Risk Management Will Become a Key Capability For producers of APT, tungsten oxides, tungsten powder, and tungsten carbide powder, raw material prices and finished product selling prices may change at different speeds. Suppose a company needs to purchase a certain quantity of APT, process it into tungsten powder, and sell the powder to customers. If APT prices rise but downstream quotations cannot be adjusted at the same pace, the company’s profit margins may be squeezed.The company could consider using futures to hedge part of its raw material price exposure. The actual effectiveness, however, depends on procurement timing, purchase volumes, the speed of downstream price adjustments, and the price differential between the futures benchmark and its own physical market. This stage of the industry chain may also require more sophisticated management. In addition to monitoring spot raw material quotations, companies will need to track futures prices, settlement benchmarks, regional price differentials, inventory costs, and hedging performance. For small and medium-sized enterprises without specialized risk management teams, indiscriminate futures trading could instead increase operating risks. (3) Cemented Carbides and Precision Manufacturing: Raw Material Risks Can Be Hedged, but Processing Margins Still Require Management Cemented carbides generally use tungsten carbide as the principal hard phase, combined with a metallic binder. Changes in tungsten powder and tungsten carbide powder prices affect the production costs of cutting tools, molds, mining tools, and precision components. If APT futures become an important international benchmark, downstream companies may use them as a reference in procurement contracts and adopt periodic price adjustments, price-linkage clauses, or partial hedging strategies to reduce raw material volatility. However, APT prices cannot fully represent the costs of tungsten carbide powder, cemented carbides, or precision components. Subsequent processes include powder treatment, pressing, sintering, precision machining, coating, quality inspection, and losses from defective products. Consequently, stable process performance, high yield rates, customer relationships, and product differentiation will remain more important than simply predicting whether tungsten prices will rise or fall. (4) End Users: Easier Cost Budgeting Does Not Necessarily Mean Lower Procurement Costs Companies in aerospace, automotive, electronics and information technology, energy equipment, mining machinery, and defense manufacturing may all be affected by tungsten raw material price movements. Futures instruments can help companies identify price risks earlier, prepare budgets, and plan inventory. However, cash-settled futures cannot guarantee physical supply. Even if a company receives financial compensation through a futures position, it may still be unable to procure raw materials on time because of shortages. For critical production processes, long-term supply agreements, qualified supplier networks, reasonable inventory levels, and assessments of substitute materials remain indispensable. Tungsten Trioxide Produced from APT, CTIA GROUP V. Implications for China’s Tungsten Industry Chain: Challenges and Opportunities 1. China’s Existing Industrial Advantages Will Not Automatically Disappear When Futures Are Listed The core competitiveness of China’s tungsten industry stems from its integrated capabilities in mineral resources, smelting and processing, powder production, cemented carbide manufacturing, and advanced processing. The launch of a financial contract by an international exchange will not directly increase overseas mine output, nor will it immediately replicate China’s mature tungsten smelting and materials manufacturing system. China Tungsten Online believes that China is not only a major global tungsten producer but also a key processing center and a major consumer. In recent years, changes in the structure of raw material imports and higher-value-added product exports have been reshaping China’s role in the international tungsten industry chain. Therefore, the listing of futures will not immediately alter the global physical supply structure. The factors that will continue to determine industrial competitiveness include access to resources, smelting efficiency, material quality, cost control, product development, and reliable delivery. 2. Chinese Spot Prices and International Futures Prices May Diverge More Significantly The relationship between Chinese spot prices and international futures prices, including the causal factors driving their movements, warrants close attention. China’s domestic tungsten market and overseas markets are not entirely independent. However, export controls, supply-demand imbalances, and changing trade conditions can create significant price differentials between them. According to China Tungsten Online’s statistics, during the rapid price increase in 2025, domestic APT prices rose significantly faster than international prices, at one point resulting in an inversion of domestic and international price relationships. The maximum price differential between Chinese and European APT approached 30%. From mid-March 2026 onward, domestic prices entered a downward cycle, while international APT prices began to rise faster than domestic prices again, with the price differential continuing to widen. As of the time of writing, European APT quotations stood at US$2,500–2,900 per metric tonne unit (mtu), equivalent to approximately RMB 1.48–1.72 million per tonne, more than 3.5 times the domestic APT price of approximately RMB 460,000 per tonne. If CME futures use APT price assessments for Rotterdam and Baltimore as their settlement benchmarks, their prices will initially reflect supply and demand, logistics, and policy conditions in those international trading markets. They will not necessarily correspond to domestic Chinese APT spot prices. Chinese companies should therefore not treat international futures prices as direct substitutes for domestic prices. A more important task will be to establish a dynamic comparison mechanism linking domestic prices, export quotations, international spot assessments, and futures prices, while continuously monitoring whether price differentials widen, narrow, or undergo structural changes. 3. International Pricing Capabilities Will Become More Important for Chinese Tungsten Exporters For companies exporting APT, tungsten oxides, tungsten powder, tungsten carbide powder, and related materials, international futures may gradually become one of the reference points used by overseas customers in inquiries and contract negotiations. This could encourage exporters to pay greater attention to international benchmark quotations, price-linkage clauses, foreign exchange risk, and delivery cost management. At the same time, companies must continue to calculate domestic raw material costs, export-related taxes and fees, logistics costs, and processing margins accurately, rather than overlooking their actual cost structures when international benchmarks change. If international buyers increasingly favor contracts linked to observable price indicators, Chinese companies will need to strengthen their international market research, risk management, and contract design capabilities instead of relying solely on traditional spot quotations. 4. Hedging May Become an Optional Tool for Chinese Mining and Smelting Companies In principle, Chinese companies with international business operations and adequate risk management capabilities may evaluate the feasibility of using overseas futures contracts. Actual participation would require consideration of trading access, brokerage channels, compliance requirements for overseas derivatives transactions, cross-border fund arrangements, accounting treatment, and the company’s internal risk management framework. More importantly, hedging is meaningful only when the company’s physical business exposure sufficiently matches the contract benchmark. For example, a company holding tungsten concentrate inventory in China would be exposed to differences in grade, processing stage, geographical location, and trading terms relative to a futures contract settled against overseas APT prices. If the price differential changes sharply, even a futures position with the correct directional view may fail to offset the physical market loss adequately. The listing of tungsten futures therefore does not mean that every Chinese tungsten company should immediately participate in trading. For many companies, establishing price monitoring, procurement budgeting, and risk exposure management systems may be a more prudent first step than directly entering the futures market. 5. International Futures May Create New Competitive Pressure for the Upgrading of China’s Tungsten Industry Over the long term, international tungsten futures may support the development of overseas raw material trading, price information services, and risk management systems.As overseas supply chains expand, some importers may increasingly favor tungsten raw materials and processed products with traceable origins and compliance with specific procurement policies. Chinese companies will need to continue strengthening product quality, machining precision, material consistency, supply chain traceability, and customer service, while extending their capabilities from raw material supply toward higher-value-added materials and end-product manufacturing. However, this development should not be interpreted as evidence that China’s tungsten industry will inevitably lose its competitive advantage. If overseas supply chains have higher production costs, longer development cycles, or less mature processing technologies, China’s established industrial clusters may remain highly competitive. The more likely outcome is a fragmented supply chain, increasingly differentiated customer segments, and the coexistence of multiple pricing systems, rather than straightforward one-way substitution. 6. Implications for Tungsten Product Futures in China China has spent a considerable period preparing for the possible introduction of tungsten product futures, particularly APT-related contracts. With CME moving toward the launch of tungsten futures, the competitive landscape for a potential Chinese futures market has become more complex. Combined with the sharp price volatility of tungsten products over the past year, the risks associated with market participation, contract complexity, timing, and competitive positioning have become increasingly difficult to assess. China Tungsten Online will refrain from commenting further on this issue at present. VI. Will Futures Allow the United States to Determine International Tungsten Prices? Futures markets can generate traded prices, but their influence depends on trading volume, open interest, participant composition, the relationship with the physical market, and the representativeness of the delivery or settlement benchmark. CME has a mature derivatives trading infrastructure, but the scale of the exchange alone does not guarantee the success of a new contract. The tungsten market differs significantly from mature bulk metal markets such as copper and aluminum. Tungsten products have numerous specifications, the industry chain involves complex processing stages, trade is relatively fragmented, and global supply is highly concentrated.If the new contract fails to attract sufficient industrial participants and genuine commercial hedging demand, it may experience inadequate liquidity, wide bid-ask spreads, or a disconnect between futures and spot prices. Furthermore, APT price assessments remain central to the settlement mechanism. If market transaction data are insufficient, the representativeness and transparency of the price assessment will become focal points of market scrutiny. Futures prices may also be influenced by macroeconomic capital flows, market expectations, and short-term trading behavior. They should not therefore be equated with the long-term fundamental value of tungsten. A more reasonable assessment is that CME tungsten futures could become an important international pricing reference. Whether they can develop into a globally influential benchmark will depend on actual trading activity after launch, industrial hedging demand, and the strength of their relationship with the physical market. This remains a sensitive issue with a high degree of uncertainty. VII. Conclusion: Tungsten Futures Are More Than a Financial Event; They Signal a Transformation in the Internationalization of the Tungsten Industry Chain CME’s plan to launch tungsten futures reflects a broader shift in the global tungsten market from a model dominated by spot trading and fragmented quotations toward one that places greater emphasis on price transparency, risk management, and supply chain security. In the short term, the contract’s principal role will be to provide a new risk management instrument for overseas tungsten raw material trading. Over the medium to long term, its implications may extend to the formation of international pricing benchmarks, procurement contract design, overseas supply chain investment, and the relationship between domestic and international prices. For China, this is neither a minor development that can be ignored nor a sign that its dominant position in the global tungsten market will immediately weaken. China retains a substantial industrial foundation in resources, smelting, powder production, cemented carbides, and advanced processing. Nevertheless, companies will need to develop a more proactive understanding of international price indicators, improve cost accounting and risk management, and continue increasing the added value of their products. For the global tungsten industry chain, futures instruments can help companies manage price risk, but they cannot create new tungsten resources or replace actual raw material supply. Competition in the international tungsten market will continue to revolve around resource security, processing capacity, technological capabilities, supply chain resilience, and end-user demand. In short, CME tungsten futures would initially expand the range of risk management tools available to the international tungsten raw material market. Their deeper significance lies in the accelerating restructuring of pricing references, trading rules, and supply security systems across the global tungsten industry chain. Chinese companies should view this development as a signal to strengthen their international market research and industrial competitiveness, rather than simply interpreting it as a transfer of pricing power. China Tungsten Online will continue to closely monitor developments relating to CME tungsten futures. Stay tuned for further updates. text: Analysis of Latest Tungsten Market from Chinatungsten Online This week, the tungsten market showed a tentative recovery driven primarily by supply-side sentiment. Prices of major tungsten products rebounded noticeably from the bottom, and liquidity along the industrial chain improved somewhat. However, transactions remained dominated by small, rigid-demand orders as the market waited for further validation from the demand side. Large tungsten producers’ concentrated purchases of ammonium paratungstate (APT) ignited firm-price sentiment on the primary raw-material side. Supply-side reluctance to sell intensified, and the steadfast guidance prices of major producers further boosted market confidence. The atmosphere in the tungsten concentrate market reversed rapidly from earlier panic selling. Concentrates grading 55% WO₃ and above found solid bottom support near RMB 300,000/standard ton, with cumulative gains of approximately 12% during the week. In the APT market, the release of orders, combined with widespread production cuts or suspensions at plants, significantly strengthened the willingness to hold and firm prices. Market psychological price levels quickly moved toward the major producers’ guidance price of RMB 500,000/ton. The tungsten scrap market responded promptly, releasing stronger upside momentum with higher price elasticity. Taking scrap tungsten carbide rods as an example, prices rose by about 19% during the week, with volatility notably greater than that of primary materials. upward momentum was driven largely by speculative positioning among traders. Sellers, facing high holding costs and a wait-and-see-for-higher-prices mindset, showed strong reluctance to sell, making low-priced material hard to find. Actual terminal digestion remained cautious, buyers inquired actively but mostly conducted small-lot, quick-turnaround cash transactions. When the upstream atmosphere transmitted to the powder and cemented-carbide segments, the pace slowed relatively. Merchants reported that some downstream customers had gradually accepted the higher levels, yet deals remained mainly small rigid-demand orders settled on a spot basis. A wait-and-see atmosphere and cautious, needs-based operations continued to dominate the market. Confidence among cemented-carbide producers and their end users in rebuilding inventories still required further restoration.
